name: John
subtitle: A Sign Made of Scripture
howToRead: John quotes the Old Testament rarely — and reads it everywhere. He opens on the first words of Genesis, “In the beginning,” and tells the rest of the story in figures: the Word who tabernacles among us as the glory once filled the tent, the Lamb of God, the serpent Moses lifted in the wilderness, the ladder of Jacob’s dream, the manna, the water from the rock, the shepherd of Ezekiel, the vine that is Israel, the Passover lamb whose bones are not broken. His handful of formal citations fall like nails — “zeal for your house,” “bread from heaven,” “they hated me without cause,” “they will look on him whom they pierced” — but the deeper argument is typological: the signs are written, and they are written to be recognized from Scripture. The chips beside each passage name the text underneath it — solid for a formal quotation, dashed for an allusion, dotted for a fainter echo, ◇ for a figural pattern that borrows no words and carries the most weight in this Gospel. A lighter chip and a trailing ? mark an echo that is faint or contested. Where John follows the Greek of the Septuagint against the Hebrew, both readings are shown.

pericopes.text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him. Without him was not anything made that has been made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: John opens with the exact phrase 'In the beginning' (en archē), the LXX incipit of Genesis 1:1, signaling a deliberate re-narration of creation. Volume is maximal (verbatim phrase in the most marked position of the Gospel) and recurrence strong (creation language saturates vv.1-5). Thematic coherence is total: John reads the Genesis creation through the lens of the Word as agent.

echoes.text: God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
echoes.note: Creation 'by the word' ('Let there be light') is recast as creation 'through him,' the Logos (v.3). The Genesis pattern of God speaking the world into being is the conceptual substrate for 'all things were made through him.' High thematic coherence between divine speech-act and the personified Word.

echoes.text: By Yahweh’s word, the heavens were made; all their army by the breath of his mouth.
echoes.note: 'By the word of the LORD the heavens were made' is the clearest OT text crediting creation to God's spoken word, the Jewish exegetical bridge from Genesis to a creative Logos. Strong thematic coherence with v.3 ('all things were made through him') and availability secure in Second-Temple liturgy.

echoes.text: “Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed. When there were no depths, I was born, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains were settled in place, before the hills, I was born; while as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the beginning of the dust of the world. When he established the heavens, I was […]
echoes.note: Personified Wisdom, 'with' God 'in the beginning' as the agent/craftsman of creation, is the primary background for the Word who 'was with God' and through whom all things were made. Recurrence of the with-God-at-creation motif and high thematic coherence; widely recognized as John's Wisdom-Christology source.

echoes.text: For she that is the architect of all things taught me, even wisdom. For there is in her a spirit quick of understanding, holy, Alone in kind, manifold, Subtil, freely moving, Clear in utterance, unpolluted, Distinct, unharmed, Loving what is good, keen, unhindered, Beneficent, loving toward man, Stedfast, sure, free from care, All-powerful, all-surveying, And penetrating through all spirits That are quick of understanding, pure, most subtle: For wisdom is […]
echoes.note: Wisdom as the 'breath of the power of God,' a pure effulgence of glory, an unspotted mirror, and the light surpassing all light underwrites John's identification of the Word with life and light (vv.4-5). Availability secure (deuterocanonical, first century) and strong thematic coherence with the light/glory motifs of the Prologue.

echoes.text: O God of the fathers, and Lord who keep your mercy, Who made all things by your word; And by your wisdom you formedst man, That he should have dominion over the creatures that were made by you,
echoes.note: 'O God... who made all things by your word, and by your wisdom formed man' explicitly pairs word and wisdom as co-agents of creation, the exact fusion John performs on the Logos. Medium confidence because it is conceptual parallel rather than verbal, but thematic coherence with v.3 is high.

echoes.text: Wisdom will praise herself, And will glory in the midst of her people. In the congregation of the Most High will she open her mouth, And glory in the presence of his power. I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, And covered the earth as a mist. I lived in high places, And my throne is in the pillar of the cloud. Alone I compassed the circuit of heaven, And walked in the depth of the abyss. In the waves of the sea, and in all the earth, And in every […]
echoes.note: Wisdom's self-praise, coming forth from the mouth of the Most High and present from the beginning, is a key model for the pre-existent Word. Sirach 24 is the most sustained Wisdom-tabernacle hymn and is recurrent across the Prologue (see also v.14). High thematic coherence.

echoes.text: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
echoes.note: The darkness over the deep before the first light is evoked by 'the light shines in the darkness' (v.5). The creation-from-darkness sequence reinforces the Genesis 1 framing; medium confidence as the verbal contact is thematic (light/darkness) rather than lexical.

echoes.text: For with you is the spring of life. In your light shall we see light.
echoes.note: 'For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we see light' fuses life and light as divine gifts, exactly the pairing of v.4 ('in him was life, and the life was the light of men'). Thematic coherence is high; flagged medium for absence of verbal borrowing.

echoes.text: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.
echoes.note: 'The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light' offers the light-shining-in-darkness topos. Low confidence and somewhat contested: the motif is broad and could derive from several light texts, but it coheres with the Prologue's darkness-versus-light contest.

echoes.text: For whoever finds me, finds life, and will obtain favor from Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Whoever finds me finds life' links personified Wisdom directly to life, supporting the life-in-the-Word claim of v.4. Faint and contested, but coherent with the broader Wisdom substrate already established.

pericopes.text: There came a man, sent from God, whose name was John. The same came as a witness, that he might testify about the light, that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but was sent that he might testify about the light. The true light that enlightens everyone was coming into the world.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'Behold, I send my messenger' frames John as the divinely sent forerunner ('there came a man, sent from God'). The sending-of-the-messenger motif is the standard prophetic preparation pattern and coheres with John's witness role; medium because the verbal link is conceptual.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: 'A light to the nations' resonates with 'the true light that enlightens everyone' (v.9), the universal scope of illumination. Low confidence: the universalizing of light is a shared Isaianic theme rather than a direct quotation.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? Yahweh is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid?
echoes.note: 'The LORD is my light and my salvation' supplies the divine-light identification that the Prologue transfers to the Logos. Faint and contested; included for recurrence of the light-as-God motif.

pericopes.text: He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world didn’t recognize him. He came to his own, and those who were his own didn’t receive him. But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name: who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.

echoes.text: With all these I sought rest; And in whose inheritance shall I lodge? Then the Creator of all things gave me a commandment; And he that created me made my tabernacle to rest, And said, Let your tabernacle be in Jacob, And your inheritance in Israel. He created me from the beginning before the world; And to the end I will not fail. In the holy tabernacle I ministered before him; And so was I established in Sion. In the beloved city likewise he gave me […]
echoes.note: Wisdom seeks a resting place among the nations and is given Israel as her inheritance; the motif of the agent of creation coming to her own people who variously receive or reject her underlies vv.10-11. Thematic coherence with the Wisdom-rejection pattern is strong; medium for lack of verbal contact.

echoes.text: Because I have called, and you have refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no one has paid attention; but you have ignored all my counsel, and wanted none of my reproof; I also will laugh at your disaster. I will mock when calamity overtakes you; when calamity overtakes you like a storm, when your disaster comes on like a whirlwind; when distress and anguish come on you. Then will they call on me, but I will not answer. They will seek me diligently, […]
echoes.note: Wisdom calls but is not received ('I called and you refused'), the rejection-of-Wisdom topos behind 'his own didn't receive him' (v.11). The motif of the personified divine agent spurned by her people coheres tightly with John's tragic note.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: Wisdom finds no dwelling place among humans and returns to heaven, the most pointed Second-Temple parallel to the Word coming to his own and being rejected (vv.10-11). Pseudepigraphal but genuinely warranted here: the Wisdom-withdrawal pattern matches John's reversal closely. Contested as to direct dependence.

echoes.text: You are the children of Yahweh your God. You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead.
echoes.note: 'You are the children of the LORD your God' supplies the divine-sonship category recast as the 'right to become God's children' (v.12). Low confidence; the sonship-of-God-people motif is broad across the OT.

echoes.text: Of the Rock who became your father, you are unmindful, and have forgotten God who gave you birth.
echoes.note: 'The God who gave you birth' offers a God-as-begetter image behind 'born... of God' (v.13). Faint and contested, but coheres with the divine-generation language that replaces ordinary descent.

echoes.text: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’
echoes.note: 'You are children of the living God,' the promise of new divine sonship to those who were not a people, resonates with becoming God's children by birth from God (vv.12-13). Low confidence; thematic rather than verbal.

pericopes.text: The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth. John testified about him. He cried out, saying, “This was he of whom I said, ‘He who comes after me has surpassed me, for he was before me.’” From his fullness we all received grace upon grace. For the law was given through Moses. Grace and truth were realized through Jesus Christ. No one has seen God at any time. The one and only Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.

echoes.text: Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them. According to all that I show you, the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all of its furniture, even so you shall make it.
echoes.note: 'The Word became flesh and lived (eskēnōsen, 'tabernacled') among us' deliberately evokes the sanctuary that God commanded so he might 'dwell among them.' The tabernacle-pitching verb is the load-bearing figural cue: the incarnate Word is the new tent of meeting. High volume and thematic coherence.

echoes.text: Then the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and Yahweh’s glory filled the tabernacle. Moses wasn’t able to enter into the Tent of Meeting, because the cloud stayed on it, and Yahweh’s glory filled the tabernacle.
echoes.note: The glory of the LORD filling the tabernacle is the template for 'we saw his glory' (v.14): the indwelling Word manifests the kabod that once filled the tent. The tabernacle-plus-glory pairing makes the figural reading near-certain. High coherence and recurrence with the Sinai cycle.

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
echoes.note: 'Full of grace and truth' renders the LXX/Hebrew formula 'abounding in steadfast love (hesed) and faithfulness ('emet)' from God's self-revelation to Moses. This is the densest verbal-conceptual borrowing of the Prologue's climax (vv.14,17). Very high thematic coherence: the glory Israel saw at Sinai is now seen in the Word.

echoes.text: He said, “Please show me your glory.” He said, “I will make all my goodness pass before you, and will proclaim Yahweh’s name before you. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy.” He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.” Yahweh also said, “Behold, there is a place by me, and you shall stand on the rock. It will happen, while my glory passes by, that I will put you in a cleft of […]
echoes.note: Moses' request to see God's glory, granted only as a passing of God's goodness while his face remains unseen, undergirds both 'we saw his glory' and 'no one has seen God at any time' (vv.14,18). The contrast (Moses denied the face; the Son makes God known) is structured directly on this scene.

echoes.text: He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.”
echoes.note: 'No one has seen God at any time' (v.18) closely restates 'you cannot see my face, for no one may see me and live.' High volume and a near-citation level of verbal coherence; the Son's making-God-known answers the Sinai limitation.

echoes.text: Then the Creator of all things gave me a commandment; And he that created me made my tabernacle to rest, And said, Let your tabernacle be in Jacob, And your inheritance in Israel.
echoes.note: Wisdom is commanded to 'pitch her tent (kataskēnōson) in Jacob,' the closest Second-Temple antecedent to the Word tabernacling among us (v.14). The tent-pitching verb plus the creation-agent identity makes Sirach 24 a primary source for the whole Prologue. High coherence and recurrence.

echoes.text: He gave to Moses, when he finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, stone tablets, written with God’s finger.
echoes.note: 'The law was given through Moses' (v.17) refers to the Sinai giving of the tablets 'written with the finger of God.' The Moses-law / Christ-grace antithesis is built on the Sinai law-giving as its foil. Secure availability and strong thematic coherence.

echoes.text: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him. When Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, behold, the skin of his face shone; and they were afraid to come near him. Moses called to them, and Aaron and all the rulers of the congregation returned to him; and Moses spoke to them. […]
echoes.note: Moses' face shining with reflected glory after seeing God contrasts with the Son who is himself the glory and declares the Father (vv.14,18). The Sinai-radiance scene reinforces the Moses-versus-Word comparison; medium for absence of direct verbal borrowing here.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to you out of the midst of the fire: you heard the voice of words, but you saw no form; you only heard a voice.
echoes.note: At Horeb Israel heard a voice but 'saw no form,' the unseen-God theme behind v.18. The motif of God unseen yet now declared by the Son coheres with John's Sinai contrast; medium confidence.

echoes.text: then I was the craftsman by his side. I was a delight day by day, always rejoicing before him,
echoes.note: Wisdom beside God as the delighting child/craftsman supports 'the one and only Son, who is in the bosom of the Father' (v.18), the intimate, eternal closeness of the agent to God. Coheres with the Wisdom substrate established in the opening; medium.

echoes.text: For she is a breath of the power of God, And a clear effluence of the glory of the Almighty; Therefore can nothing defiled find entrance into her. For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, And an unspotted mirror of the working of God, And an image of his goodness.
echoes.note: Wisdom as the radiance of God's glory and image of his goodness underlies 'we saw his glory' and the Son as the one who makes the unseen God known (vv.14,18). Reinforces the glory/visibility theme; medium for conceptual rather than verbal link.

echoes.text: ‘Yahweh is slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, forgiving iniquity and disobedience; and that will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, on the third and on the fourth generation.’
echoes.note: The 'grace and truth' (hesed-we-emet) divine-attribute formula recurs in Moses' intercession, strengthening recurrence of the Exodus 34:6 source behind v.14/17. Listed low because Exodus 34:6 is the primary locus; this is a secondary witness.

echoes.text: Mercy and truth meet together. Righteousness and peace have kissed each other.
echoes.note: 'Steadfast love and faithfulness meet together' pairs hesed and 'emet, the same word-pair behind 'grace and truth.' Faint and contested as a direct source, but evidences the recurrence of the formula in Israel's vocabulary.

pericopes.text: This is John’s testimony, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, “Who are you?” He declared, and didn’t deny, but he declared, “I am not the Christ.” They asked him, “What then? Are you Elijah?” He said, “I am not.” “Are you the prophet?” He answered, “No.” They said therefore to him, “Who are you? Give us an answer to take back to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?” He said, “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as Isaiah the prophet said.” The ones who had been sent were from the Pharisees. They asked him, “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?” John answered them, “I baptize in water, but among you stands one whom you don’t know. He is the one who comes after me, who is preferred before me, whose sandal strap I’m not worthy to loosen.” These things were done in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.

echoes.text: The voice of one who calls out, “Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness! Make a level highway in the desert for our God.
echoes.note: John explicitly quotes 'I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, Make straight the way of the Lord' (v.23) with the formula 'as Isaiah the prophet said.' This is a formal citation: maximal volume and an attributed source. Thematic coherence with John's preparatory role is exact.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: The priests' question 'Are you Elijah?' (v.21) invokes the promise that God will send Elijah before the great day of the LORD. The expectation is directly named, so the allusion is secure; John's denial plays against this eschatological script. High coherence.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: 'Are you the prophet?' (v.21) draws on Moses' promise that God would raise up 'a prophet like me,' a fixed eschatological category in Second-Temple Judaism. The interrogation triad (Christ/Elijah/the prophet) is built on this expectation. High availability and coherence.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: The messenger sent to prepare the way before the Lord stands behind both the Elijah question and the way-preparation quotation of v.23. Recurrence with Mal 4:5 strengthens the Elijah-forerunner background; medium since Isaiah 40 carries the explicit citation.

echoes.text: They answered him, “He was a hairy man, and wearing a leather belt around his waist.” He said, “It is Elijah the Tishbite.”
echoes.note: Elijah's wilderness/garb profile underlies why John is asked whether he is Elijah (v.21). Faint here (John's Gospel omits the camel-hair description) but coheres with the Elijah typology; low and somewhat contested in John specifically.

pericopes.text: The next day, he saw Jesus coming to him, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! This is he of whom I said, ‘After me comes a man who is preferred before me, for he was before me.’ I didn’t know him, but for this reason I came baptizing in water: that he would be revealed to Israel.” John testified, saying, “I have seen the Spirit descending like a dove out of heaven, and it remained on him. I didn’t recognize him, but he who sent me to baptize in water, he said to me, ‘On whomever you will see the Spirit descending, and remaining on him, the same is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’ I have seen, and have testified that this is the Son of God.”

echoes.text: Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one according to the number of the souls; according to what everyone can eat you shall make your count for the lamb. Your lamb shall be without defect, a male a year old. You […]
echoes.note: 'Behold, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world' (v.29) reads Jesus through the Passover lamb whose blood delivers Israel. John's later Passover chronology (Jesus dying as the lambs are slain, no bones broken) confirms this figural channel. High volume and thematic coherence.

echoes.text: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth.
echoes.note: The Servant 'led like a lamb to the slaughter' who bears the sin of many is the strongest source for a sin-bearing Lamb (v.29), since the Passover lamb is not explicitly sin-removing. The combination of lamb imagery with sin-bearing points decisively to the Servant Song. High coherence.

echoes.text: Abraham said, “God will provide himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.” So they both went together.
echoes.note: 'God will provide himself the lamb' (the Aqedah) supplies a God-provided sacrificial lamb that became central in Second-Temple atonement reflection, coherent with 'the Lamb of God' (the lamb God provides). Medium because the verbal link is the divine-provision phrase rather than direct quotation.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'The Spirit of the LORD shall rest on him' undergirds the Spirit 'descending and remaining on him' (vv.32-33); the abiding (not transient) anointing marks the messianic endowment. High thematic coherence with the messianic identification that follows.

echoes.text: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.
echoes.note: 'My chosen, on whom I have put my Spirit' fuses the Servant with the Spirit-resting/abiding motif of vv.32-34, and 'Son of God' (v.34, with a known variant 'chosen one') strengthens the Servant link. High coherence between Spirit-endowed Servant and the baptismal attestation.

echoes.text: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
echoes.note: The Spirit hovering over the waters at creation, evoked by the Spirit descending over the baptismal waters as a dove (v.32), ties the Spirit-baptism to a new-creation motif consonant with the Prologue's Genesis framing. Medium: the dove-over-water image is the figural cue.

echoes.text: He himself sent out a dove to see if the waters were abated from the surface of the ground, but the dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned to him into the ship, for the waters were on the surface of the whole earth. He put out his hand, and took her, and brought her to him into the ship. He waited yet another seven days; and again he sent the dove out of the ship. The dove came back to him at evening and, behold, in her mouth was a freshly […]
echoes.note: Noah's dove returning over the receding flood-waters offers a dove-over-water image often linked to the baptismal dove (v.32) and to new creation after judgment. Low and contested as a deliberate source, but recurrent in early Jewish-Christian dove symbolism.

echoes.text: “Now this is that which you shall offer on the altar: two lambs a year old day by day continually. The one lamb you shall offer in the morning; and the other lamb you shall offer at evening: and with the one lamb a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour mixed with the fourth part of a hin of beaten oil, and the fourth part of a hin of wine for a drink offering. The other lamb you shall offer at evening, and shall do to it according to the meal offering of […]
echoes.note: The daily Tamid lamb offered morning and evening provides another sacrificial-lamb backdrop for 'the Lamb of God' (v.29) alongside Passover and Isaiah 53. Low confidence; included for recurrence of cultic lamb imagery available to John.

echoes.text: But I was like a gentle lamb that is led to the slaughter; and I didn’t know that they had devised devices against me, saying, Let us destroy the tree with its fruit, and let us cut him off from the land of the living, that his name may be no more remembered.
echoes.note: 'I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter' echoes the innocent-victim lamb of v.29, reinforcing the Isaiah 53 sense. Faint and contested as an independent source but a genuine OT lamb-as-victim parallel.

pericopes.text: Again, the next day, John was standing with two of his disciples, and he looked at Jesus as he walked, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God!” The two disciples heard him speak, and they followed Jesus. Jesus turned, and saw them following, and said to them, “What are you looking for?” They said to him, “Rabbi” (which is to say, being interpreted, Teacher), “where are you staying?” He said to them, “Come, and see.” They came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day. It was about the tenth hour. One of the two who heard John, and followed him, was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother. He first found his own brother, Simon, and said to him, “We have found the Messiah!” (which is, being interpreted, Christ). He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him, and said, “You are Simon the son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas” (which is by interpretation, Peter).

echoes.text: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth.
echoes.note: The repeated 'Behold, the Lamb of God' (v.36) re-applies the same Servant-lamb identification, the recurrence of which (vv.29,36) strengthens the Isaiah 53 reading under Hays' recurrence criterion. Medium as it is a restatement of the v.29 source.

echoes.text: Neither will your name any more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.
echoes.note: Jesus' renaming of Simon to Cephas/Peter (v.42) follows the OT pattern of God renaming at covenant calling (Abram to Abraham). The name-change-as-vocation motif coheres with the call narrative; low because no single text is quoted.

echoes.text: He said, “Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have fought with God and with men, and have prevailed.”
echoes.note: Jacob renamed Israel after the encounter at the Jabbok is a second instance of the divine-renaming pattern behind Simon to Cephas (v.42), and anticipates the Jacob/Israel motifs that culminate in v.51. Low and contested as a direct source.

pericopes.text: On the next day, he was determined to go out into Galilee, and he found Philip. Jesus said to him, “Follow me.” Now Philip was from Bethsaida, of the city of Andrew and Peter. Philip found Nathanael, and said to him, “We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, wrote: Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.” Nathanael said to him, “Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.” Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and said about him, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit!” Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.” Nathanael answered him, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are King of Israel!” Jesus answered him, “Because I told you, ‘I saw you underneath the fig tree,’ do you believe? You will see greater things than these!” He said to him, “Most certainly, I tell you, hereafter you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”

echoes.text: He dreamed. Behold, a stairway set upon the earth, and its top reached to heaven. Behold, the angels of God ascending and descending on it.
echoes.note: 'You will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man' (v.51) is an explicit re-reading of Jacob's ladder, with the verbs 'ascending and descending' lifted from the dream. John relocates the ladder onto the Son of Man, who becomes the bridge between heaven and earth. Maximal figural volume and coherence.

echoes.text: I will raise them up a prophet from among their brothers, like you. I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I shall command him.
echoes.note: Philip's 'him of whom Moses in the law... wrote' (v.45) identifies Jesus as the prophet-like-Moses, the figure promised in Moses' words. Secure availability and high coherence with the messianic-fulfillment claim that frames the disciple-gathering.

echoes.text: He said, “Your brother came with deceit, and has taken away your blessing.”
echoes.note: 'An Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit' (v.47) plays on Jacob, of whom Isaac said 'your brother came with deceit'; Nathanael is the true Israel without the guile that named Jacob. The Jacob contrast prepares directly for the Jacob's-ladder saying of v.51. Strong figural coherence and recurrence.

echoes.text: But they will sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and no one will make them afraid: For the mouth of Yahweh of Armies has spoken.
echoes.note: 'Every man under his vine and under his fig tree' is the eschatological-peace idiom evoked by Nathanael 'under the fig tree' (v.48), suggesting a pious Israelite awaiting the messianic age, possibly studying Torah. Medium: the fig-tree setting is the cue, common to several peace texts.

echoes.text: In that day,’ says Yahweh of Armies, ‘you will invite every man his neighbor under the vine and under the fig tree.’”
echoes.note: 'You will invite one another under the vine and under the fig tree,' the messianic-day promise, reinforces the 'under the fig tree' setting of v.48 as a sign of the dawning messianic peace Nathanael recognizes in his confession. Medium, recurrent with Micah 4:4.

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: Nathanael's confession 'you are the Son of God! You are King of Israel!' (v.49) draws on the royal coronation oracle naming the Davidic king God's son. Strong coherence between Son-of-God and King titles; medium for the conceptual rather than verbal link.

echoes.text: The remnant of Israel will not do iniquity, nor speak lies, neither will a deceitful tongue be found in their mouth, for they will feed and lie down, and no one will make them afraid.”
echoes.note: The remnant of Israel 'shall do no injustice and speak no lies; nor shall a deceitful tongue be found' supplies the no-deceit ideal of the true Israelite applied to Nathanael (v.47). Coheres with the genuine-Israel motif; medium.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man to whom Yahweh doesn’t impute iniquity, in whose spirit there is no deceit.
echoes.note: 'Blessed is the man... in whose spirit there is no deceit' offers the no-guile ideal behind 'in whom is no deceit' (v.47). Low and contested as a direct source but a genuine parallel to the guileless-Israelite commendation.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: The title 'Son of Man' coming with heaven (v.51) draws on the heavenly one 'like a son of man' who approaches the Ancient of Days. John fuses the Danielic Son of Man with the Jacob's-ladder vision; medium because the borrowing is the title and the opened-heaven setting rather than a quotation.

echoes.text: He was afraid, and said, “How dreadful is this place! This is none other than God’s house, and this is the gate of heaven.”
echoes.note: Jacob's 'this is the gate of heaven' at Bethel undergirds 'heaven opened' (v.51), reinforcing the Bethel-ladder figural reading where the Son of Man is the locus of access to heaven. Medium, recurrent with Genesis 28:12.

echoes.text: Now in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, in the fifth of the month, as I was among the captives by the river Chebar, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.
echoes.note: 'The heavens were opened and I saw visions of God' supplies the opened-heaven apocalyptic idiom of v.51. Low confidence: a standard visionary formula rather than a specific source, but coherent with the heavenly disclosure promised.

pericopes.text: The third day, there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee. Jesus’ mother was there. Jesus also was invited, with his disciples, to the marriage. When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother said to him, “They have no wine.” Jesus said to her, “Woman, what does that have to do with you and me? My hour has not yet come.” His mother said to the servants, “Whatever he says to you, do it.” Now there were six water pots of stone set there after the Jews’ way of purifying, containing two or three metretes apiece. Jesus said to them, “Fill the water pots with water.” They filled them up to the brim. He said to them, “Now draw some out, and take it to the ruler of the feast.” So they took it. When the ruler of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and didn’t know where it came from (but the servants who had drawn the water knew), the ruler of the feast called the bridegroom, and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and when the guests have drunk freely, then that which is worse. You have kept the good wine until now!” This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.

echoes.text: “Behold, the days come,” says Yahweh, “that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the one treading grapes him who sows seed; and sweet wine will drip from the mountains, and flow from the hills. I will bring my people Israel back from captivity, and they will rebuild the ruined cities, and inhabit them; and they will plant vineyards, and drink wine from them. They shall also make gardens, and eat their fruit.
echoes.note: The eschatological promise that the mountains shall drip sweet wine and the hills flow with it stands behind Cana's superabundance (six jars of 20-30 gallons each become the best wine). Coherence is high: John frames the sign as the dawn of the messianic age in which the prophets' image of overflowing wine is realized. Availability and Recurrence of the wine-of-the-age topos across the prophets strengthen the echo.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day, that the mountains will drop down sweet wine, the hills will flow with milk, all the brooks of Judah will flow with waters, and a fountain will flow out from Yahweh’s house, and will water the valley of Shittim.
echoes.note: Joel's day-of-the-Lord vision of mountains dripping with new wine belongs to the same prophetic abundance-of-wine cluster that informs Cana. The figural logic is that Jesus' first sign inaugurates that promised day. Coherence with John's 'his hour' / eschatological framing supports the reading though the verbal contact is thematic not lexical.

echoes.text: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines.
echoes.note: Isaiah's eschatological banquet on Zion of rich food and well-aged wines for all peoples is the messianic-feast type that Cana's wedding banquet enacts. Volume is moderate (banquet + choice wine); Coherence is strong since the ruler praises the 'good wine kept until now,' echoing the aged-wine motif. The wedding setting reinforces the feast typology.

echoes.text: They shall come and sing in the height of Zion, and shall flow to the goodness of Yahweh, to the grain, and to the new wine, and to the oil, and to the young of the flock and of the herd: and their soul shall be as a watered garden; and they shall not sorrow any more at all.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's restoration oracle promises radiance over the LORD's goodness, the grain, the wine, and the oil, with mourning turned to joy. The new-covenant abundance (same chapter as the new covenant) coheres with John's inaugural sign of joy and wine. The contact is thematic and the echo faint.

echoes.text: Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine; he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes. His eyes will be red with wine, his teeth white with milk.
echoes.note: Jacob's blessing of Judah, who 'washes his garments in wine' with eyes darker than wine, is a classic messianic-Davidic prophecy of wine-abundance attached to the coming ruler from Judah. Second-Temple readers (cf. Targums) read this messianically, so Availability is strong. Cana's prodigal wine figurally fulfills the Shiloh oracle's vinous excess.

echoes.text: I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride. I have gathered my myrrh with my spice; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Friends Eat, friends! Drink, yes, drink abundantly, beloved. Beloved
echoes.note: The Song's wedding/erotic imagery of wine ('your love is better than wine,' the bridegroom and bride) supplies a nuptial-wine matrix that John's wedding sign may evoke, especially given the bridegroom motif. Volume is diffuse and the echo is faint and contested, but Coherence with John's broader bridegroom Christology (cf. 3:29) supports listing it.

echoes.text: You shall no more be termed Forsaken; neither shall your land any more be termed Desolate: but you shall be called Hephzibah, and your land Beulah; for Yahweh delights in you, and your land shall be married. For as a young man marries a virgin, so your sons shall marry you; and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God will rejoice over you.
echoes.note: Isaiah names restored Zion 'married' (Beulah) and depicts God rejoicing over her as a bridegroom over a bride. The Cana wedding, where the bridegroom motif surfaces and Jesus implicitly assumes the true bridegroom's role, figurally enacts this nuptial covenant imagery. Coherence with John's bridegroom Christology strengthens the link.

echoes.text: I will betroth you to me forever. Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion. I will even betroth you to me in faithfulness; and you shall know Yahweh.
echoes.note: Hosea's promise that the LORD will betroth Israel to himself forever in righteousness and faithfulness is foundational to the YHWH-as-bridegroom typology activated at a wedding where Jesus quietly occupies the bridegroom's place. Availability and Recurrence of the divine-marriage theme support a figural echo. Hosea 2:21-22 also pairs betrothal with abundance of grain, wine, and oil.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them, “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘These are the living things which you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof, and is cloven-footed, and chews the cud among the animals, that you may eat. “‘Nevertheless these you shall not eat of those that chew the cud, or of those who part the hoof: the camel, because he chews the cud but doesn’t have a parted hoof, he is […]
echoes.note: John explicitly notes the six stone jars were set 'after the Jews' way of purifying'; the Levitical purity code (clean/unclean, washings) is the institution being named. Volume is high (direct reference to the purification system) and Coherence is strong: Jesus transforms the water of ritual purification into the wine of the new age, signaling supersession of the old cleansing rites.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, “This is the statute of the law which Yahweh has commanded. Tell the children of Israel to bring you a red heifer without spot, in which is no defect, and which was never yoked. You shall give her to Eleazar the priest, and he shall bring her outside of the camp, and one shall kill her before his face. Eleazar the priest shall take some of her blood with his finger, and sprinkle her blood toward the front of the […]
echoes.note: The water of purification / red-heifer lustration ordinance is part of the specific 'purifying' system John references with the stone jars (stone vessels in particular resisted impurity per Second-Temple halakhah). Coherence supports it: the water-for-cleansing motif is precisely what Jesus repurposes. Slightly lower volume than Leviticus since John's phrase is general.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, “In this you shall know that I am Yahweh. Behold, I will strike with the rod that is in my hand on the waters which are in the river, and they shall be turned to blood. The fish that are in the river shall die, and the river shall become foul; and the Egyptians shall loathe to drink water from the river.”’” Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Take your rod, and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, over their […]
echoes.note: The first Mosaic sign turned water into blood; John's first sign turns water into wine, a possible deliberate Moses/Jesus typological inversion (curse vs. joy). Coherence with John's broader Moses Christology (1:17) gives it some weight, but the contrast is subtle and the echo contested.

echoes.text: Go your way—eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart; for God has already accepted your works.
echoes.note: The sapiential exhortation to drink wine with a merry heart as God's gift frames wine as a sign of divine favor and joy, the affective register of Cana's abundance. Volume is low and the link diffuse; listed as a faint wisdom-tradition resonance.

echoes.text: Wine is as good as life to men, If you drink it in its measure: What life is there to a man that is without wine? And it has been created to make men glad. Wine drunk in season and to satisfy Is joy of heart, and gladness of soul:
echoes.note: Ben Sira's praise of wine as gladness of heart 'created from the beginning for joy,' drunk in season, supplies a deuterocanonical wisdom backdrop to Cana's celebratory wine. Availability is solid (Second-Temple sapiential text); the echo is thematic and faint.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: John 2:1 'on the third day' may complete John's opening week (day-counting from 1:29, 35, 43) evoking the seven-day creation framework that the Prologue's 'In the beginning' inaugurates, making Cana a new-creation climax. The echo is structural and contested but coherent with John's deliberate Genesis 1 architecture.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'On the third day' as a marker of restoration/raising ('on the third day he will raise us up that we may live before him') may color John's 'third day' at Cana, anticipating resurrection-glory language that returns at 2:19-22. Coherence with the chapter's later three-days-temple saying supports a faint thematic echo.

pericopes.text: After this, he went down to Capernaum, he, and his mother, his brothers, and his disciples; and they stayed there a few days.

The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. He found in the temple those who sold oxen, sheep, and doves, and the changers of money sitting. He made a whip of cords, and threw all out of the temple, both the sheep and the oxen; and he poured out the changers’ money, and overthrew their tables. To those who sold the doves, he said, “Take these things out of here! Don’t make my Father’s house a marketplace!” His disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will eat me up.” The Jews therefore answered him, “What sign do you show us, seeing that you do these things?” Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” The Jews therefore said, “It took forty-six years to build this temple! Will you raise it up in three days?” But he spoke of the temple of his body. When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he said this, and they believed the Scripture, and the word which Jesus had said.

echoes.text: For the zeal of your house consumes me. The reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me.
echoes.note: John 2:17 explicitly cites 'Zeal for your house will eat me up' (gegraptai), a verbatim quotation of Psalm 69:9a. Volume is maximal (formal citation), and Psalm 69 is a major Johannine passion testimony (cf. the vinegar of 19:28-29 from Ps 69:21), giving high Recurrence and Coherence within John's passion typology.

echoes.text: Yes, every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah will be holy to Yahweh of Armies; and all those who sacrifice will come and take of them, and cook in them. In that day there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: Zechariah's eschatological vision ends 'there shall no longer be a trader in the house of the LORD of hosts on that day' when all vessels in the temple become holy. Jesus' expulsion of the sellers and his 'do not make my Father's house a marketplace' directly enacts this oracle. Volume and Coherence are strong; the day-of-the-LORD purification of the temple is precisely the action depicted.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies. “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap; and he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi, and […]
echoes.note: Malachi's prophecy that 'the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple' to purify the sons of Levi like a refiner is enacted as Jesus comes to the temple in judgment. Coherence is strong (sudden coming, purgation of temple commerce/cult) and Recurrence high in the gospels' temple theology. The refining-judgment frame fits the whip and overturning of tables.

echoes.text: “All their wickedness is in Gilgal; for there I hated them. Because of the wickedness of their deeds I will drive them out of my house! I will love them no more. All their princes are rebels.
echoes.note: Hosea's 'I will drive them out of my house' for their wickedness offers a prophetic precedent for expulsion from God's house, resonating with Jesus throwing the merchants out of the temple. Volume is low and verbal contact partial; listed as a faint judgment-on-the-temple echo.

echoes.text: In the twenty-fifth year of our captivity, in the beginning of the year, in the tenth day of the month, in the fourteenth year after that the city was struck, in the same day, the hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me there. In the visions of God brought he me into the land of Israel, and set me down on a very high mountain, whereon was as it were the frame of a city on the south. He brought me there; and, behold, there was a man, whose appearance […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel's vision of the new, purified eschatological temple (and the life-giving water flowing from it) stands behind Jesus' 'destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it,' interpreted as the temple of his body replacing the building. Coherence is strong with John's temple-replacement Christology; the figural new-temple typology supports a medium-confidence link.

echoes.text: Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I, even I, have seen it,” says Yahweh.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's temple sermon denounces those who make the LORD's house 'a den of robbers'; Jesus' 'do not make my Father's house a marketplace' belongs to the same prophetic critique of commercializing/profaning the temple. The synoptics quote Jer 7:11 directly; John's wording diverges ('marketplace' vs. 'den of robbers') but the underlying allusion is strong.

echoes.text: and speak to him, saying, ‘Thus says Yahweh of Armies, “Behold, the man whose name is the Branch: and he shall grow up out of his place; and he shall build Yahweh’s temple; even he shall build Yahweh’s temple; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule on his throne; and he shall be a priest on his throne; and the counsel of peace shall be between them both.
echoes.note: The Branch who 'shall build the temple of the LORD' may inform John's claim that Jesus will raise the temple in three days, identifying him as the messianic temple-builder. Coherence with the new-temple Christology supports it, but verbal contact is faint and the link contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]
echoes.note: John dates the cleansing to 'the Passover of the Jews' (2:13), invoking the Exodus Passover institution that frames Jesus' whole Jerusalem ministry and ultimately his death as the true paschal lamb (cf. 19:36). Volume is moderate (explicit feast reference) and Coherence high within John's paschal Christology.

echoes.text: and I came to Jerusalem, and understood the evil that Eliashib had done for Tobiah, in preparing him a room in the courts of God’s house. It grieved me severely: therefore I threw all the household stuff of Tobiah out of the room. Then I commanded, and they cleansed the rooms: and there brought I again the vessels of God’s house, with the meal offerings and the frankincense.
echoes.note: Nehemiah's zealous cleansing of the temple chambers of Tobiah's goods provides a scriptural model of reforming zeal that purges the temple of intrusion, resonating with Jesus' 'zeal' and his expulsion of the traders. The echo is faint and typological rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Your statutes stand firm. Holiness adorns your house, Yahweh, forever more.
echoes.note: 'Holiness befits your house, O LORD, forevermore' undergirds the indignation at profaning the Father's house, the principle Jesus enforces. Volume is low and the connection conceptual; included as a faint sanctity-of-the-house resonance.

pericopes.text: Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, during the feast, many believed in his name, observing his signs which he did. But Jesus didn’t trust himself to them, because he knew everyone, and because he didn’t need for anyone to testify concerning man; for he himself knew what was in man.

echoes.text: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
echoes.note: 'The LORD looks on the heart' while man looks on outward appearance is the classic text for divine knowledge of the inner person, directly behind 'he knew what was in man.' Volume and Coherence are strong: Jesus exercises the uniquely divine prerogative of reading hearts, a Johannine claim to his deity. The conceptual contact is precise.

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: 'I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways' ascribes heart-searching to YHWH alone; John applies this to Jesus, who 'knew everyone' and needed no testimony about man. Coherence is high within John's high Christology; the divine heart-searcher motif is the operative background.

echoes.text: Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down, and are acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word on my tongue, but, behold, Yahweh, you know it altogether.
echoes.note: The psalm's confession that the LORD searches and knows everything, discerning thoughts from afar before a word is spoken, is the paradigmatic statement of omniscient knowledge of persons that John attributes to Jesus. Volume and Coherence are strong; this is a leading text for the divine knowledge Jesus possesses.

echoes.text: then hear in heaven, your dwelling place, and forgive, and do, and render to every man according to all his ways, whose heart you know; (for you, even you only, know the hearts of all the children of men;)
echoes.note: Solomon's temple prayer affirms that God alone 'knows the hearts of all the children of mankind.' Set against the temple context just preceding (2:13-22), Jesus' knowledge of all hearts pointedly claims the prerogative Solomon reserved to God alone, reinforcing the divine-knowledge Christology. Coherence with the chapter's temple frame strengthens it.

echoes.text: But, Yahweh of Armies, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind, I shall see your vengeance on them; for to you have I revealed my cause.
echoes.note: 'O LORD of hosts, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind' is another heart-testing formula in the same cluster as 17:10; it reinforces the divine-omniscience background without distinct verbal contact of its own. Listed as a corroborating faint echo.

echoes.text: He searcheth out the deep, and the heart, And he has understanding of their cunning plans: For the Most High knows all knowledge, And he looks into the signs of the world, Declaring the things that are past, and the things that shall be, And revealing the traces of hidden things. No thought escapes him; There is not a word hid from him.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's praise of the Most High who 'searches out the abyss and the human heart' and from whom no thought is hidden offers a deuterocanonical parallel to Jesus knowing what is in man. Availability is good; the echo is thematic, reinforcing the omniscience motif rather than supplying a direct source.

pericopes.text: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. The same came to him by night, and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do, unless God is with him.” Jesus answered him, “Most certainly, I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see the Kingdom of God.” Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb, and be born?” Jesus answered, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born of water and spirit, he can’t enter into the Kingdom of God! That which is born of the flesh is flesh. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit. Don’t marvel that I said to you, ‘You must be born anew.’ The windblows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

echoes.text: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you. I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: Being 'born of water and spirit' fuses the two halves of Ezekiel's new-covenant oracle: God sprinkles 'clean water' for cleansing and puts a 'new spirit' within. The water-then-spirit sequence and the regeneration theme give high volume and coherence; Jesus' rebuke that 'the teacher of Israel' should know this presumes a known prophetic text.

echoes.text: Then he said to me, Prophesy to the wind, prophesy, son of man, and tell the wind, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Come from the four winds, breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live. So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army. Then he said to me, Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel: behold, they say, Our bones are dried up, and our hope […]
echoes.note: The wind that 'blows where it wants to' and the one 'born of the Spirit' echo Ezekiel's valley vision where the ruach/breath comes from the four winds to give life. The Hebrew ruach pun (wind/spirit/breath) underlies both Ezek 37 and John 3:8; high coherence with the new-creation/resurrection motif of new birth.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:
echoes.note: The new-covenant promise of an inward, Spirit-written law ('I will put my law within them') coheres with regeneration 'from above.' Recurrence of new-covenant texts (alongside Ezek 36-37) strengthens the cluster, though John makes no verbal quotation.

echoes.text: “For the unclean, they shall take of the ashes of the burning of the sin offering; and running water shall be poured into a vessel. A clean person shall take hyssop, dip it in the water, and sprinkle it on the tent, on all the vessels, on the persons who were there, and on him who touched the bone, or the slain, or the dead, or the grave. The clean person shall sprinkle on the unclean on the third day, and on the seventh day. On the seventh day, he shall […]
echoes.note: The 'water of cleansing' / sprinkling rite for purification may stand behind 'born of water,' especially given v.25's dispute 'about purification.' Faint and contested; the water imagery is more naturally Ezekiel's, but the purification context raises availability.

echoes.text: As you don’t know what is the way of the wind, nor how the bones grow in the womb of her who is with child; even so you don’t know the work of God who does all.
echoes.note: 'As you do not know the way of the wind (ruach)... so you do not know the work of God' supplies the exact analogy of 3:8: the unknowable course of the wind/spirit mirrors the mystery of divine begetting in the womb. High coherence and a shared sapiential ruach-pun; verbal volume is moderate.

echoes.text: He lays the beams of his rooms in the waters. He makes the clouds his chariot. He walks on the wings of the wind. He makes his messengers winds; his servants flames of fire.
echoes.note: The Psalm makes winds God's messengers and 'when you send forth your Spirit (ruach), they are created.' Resonates with wind/Spirit/new-creation in 3:5-8 but is faint and diffuse.

echoes.text: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
echoes.note: The Spirit/wind (ruach) hovering at creation undergirds 'born of the Spirit' as new creation; coheres with John's creation framing (1:1-3) but verbal contact with ch.3 is faint.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: God breathing the breath of life to make the man a living being stands behind Spirit-begetting as the giving of new life; low volume, drawn in by the ruach/breath cluster of 3:6-8.

pericopes.text: Nicodemus answered him, “How can these things be?” Jesus answered him, “Are you the teacher of Israel, and don’t understand these things? Most certainly I tell you, we speak that which we know, and testify of that which we have seen, and you don’t receive our witness. If I told you earthly things and you don’t believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? No one has ascended into heaven, but he who descended out of heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.

echoes.text: Who has ascended up into heaven, and descended? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has bound the waters in his garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son’s name, if you know?
echoes.note: 'Who has ascended to heaven and come down? ... What is his name, and his son's name?' is strikingly answered by 3:13 ('No one has ascended... but he who descended, the Son of Man'). High volume of shared ascent/descent language plus the 'son' motif; a recognized wisdom backdrop.

echoes.text: It is not in heaven, that you should say, “Who will go up for us to heaven, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?”
echoes.note: 'Who will ascend to heaven for us to bring it down?' frames revelation as something no human can fetch from heaven; 3:13 inverts this — the Son of Man alone has descended bearing heavenly things. Coherent revelation-from-above theme; moderate verbal contact.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: 'Son of Man' coming with the clouds of heaven supplies the title and the heaven-earth movement that John reworks as descent/ascent. Recurrent Johannine Son-of-Man usage gives coherence, though here the motion is reversed.

echoes.text: The ox knows his owner, and the donkey his master’s crib; but Israel doesn’t know, my people don’t consider.”
echoes.note: 'Israel does not know, my people do not understand' may color Jesus' rebuke of 'the teacher of Israel' who does not understand (3:10). Faint thematic echo of Israel's failure to perceive.

echoes.text: And hardly do we divine the things that are on earth, And the things that are close at hand we find with labor; But the things that are in the heavens who ever yet traced out? And who ever gained knowledge of your counsel, except you gave wisdom, And sent your holy spirit from on high?
echoes.note: 'We can hardly guess at what is on earth... but who has traced out what is in the heavens? Who has learned your counsel unless you have given wisdom and sent your holy spirit?' closely parallels 3:12's earthly-vs-heavenly things and the Spirit-given knowledge of 3:8-11. Strong conceptual coherence (Second-Temple availability).

echoes.text: I have not learned wisdom, neither do I have the knowledge of the Holy One.
echoes.note: 'I have not learned wisdom, nor have I knowledge of the Holy One' immediately precedes the ascent question and reinforces the human inability to grasp heavenly things (3:12); faint, drawn in with v.4.

pericopes.text: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Make a fiery serpent, and set it on a pole. It shall happen, that everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live.” Moses made a serpent of brass, and set it on the pole. If a serpent had bitten any man, when he looked at the serpent of brass, he lived.
echoes.note: The explicit typological centerpiece: 'As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up.' Direct verbal and figural correspondence — the lifted bronze serpent that the snake-bitten looked to and lived prefigures the crucified Son giving eternal life to those who believe. Maximal volume and coherence.

echoes.text: For even when terrible raging of wild beasts came upon your people, And they were perishing by the bites of crooked serpents, Your wrath continued not to the uttermost; But for admonition were they troubled for a short space, Having a token of salvation, To put them in remembrance of the commandment of your law: For he that turned toward it was not saved because of that which was seen, But because of you, the Saviour of all.
echoes.note: The Wisdom midrash on Numbers 21 clarifies that 'the one who turned toward it was saved, not by what was seen, but by you, the Savior of all' — exactly John's point that the serpent saves by directing faith beyond itself to God. Strong Second-Temple interpretive parallel, high coherence with 3:15's believing-and-living.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
echoes.note: The Servant who is 'lifted up (hypsothesetai) and exalted' supplies the double sense of John's hypsoo (crucified/exalted) Son of Man. LXX verbal contact with the lifting-up vocabulary that John deploys here and in 8:28; 12:32-34.

echoes.text: He removed the high places, and broke the pillars, and cut down the Asherah: and he broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made; for in those days the children of Israel burned incense to it; and he called it Nehushtan.
echoes.note: Hezekiah's destruction of the bronze serpent (Nehushtan) is part of the object's canonical afterlife and may inform the careful 'not the bronze itself but faith' nuance; faint, supplementary to Num 21.

pericopes.text: For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him. He who believes in him is not judged. He who doesn’t believe has been judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the one and only Son of God. This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light; for their works were evil. For everyone who does evil hates the light, and doesn’t come to the light, lest his works would be exposed. But he who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be revealed, that they have been done in God.”

echoes.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
echoes.note: 'God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son' echoes the Aqedah where God says of Isaac 'your son, your only son, whom you love' and credits Abraham who 'did not withhold' him. The LXX agapetos / monogenes-equivalent and the giving of the beloved only son give strong figural volume and coherence.

echoes.text: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.
echoes.note: 'The light has come into the world' and nations coming to the light coheres with Isaiah's 'Arise, shine, for your light has come.' Recurrent Johannine light-coming-into-the-world motif (cf. 1:9; 8:12); moderate verbal contact.

echoes.text: “These are of those who rebel against the light. They don’t know its ways, nor stay in its paths. The murderer rises with the light. He kills the poor and needy. In the night he is like a thief. The eye also of the adulterer waits for the twilight, saying, ‘No eye shall see me.’ He disguises his face. In the dark they dig through houses. They shut themselves up in the daytime. They don’t know the light. For the morning is to all of them like thick […]
echoes.note: The evildoers who 'rebel against the light,' who do their deeds in darkness and for whom 'morning is like deep darkness,' closely parallel 3:19-20: those who do evil hate the light lest their works be exposed. Strong thematic coherence of light/darkness moral exposure.

echoes.text: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.
echoes.note: 'The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light' supplies the light-into-darkness frame of 3:19; faint, part of the broader Isaianic light cluster.

echoes.text: For whoever finds me, finds life, and will obtain favor from Yahweh. But he who sins against me wrongs his own soul. All those who hate me love death.”
echoes.note: 'Whoever finds me finds life... all who hate me love death' parallels the believe-and-live / hate-the-light-love-darkness antithesis of 3:16-20 in a wisdom register; faint.

echoes.text: But for admonition were they troubled for a short space, Having a token of salvation, To put them in remembrance of the commandment of your law: For he that turned toward it was not saved because of that which was seen, But because of you, the Saviour of all.
echoes.note: The salvific 'looking' that brings life carries over from 3:14-15 into the believing-for-eternal-life of 3:15-16; low independent volume here, recurrence within the pericope cluster.

echoes.text: Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.
echoes.note: 'Their works were evil' (3:19) faintly recalls the flood-judgment verdict that human deeds were continually evil; low volume, judgment register.

pericopes.text: After these things, Jesus came with his disciples into the land of Judea. He stayed there with them, and baptized. John also was baptizing in Enon near Salim, because there was much water there. They came, and were baptized. For John was not yet thrown into prison. There arose therefore a questioning on the part of John’s disciples with some Jews about purification. They came to John, and said to him, “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, the same baptizes, and everyone is coming to him.” John answered, “A man can receive nothing, unless it has been given him from heaven. You yourselves testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ,’ but, ‘I have been sent before him.’ He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full. He must increase, but I must decrease.

echoes.text: the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the voice of those who say, Give thanks to Yahweh of Armies, for Yahweh is good, for his loving kindness endures forever; who bring thanksgiving into Yahweh’s house. For I will cause the captivity of the land to return as at the first, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'The voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride' as the sound of restored joy underlies the Baptist as 'friend of the bridegroom' who rejoices at the bridegroom's voice (3:29). Coherent eschatological-wedding-joy motif; moderate verbal contact via 'voice of the bridegroom.'

echoes.text: For as a young man marries a virgin, so your sons shall marry you; and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God will rejoice over you.
echoes.note: 'As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you' establishes God/Messiah as bridegroom to his people; John casts Jesus as that bridegroom 'who has the bride.' Strong thematic coherence within the OT marriage-of-YHWH typology.

echoes.text: I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride. I have gathered my myrrh with my spice; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Friends Eat, friends! Drink, yes, drink abundantly, beloved. Beloved
echoes.note: The bridegroom and his companions/'friends' at the wedding feast resonate with the 'friend of the bridegroom' figure; faint, supplies the nuptial-companion role.

echoes.text: I will betroth you to me forever. Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion. I will even betroth you to me in faithfulness; and you shall know Yahweh.
echoes.note: YHWH betrothing Israel to himself stands within the marriage typology that makes the messianic-bridegroom image legible; faint background, no verbal contact.

echoes.text: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding;
echoes.note: 'A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven' (3:27) coheres with the sapiential/apocalyptic axiom that God gives and removes authority (cf. Dan 2:21,37); faint, conceptual.

pericopes.text: He who comes from above is above all. He who is from the earth belongs to the earth, and speaks of the earth. He who comes from heaven is above all. What he has seen and heard, of that he testifies; and no one receives his witness. He who has received his witness has set his seal to this, that God is true. For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God; for God gives the Spirit without measure. The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand. One who believes in the Son has eternal life, but one who disobeys the Son won’t see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.”

echoes.text: Who has ascended up into heaven, and descended? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has bound the waters in his garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son’s name, if you know?
echoes.note: 'He who comes from above/from heaven is above all' recapitulates the ascent/descent and heavenly-origin question of Prov 30:4 already invoked at 3:13; recurrence within the chapter strengthens the link.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'God gives the Spirit without measure' (3:34) contrasts/develops the Spirit resting on the messianic shoot; Isaiah's lavish Spirit-endowment of the anointed coheres with the immeasurable Spirit on the sent one. Moderate thematic volume.

echoes.text: I will raise them up a prophet from among their brothers, like you. I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I shall command him.
echoes.note: 'He whom God has sent speaks the words of God' (3:34) echoes the promised prophet-like-Moses in whose mouth God puts his words. Coherent with John's sent-one-speaks-God's-words theme; moderate verbal contact.

echoes.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
echoes.note: 'The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand' (3:35) recapitulates the beloved-Son giving of 3:16 / the Aqedah; recurrence within the chapter, low independent volume.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'Given all things into his hand' resonates with the Son of Man given dominion and all peoples serving him; faint, draws on the Danielic enthronement already present at 3:13-14.

echoes.text: Give sincere homage to the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish on the way, for his wrath will soon be kindled. Blessed are all those who take refuge in him.
echoes.note: The wrath that 'remains' on the one who disobeys the Son (3:36) faintly echoes 'kiss the Son lest he be angry'—submit to the Son or face wrath. Low verbal volume, coherent judgment register.

echoes.text: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.
echoes.note: 'The one who believes... has life' vs. the disobedient who 'won't see life' faintly mirrors the righteous living by faith over against the unbelieving; faint, conceptual.

pericopes.text: Therefore when the Lord knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John (although Jesus himself didn’t baptize, but his disciples), he left Judea, and departed into Galilee. He needed to pass through Samaria. So he came to a city of Samaria, called Sychar, near the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son, Joseph. Jacob’s well was there.
