Jesus therefore, being tired from his journey, sat down by the well. It was about the sixth hour.

echoes.text: Jacob came in peace to the city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Paddan Aram; and encamped before the city. He bought the parcel of ground where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for one hundred pieces of money.
echoes.note: Sychar lies near the plot of ground at Shechem that Jacob purchased; v5's 'parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph' anchors the scene in this patriarchal land-grant. High Volume (named geography) and Coherence with John's Jacob/Joseph framing.

echoes.text: Moreover I have given to you one portion above your brothers, which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow.”
echoes.note: Jacob's deathbed gift of an extra 'portion' (shekem/Shechem) to Joseph is the explicit referent of v5, where the well stands on land Jacob gave Joseph. Strong verbal-thematic Coherence; the giving-of-portion motif underwrites the woman's later 'our father Jacob who gave us the well.'

echoes.text: They buried the bones of Joseph, which the children of Israel brought up out of Egypt, in Shechem, in the parcel of ground which Jacob bought of the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred pieces of money. They became the inheritance of the children of Joseph.
echoes.note: Joseph's bones were buried in the parcel at Shechem that Jacob bought, the same patriarchal plot John names. Availability and Coherence are strong; it reinforces the Jacob-Joseph-Shechem matrix even if John cites no text.

echoes.text: Then Jacob went on his journey, and came to the land of the children of the east. He looked, and behold, a well in the field, and, behold, three flocks of sheep lying there by it. For out of that well they watered the flocks. The stone on the well’s mouth was large. There all the flocks were gathered. They rolled the stone from the well’s mouth, and watered the sheep, and put the stone again on the well’s mouth in its place. Jacob said to them, “My […]
echoes.note: The classic betrothal type-scene: a man journeys, sits/stops at a well, a woman comes to draw, water is given, she runs to tell her household. v6 'sat down by the well' mirrors Jacob meeting Rachel at the well. High Recurrence (three OT instances) and Volume; the reader primed for betrothal finds a startling inversion.

echoes.text: The servant took ten camels, of his master’s camels, and departed, having a variety of good things of his master’s with him. He arose, and went to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor. He made the camels kneel down outside the city by the well of water at the time of evening, the time that women go out to draw water. He said, “Yahweh, the God of my master Abraham, please give me success this day, and show kindness to my master Abraham. Behold, I am standing […]
echoes.note: The Rebekah betrothal scene at the well: servant asks 'give me a drink,' woman draws, kinship and marriage follow. John's scene reuses the well-meeting template down to the request for water (v7). Strong Volume and Recurrence; coheres with the type-scene channel John exploits.

echoes.text: Now when Pharaoh heard this thing, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and lived in the land of Midian, and he sat down by a well. Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came and drew water, and filled the troughs to water their father’s flock. The shepherds came and drove them away; but Moses stood up and helped them, and watered their flock. When they came to Reuel, their father, he said, “How is it that you […]
echoes.note: Moses, a stranger in foreign territory (Midian), sits by a well where women come to draw; betrothal to Zipporah follows. As the third betrothal-at-well scene it raises Recurrence, strengthening the type even if the verbal contact with John is looser than Genesis 24/29.

pericopes.text: A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.” For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food. The Samaritan woman therefore said to him, “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.) Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” The woman said to him, “Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. From where then have you that living water? Are you greater than our father, Jacob, who gave us the well, and drank of it himself, as did his children, and his livestock?” Jesus answered her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.” The woman said to him, “Sir, give me this water, so that I don’t get thirsty, neither come all the way here to draw.”

echoes.text: The servant ran to meet her, and said, “Please give me a drink, a little water from your pitcher.”
echoes.note: Eliezer's 'Let me drink, I pray thee' to Rebekah at the well is verbally echoed by Jesus' 'Give me a drink' (v7), continuing the betrothal type-scene into the dialogue itself. Volume is moderate (short shared phrase) but Coherence with the well-meeting frame is high.

echoes.text: “For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
echoes.note: Israel forsook the LORD, 'the fountain of living waters,' for broken cisterns; Jesus offers the 'living water' (hydor zon) the woman cannot draw from a deep well. High Volume (rare exact phrase 'living water/fountain of living waters') and Coherence: Jesus is the true fountain over against a cistern that cannot hold.

echoes.text: Yahweh, the hope of Israel, all who forsake you shall be disappointed. Those who depart from me shall be written in the earth, because they have forsaken Yahweh, the spring of living waters.
echoes.note: Those who forsake the LORD have forsaken 'the fountain of living waters'; the doubled Jeremianic phrase raises Recurrence and makes the divine self-identification as living-water source the most likely source-pool for v10-14.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day, that living waters will go out from Jerusalem; half of them toward the eastern sea, and half of them toward the western sea; in summer and in winter will it be.
echoes.note: On the eschatological day 'living waters shall go out from Jerusalem.' Jesus relocates that eschatological living water into himself given to a Samaritan, fitting John's realized-eschatology and the 'hour comes and now is' just ahead. Moderate Volume, strong thematic Coherence.

echoes.text: Therefore with joy you will draw water out of the wells of salvation.
echoes.note: 'With joy shall you draw water out of the wells of salvation' joins drawing water (the woman's task) to salvation (v22 'salvation is from the Jews'). Coherence is good; the drawing-water verb links the literal and figural planes.

echoes.text: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
echoes.note: 'Everyone who thirsts, come to the waters... without money' parallels Jesus' free 'gift of God' (v10) of water that ends thirst (v14). Strong Coherence with John's thirst/gift language; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: and Yahweh will guide you continually, and satisfy your soul in dry places, and make strong your bones; and you shall be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters don’t fail.
echoes.note: The blessed will be 'like a spring of water, whose waters fail not' — the interior, never-failing spring matches v14's 'well of water springing up to eternal life.' Coherence high on the perpetual-inner-spring image; Volume modest.

echoes.text: They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun strike them: for he who has mercy on them will lead them, even by springs of water he will guide them.
echoes.note: The redeemed 'shall not hunger nor thirst,' for God leads them by springs of water — paralleling 'never thirst again' (v14). Faint, but coherent with the never-thirst promise.

echoes.text: He brought me back to the door of the house; and behold, waters issued out from under the threshold of the house eastward; (for the forefront of the house was toward the east;) and the waters came down from under, from the right side of the house, on the south of the altar. Then he brought me out by the way of the gate northward, and led me round by the way outside to the outer gate, by the way of the gate that looks toward the east; and behold, there ran […]
echoes.note: The life-giving river flowing from the temple, deepening and bringing life, is a leading source for NT living-water imagery. John makes Jesus the temple-source of the eschatological water; moderate Volume, strong Coherence with the temple/water/life nexus.

echoes.text: For with you is the spring of life. In your light shall we see light.
echoes.note: 'With you is the fountain of life' grounds the divine-fountain motif; Jesus' gift becomes 'a well of water springing up to eternal life' (v14). Coherence with the life-fountain image is high; Volume modest.

echoes.text: The words of a man’s mouth are like deep waters. The fountain of wisdom is like a flowing brook.
echoes.note: 'The wellspring of wisdom is a flowing brook' and Proverbs' fountain-of-life sayings supply the sapiential backdrop for water = life/wisdom. Faint verbal contact; contributes to the broader well/fountain field.

echoes.text: a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, flowing streams from Lebanon. Beloved
echoes.note: The beloved is 'a well of living waters' — a rare exact match to 'living water,' and, given the betrothal type-scene already in play, a thematically apt nuptial overtone. Volume on the phrase is notable but the connection is contested.

echoes.text: Isaac’s servants dug in the valley, and found there a well of springing water.
echoes.note: Isaac's servants find 'a well of springing water' (be'er mayim chayyim) — the same idiom rendered 'well of water springing up' in v14, set again in patriarchal well-digging. Reinforces the patriarchal-well + living-water overlap.

echoes.text: They that eat me will yet be hungry; And those who drink me will yet be thirsty.
echoes.note: Wisdom says 'those who drink me will thirst for more'; Jesus inverts it — whoever drinks his water 'will never thirst again' (v14). Likely deliberate contrast with the sapiential tradition; Availability secure as Second-Temple deuterocanon.

pericopes.text: Jesus said to her, “Go, call your husband, and come here.” The woman answered, “I have no husband.” Jesus said to her, “You said well, ‘I have no husband,’ for you have had five husbands; and he whom you now have is not your husband. This you have said truly.” The woman said to him, “Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet.

echoes.text: The king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Avva, and from Hamath and Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel; and they possessed Samaria, and lived in the cities of it. So it was, at the beginning of their dwelling there, that they didn’t fear Yahweh: therefore Yahweh sent lions among them, which killed some of them. Therefore they spoke to the king of Assyria, saying, “The […]
echoes.note: The Samaritans were resettled foreign peoples who 'feared the LORD and served their own gods'; the woman's 'five husbands' has long been read as a figure for this syncretism (Josephus counts five settler nations/deities). Coherence with John's Samaritan setting is high, though the allegory of the number is debated.

echoes.text: Contend with your mother! Contend, for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband; and let her put away her prostitution from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts; Lest I strip her naked, and make her bare as in the day that she was born, and make her like a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and kill her with thirst. Indeed, on her children I will have no mercy; for they are children of unfaithfulness; For their mother has played […]
echoes.note: Israel as the adulterous wife pursuing many lovers/baalim supplies the prophetic marriage-and-apostasy grammar behind the husbands motif. Faint and contested, but coherent with reading the woman's marital history as covenantal figure.

echoes.text: (In earlier times in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God, thus he said, “Come, and let us go to the seer”; for he who is now called a prophet was before called a Seer.)
echoes.note: The prophet as 'seer' who knows hidden things lies behind the woman's 'I perceive you are a prophet' (v19) after Jesus discloses her secret. Faint lexical contact; supports the prophet-recognition motif.

pericopes.text: Our fathers worshiped in this mountain, and you Jews say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship.” Jesus said to her, “Woman, believe me, the hour comes, when neither in this mountain, nor in Jerusalem, will you worship the Father. You worship that which you don’t know. We worship that which we know; for salvation is from the Jews. But the hour comes, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such to be his worshipers. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.” The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah comes, he who is called Christ. When he has come, he will declare to us all things.” Jesus said to her, “I am he, the one who speaks to you.”

echoes.text: It shall happen, when Yahweh your God brings you into the land where you go to possess it, that you shall set the blessing on Mount Gerizim, and the curse on Mount Ebal.
echoes.note: The blessing was set on Mount Gerizim, the Samaritan holy mountain the woman means by 'this mountain' (v20). High Volume and Availability: the Gerizim/Jerusalem dispute is the precise OT fault-line John dramatizes.

echoes.text: “These shall stand on Mount Gerizim to bless the people, when you have passed over the Jordan: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin.
echoes.note: Six tribes stand on Gerizim to pronounce blessing, grounding the Samaritan claim that 'our fathers worshiped in this mountain.' Coheres with v20; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: But to the place which Yahweh your God shall choose out of all your tribes, to put his name there, you shall seek his habitation, and there you shall come. There you shall bring your burnt offerings, your sacrifices, your tithes, the wave offering of your hand, your vows, your freewill offerings, and the firstborn of your herd and of your flock. There you shall eat before Yahweh your God, and you shall rejoice in all that you put your hand to, you and […]
echoes.note: Worship is to be at 'the place the LORD shall choose,' the Deuteronomic charter behind the Jewish claim that 'in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship' (v20). High Coherence: Jesus transcends the very 'place' debate this text founds (v21-23).

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him. This is according to all that you desired of Yahweh your God in Horeb in the day of the assembly, saying, “Let me not hear again the voice of Yahweh my God, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I not die.” Yahweh said to me, “They have well said that which they have spoken. I will raise them up a prophet from among their […]
echoes.note: Moses promised a prophet 'like me' who would speak all God commands; the Samaritan Taheb expectation rests here, matching the woman's 'when Messiah comes he will declare to us all things' (v25). High Coherence with Samaritan messianism and Jesus' 'I am he' (v26).

echoes.text: Therefore my people shall know my name. Therefore they shall know in that day that I am he who speaks; behold, it is I.”
echoes.note: 'My people shall know my name... that I am he that speaks' supplies the divine 'I am he' (ego eimi ho lalon) Jesus uses in v26, knitting revelation-of-name to direct speech. Volume is strong on the unusual 'he that speaks / I am he' formula.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”
echoes.note: The divine self-naming 'I AM' stands behind John's recurring ego eimi, here in v26. Faint at this point (the absolute uses come later in John), but Availability and Coherence with John's theme are real.

echoes.text: Now the Egyptians are men, and not God; and their horses flesh, and not spirit. When Yahweh stretches out his hand, both he who helps shall stumble, and he who is helped shall fall, and they all shall be consumed together.
echoes.note: 'The Egyptians are flesh, and not spirit' gives the flesh/spirit contrast informing 'God is spirit' (v24). Faint and contested, but a plausible OT seed for the spirit-worship claim.

echoes.text: It shall happen in the latter days, that the mountain of Yahweh’s house shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it. Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For out of Zion the law shall go out, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.
echoes.note: Nations stream to Zion, for 'out of Zion shall go forth the law' — backing 'salvation is from the Jews' (v22). Coherence good for the Jew-as-source-of-salvation claim; moderate Volume.

pericopes.text: At this, his disciples came. They marveled that he was speaking with a woman; yet no one said, “What are you looking for?” or, “Why do you speak with her?” So the woman left her water pot, and went away into the city, and said to the people, “Come, see a man who told me everything that I did. Can this be the Christ?” They went out of the city, and were coming to him.

echoes.text: The young lady ran, and told her mother’s house about these words.
echoes.note: Rebekah 'ran and told' her household after the well encounter; the woman leaves her water pot and runs to tell the city (v28-29), completing the betrothal type-scene's go-and-announce beat. Faint verbal contact but coherent with the type-scene already established.

pericopes.text: In the meanwhile, the disciples urged him, saying, “Rabbi, eat.” But he said to them, “I have food to eat that you don’t know about.” The disciples therefore said one to another, “Has anyone brought him something to eat?” Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to accomplish his work. Don’t you say, ‘There are yet four months until the harvest?’ Behold, I tell you, lift up your eyes, and look at the fields, that they are white for harvest already. He who reaps receives wages, and gathers fruit to eternal life; that both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together. For in this the saying is true, ‘One sows, and another reaps.’ I sent you to reap that for which you haven’t labored. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”

echoes.text: He humbled you, and allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know; that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh’s mouth.
echoes.note: Man lives not by bread alone but by what proceeds from God's mouth; Jesus' 'I have food you don't know about... to do the will of him who sent me' (v32-34) reuses this contrast of bodily food with God's word/will. Strong Coherence; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: I haven’t gone back from the commandment of his lips. I have treasured up the words of his mouth more than my necessary food.
echoes.note: 'I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary food' parallels Jesus' food-as-doing-God's-will. Faint, supporting the word/will-over-food motif.

echoes.text: “Behold, the days come,” says Yahweh, “that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the one treading grapes him who sows seed; and sweet wine will drip from the mountains, and flow from the hills.
echoes.note: The eschatological harvest where 'the plowman overtakes the reaper' — sowing and reaping collapse together — underlies 'fields white for harvest already' and sower-and-reaper rejoicing together (v35-36). High Coherence with realized harvest; Volume strong on the compressed-harvest image.

echoes.text: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”
echoes.note: 'Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe' supplies the ripe/ready harvest call behind v35. Coherence is good, though Joel's harvest is judgment, making the transfer to mission-harvest somewhat contested.

echoes.text: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.
echoes.note: Those who sow in tears reap in joy, going out and returning rejoicing — matching 'he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together' (v36). Coherence good on the joint sow/reap rejoicing; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: You will sow, but won’t reap. You will tread the olives, but won’t anoint yourself with oil; and crush grapes, but won’t drink the wine.
echoes.note: 'You shall sow but not reap' typifies the sow-one/reap-another proverb cited in v37. One of several covenant-curse/proverb backgrounds; faint individually.

echoes.text: then let me sow, and let another eat. Yes, let the produce of my field be rooted out.
echoes.note: 'Let me sow, and another eat' is a close formal analogue to the proverb 'one sows and another reaps' (v37). Faint but apt for the sowing/reaping-by-different-parties saying.

pericopes.text: From that city many of the Samaritans believed in him because of the word of the woman, who testified, “He told me everything that I did.” So when the Samaritans came to him, they begged him to stay with them. He stayed there two days. Many more believed because of his word. They said to the woman, “Now we believe, not because of your speaking; for we have heard for ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world.”

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: The Servant made 'salvation to the ends of the earth' / light to the nations stands behind 'the Savior of the world' confessed by Samaritans (v42), extending salvation beyond Israel. Strong Coherence with the universal-salvation theme; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me. “Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other.
echoes.note: 'A just God and a Savior... look unto me, all the ends of the earth' is the OT locus for God as universal Savior, reframed as 'Savior of the world.' Volume good on the Savior-for-all-earth formula.

echoes.text: Yahweh has made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.
echoes.note: 'All the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God' supports the world-wide Savior confession in v42. Faint but coherent with the universalizing of salvation.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'After two days he will revive us' may color the deliberate 'he stayed there two days' (v40) before life/belief spreads, given John's symbolic use of time. Faint and contested.

pericopes.text: After the two days he went out from there and went into Galilee. For Jesus himself testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country. So when he came into Galilee, the Galileans received him, having seen all the things that he did in Jerusalem at the feast, for they also went to the feast.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says Yahweh concerning the men of Anathoth, who seek your life, saying, You shall not prophesy in Yahweh’s name, that you not die by our hand;
echoes.note: The men of Jeremiah's own town Anathoth sought his life, illustrating the prophet dishonored in his own country (v44). Offered as an OT exemplar of the rejected-prophet motif rather than a verbal source; faint and contested.

pericopes.text: Jesus came therefore again to Cana of Galilee, where he made the water into wine. There was a certain nobleman whose son was sick at Capernaum. When he heard that Jesus had come out of Judea into Galilee, he went to him, and begged him that he would come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death. Jesus therefore said to him, “Unless you see signs and wonders, you will in no way believe.” The nobleman said to him, “Sir, come down before my child dies.” Jesus said to him, “Go your way. Your son lives.” The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him, and he went his way. As he was now going down, his servants met him and reported, saying “Your child lives!” So he inquired of them the hour when he began to get better. They said therefore to him, “Yesterday at the seventh hour, the fever left him.” So the father knew that it was at that hour in which Jesus said to him, “Your son lives.” He believed, as did his whole house. This is again the second sign that Jesus did, having come out of Judea into Galilee.

echoes.text: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]
echoes.note: Elijah revives the widow's dying son and the mother's faith follows; Jesus' word 'your son lives' (v50-53) reprises the prophet who restores a son at the point of death. High Coherence and a strong type for the life-giving prophetic word; the 'son lives' acclamation closely matches.

echoes.text: When the child was grown, one day he went out to his father to the reapers. He said to his father, “My head! My head!” He said to his servant, “Carry him to his mother.” When he had taken him, and brought him to his mother, he sat on her knees until noon, and then died. She went up and laid him on the bed of the man of God, and shut the door on him, and went out. She called to her husband, and said, “Please send me one of the servants, and one of the […]
echoes.note: Elisha restores the Shunammite's dead son, again a prophet giving life to a child amid a parent's plea. Reinforces (with 1 Kings 17) the son-restored-by-prophetic-word type; high Recurrence strengthens the channel.

echoes.text: He sends his word, and heals them, and delivers them from their graves.
echoes.note: 'He sent his word, and healed them' precisely captures the healing-at-a-distance by bare word (v50-53), where the father believes 'the word that Jesus spoke.' Strong Coherence on word-as-healing-agent; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: Now Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honorable, because by him Yahweh had given victory to Syria: he was also a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper. The Syrians had gone out in bands, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maiden; and she waited on Naaman’s wife. She said to her mistress, “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would heal him […]
echoes.note: Naaman, a Gentile official, is healed at a distance through the prophet's word without the prophet's presence — paralleling the royal official whose son is healed by Jesus' remote command. Coherence good on official-faith-by-word; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: In those days was Hezekiah sick to death. Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came to him, and said to him, “Thus says Yahweh, ‘Set your house in order; for you shall die, and not live.’” Then he turned his face to the wall, and prayed to Yahweh, saying, “Remember now, Yahweh, I beg you, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done that which is good in your sight.” Hezekiah wept bitterly. Before Isaiah had gone out into […]
echoes.note: Hezekiah is 'sick unto death' and healed by the prophet's word, with the recovery confirmed by a sign tied to a precise hour — echoing the son 'at the point of death' (v47) and the verified 'seventh hour' of recovery (v52). Coherence good on the point-of-death/hour-confirmed pattern.

pericopes.text: After these things, there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now in Jerusalem by the sheep gate, there is a pool, which is called in Hebrew, “Bethesda”, having five porches. In these lay a great multitude of those who were sick, blind, lame, or paralyzed, waiting for the moving of the water; for an angel went down at certain times into the pool, and stirred up the water. Whoever stepped in first after the stirring of the water was healed of whatever disease he had. A certain man was there, who had been sick for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him lying there, and knew that he had been sick for a long time, he asked him, “Do you want to be made well?” The sick man answered him, “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, but while I’m coming, another steps down before me.” Jesus said to him, “Arise, take up your mat, and walk.” Immediately, the man was made well, and took up his mat and walked. Now it was the Sabbath on that day.

echoes.text: The days in which we came from Kadesh Barnea, until we had come over the brook Zered, were thirty-eight years; until all the generation of the men of war were consumed from the midst of the camp, as Yahweh swore to them.
echoes.note: The man has been infirm 'thirty-eight years.' Volume: the number is exact and otherwise unmotivated, and Deut 2:14 marks precisely thirty-eight years from Kadesh-barnea until the wilderness generation that could not enter the land had died off. Coherence: John repeatedly frames Jesus' signs against an exodus/wilderness backdrop (manna in ch. 6, water in ch. 7, serpent in 3:14), so a paralytic stranded thirty-eight years beside healing water he cannot reach evokes the generation barred from the promised land's rest. Recurrence: low (the figure is unique to this scene), and many read the number as merely realistic, so contested but the coincidence with the sole OT '38 years' is striking.

echoes.text: He brought me back to the door of the house; and behold, waters issued out from under the threshold of the house eastward; (for the forefront of the house was toward the east;) and the waters came down from under, from the right side of the house, on the south of the altar. Then he brought me out by the way of the gate northward, and led me round by the way outside to the outer gate, by the way of the gate that looks toward the east; and behold, there ran […]
echoes.note: Healing water by the temple/sheep gate, a pool whose stirring brings cure, faintly recalls Ezekiel's eschatological river flowing from the temple that heals all it touches. Volume is low (no shared wording) and Recurrence weak, but Coherence with John's temple-and-water typology (cf. 7:38) gives it some force. Faint and contested; the immediate Bethesda tradition is folk-medical rather than scriptural.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
echoes.note: The gathered 'blind, lame, paralyzed' and the command to the lame man to rise and walk echoes Isaiah's promise that in the day of salvation 'the lame shall leap like a deer.' Volume thematic only; Coherence high with the sign's meaning (Jesus as the one who fulfills the healing of the eschaton). Recurrence low within John. Honestly faint.

echoes.text: and he said, “If you will diligently listen to Yahweh your God’s voice, and will do that which is right in his eyes, and will pay attention to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will put none of the diseases on you, which I have put on the Egyptians; for I am Yahweh who heals you.”
echoes.note: 'I am the LORD who heals you' stands behind the whole motif of God as healer at the waters; the angel-stirred pool offers a counterfeit/lesser healing that Jesus' word transcends. Volume low, Recurrence low; included as a maximal, faint candidate for the divine-healer background.

pericopes.text: So the Jews said to him who was cured, “It is the Sabbath. It is not lawful for you to carry the mat.” He answered them, “He who made me well, the same said to me, ‘Take up your mat, and walk.’” Then they asked him, “Who is the man who said to you, ‘Take up your mat, and walk’?” But he who was healed didn’t know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, a crowd being in the place. Afterward Jesus found him in the temple, and said to him, “Behold, you are made well. Sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you.” The man went away, and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well. For this cause the Jews persecuted Jesus, and sought to kill him, because he did these things on the Sabbath. But Jesus answered them, “My Father is still working, so I am working, too.” For this cause therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Be careful, and bear no burden on the Sabbath day, nor bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem; neither carry a burden out of your houses on the Sabbath day, neither do any work: but make the Sabbath day holy, as I commanded your fathers.
echoes.note: The objection 'It is not lawful for you to carry the mat' on the Sabbath rests directly on the prophetic Sabbath law forbidding bearing a burden on the Sabbath day. Volume: the specific prohibition of carrying a load on the Sabbath is verbal and conceptual bedrock here; Jeremiah is the sharpest scriptural articulation. Coherence: the entire pericope turns on Sabbath legality. Recurrence: the same burden-bearing prohibition recurs (Neh 13:15-19), so the charge is grounded in available scripture, not later tradition alone.

echoes.text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed […]
echoes.note: The Sabbath controversy ('because he did these things on the Sabbath') invokes the Decalogue Sabbath command. Volume: foundational; the legal framework the Jews enforce is the fourth commandment. Coherence: high, the dispute is explicitly about Sabbath observance. Recurrence: the parallel Deut 5:12-15 reinforces availability. This is the law Jesus is accused of breaking, making it load-bearing for the whole chapter.

echoes.text: On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done. God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.
echoes.note: 'My Father is still working, so I am working, too' answers the Sabbath charge by appeal to creation: God rested on the seventh day, yet (so the live Second-Temple debate, e.g. Philo, Leg. All. 1.5-6; later rabbinic discussion) God never ceases the works of giving life and rendering judgment, which alone are his prerogative even on the Sabbath. Volume: the rest of Gen 2:2-3 is exactly the premise Jesus' claim contests. Coherence: very high — it generates the equal-with-God charge in v.18 and the life/judgment exposition that follows. Recurrence: the creation Sabbath underlies the whole Bethesda-on-the-Sabbath structure. Availability: the 'God works even on the Sabbath' tradition is attested in Second-Temple/early-rabbinic sources.

echoes.text: We were accounted of him as worthless metal, And he abstains from our ways as from uncleannesses. The latter end of the righteous he calls happy; And he vaunts that God is his father. Let us see if his words be true, And let us try what shall befall in the ending of his life. For if the righteous man is God’s son, he will uphold him, And he will deliver him out of the hand of his adversaries.
echoes.note: Jesus 'called God his own Father, making himself equal with God,' provoking a death plot — closely paralleling the ungodly in Wisdom who plot against the righteous one precisely because 'he calls himself a child of the Lord' and 'boasts that God is his father.' Volume: strong conceptual and near-verbal overlap on the Father-claim provoking lethal hostility. Coherence: high with John's righteous-sufferer framing. Recurrence: the Wisdom passage informs passion narratives broadly. A deuterocanonical source, hence flagged but well-grounded.

echoes.text: I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!”
echoes.note: The charge that Jesus made 'himself equal with God' could be heard against the background of the proud one who said 'I will make myself like the Most High' — the accusers frame Jesus' self-equation as that blasphemous presumption. Volume low and the resonance is in the accusers' mouths, not the narrator's. Coherence moderate; included as a faint, contested candidate for the 'equal with God' polemic.

pericopes.text: Jesus therefore answered them, “Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise. For the Father has affection for the Son, and shows him all things that he himself does. He will show him greater works than these, that you may marvel. For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, even so the Son also gives life to whom he desires. For the Father judges no one, but he has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son, even as they honor the Father. He who doesn’t honor the Son doesn’t honor the Father who sent him.

echoes.text: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.
echoes.note: 'As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, even so the Son also gives life' draws on the Song of Moses' exclusive divine self-claim, 'I kill and I make alive,' which makes giving life and putting to death God's sole prerogative. Volume: strong conceptual identity (raising the dead / making alive). Coherence: very high — this is the theological warrant for the equal-with-God claim, transferring the uniquely divine life-giving power to the Son. Recurrence: the make-alive formula recurs (1 Sam 2:6; cf. v.21,24-29 below).

echoes.text: “Yahweh kills, and makes alive. He brings down to Sheol, and brings up.
echoes.note: Hannah's confession 'The LORD kills and makes alive; he brings down to Sheol and raises up' supplies the same death-and-resurrection-as-divine-act idiom undergirding 'the Father raises the dead.' Volume: shared raise/make-alive language. Coherence: high. Recurrence: reinforces Deut 32:39; together they establish that life-giving is an exclusively divine work now exercised by the Son.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'The Father... has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son even as they honor the Father' reflects Daniel's one like a son of man to whom is given dominion and the worship/service of all peoples. Volume: conceptual (universal honor/authority granted by God to a son-of-man figure), made explicit when v.27 names him 'son of man.' Coherence: high with John's transfer of judgment and honor. Recurrence: Danielic son-of-man framing recurs across the Gospel tradition; here it grounds the demand that all honor the Son.

pericopes.text: “Most certainly I tell you, he who hears my word, and believes him who sent me, has eternal life, and doesn’t come into judgment, but has passed out of death into life. Most certainly, I tell you, the hour comes, and now is, when the dead will hear the Son of God’s voice; and those who hear will live. For as the Father has life in himself, even so he gave to the Son also to have life in himself. He also gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is a son of man. Don’t marvel at this, for the hour comes, in which all that are in the tombs will hear his voice, and will come out; those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; and those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: 'All who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment' is John's closest verbal-conceptual echo of Daniel's 'many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, some to shame and everlasting contempt.' Volume: high — the two-outcome resurrection of the dead is distinctively Daniel's. Coherence: very high with the life/judgment theme. Recurrence: Daniel 12 is the seminal OT resurrection text and is the available source for the double resurrection.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'He gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is a son of man' explicitly grounds the Son's judging authority in the Danielic son-of-man who receives dominion and an everlasting kingdom from the Ancient of Days. Volume: the anarthrous 'son of man' plus granted judging authority is a direct Danielic signal. Coherence: very high. Recurrence: ties the resurrection-judgment scene to the dominion granted in Dan 7. This is the clearest figural citation in the discourse.

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]
echoes.note: The dead hearing the life-giving voice of the Son of God and coming alive from the tombs resonates with Ezekiel's valley of dry bones, where God's word/breath summons the dead to life and opens the graves ('I will open your graves and raise you'). Volume: shared open-graves and voice-summons imagery. Coherence: high with the resurrection theme. Recurrence: Ezekiel 37 is a stock resurrection-of-Israel text; somewhat less verbally precise than Dan 12, hence medium.

echoes.text: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
echoes.note: 'Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise... the earth will give birth to the dead' is another available resurrection oracle behind 'those in the tombs will come out.' Volume thematic; Coherence high; Recurrence modest. A genuine but secondary candidate to Daniel 12, flagged faint.

pericopes.text: I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous; because I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me. “If I testify about myself, my witness is not valid. It is another who testifies about me. I know that the testimony which he testifies about me is true. You have sent to John, and he has testified to the truth. But the testimony which I receive is not from man. However, I say these things that you may be saved. He was the burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light. But the testimony which I have is greater than that of John, for the works which the Father gave me to accomplish, the very works that I do, testify about me, that the Father has sent me. The Father himself, who sent me, has testified about me. You have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his form. You don’t have his word living in you; because you don’t believe him whom he sent.

echoes.text: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.
echoes.note: The whole witness section ('If I testify about myself, my witness is not valid... It is another who testifies about me') applies the Torah's rule that a matter is established only by two or three witnesses. Volume: the legal principle is structurally determinative — Jesus marshals multiple corroborating witnesses (John, the works, the Father, the Scriptures) precisely to satisfy this requirement. Coherence: very high. Recurrence: the two-witness rule recurs (Deut 17:6; Num 35:30) and is invoked elsewhere in John (8:17).

echoes.text: He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.”
echoes.note: 'You have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his form' inverts and presupposes the Sinai tradition that no one can see God's face/form and live, and that Israel heard the voice but saw no form (Deut 4:12). Volume: the voice/form pairing is a deliberate scriptural touchstone. Coherence: high — the point is that the accusers, unlike the Son, have no immediate access to the Father. Recurrence: the no-form motif is firmly grounded in the Sinai narratives.

echoes.text: There I will make the horn of David to bud. I have ordained a lamp for my anointed.
echoes.note: John the Baptist as 'the burning and shining lamp' may echo the prepared 'lamp for my anointed' set before the messianic king, casting John as the lamp pointing to the coming one. Volume low (single image), Recurrence low; Coherence moderate with John's witness-to-the-light theme (cf. 1:8). Faint and contested.

pericopes.text: “You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me. Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life. I don’t receive glory from men. But I know you, that you don’t have God’s love in yourselves. I have come in my Father’s name, and you don’t receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him. How can you believe, who receive glory from one another, and you don’t seek the glory that comes from the only God? “Don’t think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you, even Moses, on whom you have set your hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote about me. But if you don’t believe his writings, how will you believe my words?”

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him. This is according to all that you desired of Yahweh your God in Horeb in the day of the assembly, saying, “Let me not hear again the voice of Yahweh my God, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I not die.” Yahweh said to me, “They have well said that which they have spoken. I will raise them up a prophet from among their […]
echoes.note: 'Moses wrote about me... if you believed Moses you would believe me' centers on the Pentateuch as christological witness, with the prophet-like-Moses promise the prime text Jesus claims Moses 'wrote' concerning him. Volume: conceptual but specific — the expectation of a coming prophet whom Israel must heed. Coherence: very high; the chapter's climax makes Moses Jesus' chief scriptural witness and accuser. Recurrence: Deut 18 is the standard prophet-like-Moses proof-text in the NT (cf. Acts 3:22).

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
echoes.note: Among the things 'Moses wrote' about Christ, the protoevangelium (the seed of the woman crushing the serpent) is a candidate text for what Jesus claims the Pentateuch foretells of him. Volume: low (not quoted); the verse names no specific passage. Coherence: moderate within a figural reading of Genesis as messianic. Recurrence: low in John. Included as a maximal, contested specification of 'he wrote about me.'

echoes.text: Moses returned to Yahweh, and said, “Oh, this people have sinned a great sin, and have made themselves gods of gold. Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.”
echoes.note: 'There is one who accuses you, even Moses, on whom you have set your hope' ironically reverses Moses' role as Israel's intercessor who pleaded for the people; the very mediator they trust becomes their accuser. Volume low, Recurrence low, but Coherence moderate with the reversal motif. Faint and contested.

echoes.text: “Take this book of the law, and put it by the side of the ark of the covenant of Yahweh your God, that it may be there for a witness against you. For I know your rebellion, and your stiff neck. Behold, while I am yet alive with you this day, you have been rebellious against Yahweh. How much more after my death?
echoes.note: Moses as accuser fits the Torah's own provision that the book of the law be placed 'as a witness against you' because of Israel's rebellion. Volume: conceptual but apt — Moses' writings testify against unbelief, exactly Jesus' charge ('if you don't believe his writings'). Coherence: high with the witness/accusation framing. Recurrence: moderate; strengthens the figural reading of Moses-as-witness.

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one. You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: 'You don't have God's love in yourselves' and 'how can you believe, who... don't seek the glory from the only God' resonate with the Shema's call to love the one God with whole heart. Volume low (no quotation), but Coherence moderate: the indictment is that those who recite love of the one God fail to love and honor him. Faint, contested, included for completeness.

pericopes.text: After these things, Jesus went away to the other side of the sea of Galilee, which is also called the Sea of Tiberias. A great multitude followed him, because they saw his signs which he did on those who were sick. Jesus went up into the mountain, and he sat there with his disciples. Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand. Jesus therefore lifting up his eyes, and seeing that a great multitude was coming to him, said to Philip, “Where are we to buy bread, that these may eat?” This he said to test him, for he himself knew what he would do. Philip answered him, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread is not sufficient for them, that everyone of them may receive a little.” One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him, “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these among so many?” Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” Now there was much grass in that place. So the men sat down, in number about five thousand. Jesus took the loaves; and having given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to those who were sitting down; likewise also of the fish as much as they desired. When they were filled, he said to his disciples, “Gather up the broken pieces which are left over, that nothing be lost.” So they gathered them up, and filled twelve baskets with broken pieces from the five barley loaves, which were left over by those who had eaten. When therefore the people saw the sign which Jesus did, they said, “This is truly the prophet who comes into the world.” Jesus therefore, perceiving that they were about to come and take him by force, to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not. It shall come to pass on the sixth day, that they shall prepare that which they bring in, and it shall be twice as much as they gather daily.” Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel, “At evening, then you shall know that Yahweh has brought […]
echoes.note: The wilderness feeding of a great multitude with miraculous bread sets the controlling type that the chapter will name explicitly in v.31. High Volume and total Coherence with the manna economy (bread, gathering, leftovers, no waste); the feeding scene is the narrative enactment of the manna gift Jesus later interprets.

echoes.text: Where could I get meat to give to all this people? For they weep to me, saying, ‘Give us meat, that we may eat.’ I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me. If you treat me this way, please kill me right now, if I have found favor in your sight; and don’t let me see my wretchedness.” Yahweh said to Moses, “Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people, and officers over […]
echoes.note: Philip's 'Where are we to buy bread... not sufficient' (v.7) closely mirrors Moses' despairing 'Where am I to get meat... shall flocks and herds be slaughtered to suffice them?' Strong structural and verbal Coherence: a leader confronted with an impossible crowd, mountain setting, and divine provision overriding human arithmetic.

echoes.text: A man from Baal Shalishah came, and brought the man of God bread of the first fruits, twenty loaves of barley, and fresh ears of grain in his sack. He said, “Give to the people, that they may eat.” His servant said, “What, should I set this before a hundred men?” But he said, “Give the people, that they may eat; for thus says Yahweh, ‘They will eat, and will have some left over.’” So he set it before them, and they ate, and left some of it, according to […]
echoes.note: Elisha multiplies twenty barley loaves to feed a hundred with leftovers, dismissing a servant's 'How can I set this before a hundred?' John alone specifies 'barley loaves' and 'what are these among so many?', and adds the leftovers motif. High Volume and verbal Recurrence make this the closest single OT analogue to the miracle's mechanics.

echoes.text: He rained down manna on them to eat, and gave them food from the sky. Man ate the bread of angels. He sent them food to the full.
echoes.note: Asaph's 'he rained down manna... gave them grain of heaven... bread of the angels' is the psalm John will quote at v.31; its presence governs the feeding as the eschatological manna. High Coherence: the crowd reads the sign as a renewed wilderness banquet.

echoes.text: They asked, and he brought quails, and satisfied them with the bread of the sky.
echoes.note: 'He gave them bread from heaven in abundance' — a second psalmic celebration of the manna, reinforcing the satisfied-fullness motif ('when they were filled,' v.12). Lower distinctiveness than Ps 78 but adds Recurrence to the manna tradition active here.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: The crowd's acclamation 'This is truly the prophet who comes into the world' (v.14) invokes the promised prophet-like-Moses. The Mosaic feeding miracle triggers a Mosaic-prophet expectation; high Coherence with John's prophet-and-king Christology.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]
echoes.note: John's editorial note 'Now the Passover was at hand' (v.4) frames the whole chapter under the paschal lamb, preparing the flesh-and-blood discourse (vv.51-56). Availability and Coherence are strong; the Passover anchor is authorial, though the feeding scene itself does not verbally cite Exodus 12.

echoes.text: He said to Moses, “Come up to Yahweh, you, and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel; and worship from a distance. Moses alone shall come near to Yahweh, but they shall not come near, neither shall the people go up with him.” Moses came and told the people all Yahweh’s words, and all the ordinances; and all the people answered with one voice, and said, “All the words which Yahweh has spoken will we do.” Moses wrote all Yahweh’s […]
echoes.note: Jesus 'went up into the mountain and sat there with his disciples' (v.3) before a meal faintly recalls Moses ascending Sinai where the elders 'beheld God and ate and drank.' Suggestive of a covenant-meal-on-the-mountain pattern but low Volume; contested.

echoes.text: and they said to him, “Behold, you are old, and your sons don’t walk in your ways: now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.” But the thing displeased Samuel, when they said, “Give us a king to judge us.” Samuel prayed to Yahweh. Yahweh said to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they tell you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not be king over them.
echoes.note: The crowd's move to 'take him by force, to make him king' (v.15) faintly evokes Israel's improper demand for a king, which the LORD treats as rejection of his rule. Thematic rather than verbal; offered as a contested background to Jesus' refusal of a politicized kingship.

pericopes.text: When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea, and they entered into the boat, and were going over the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not come to them. The sea was tossed by a great wind blowing. When therefore they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they saw Jesus walking on the sea, and drawing near to the boat; and they were afraid. But he said to them, “It is I. Don’t be afraid.” They were willing therefore to receive him into the boat. Immediately the boat was at the land where they were going.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”
echoes.note: Jesus' 'It is I (ego eimi); do not be afraid' atop the storm reads, in John's idiom, as the divine self-naming 'I AM.' High Coherence with the chapter's later absolute 'I am' sayings; the theophanic-on-the-water setting elevates the otherwise ordinary phrase to divine self-disclosure.

echoes.text: He alone stretches out the heavens, and treads on the waves of the sea.
echoes.note: 'who alone... treads on the waves of the sea' ascribes sea-trampling to God alone. Jesus 'walking on the sea' enacts a prerogative the OT reserves for the Creator; strong Volume and Coherence with the I-AM disclosure that accompanies it.

echoes.text: Your way was through the sea; your paths through the great waters. Your footsteps were not known.
echoes.note: 'Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters, yet your footprints were unseen' — a hymn of God's exodus march across the deep. Coheres with Jesus pathless on the water; the psalm's exodus frame fits John's Passover setting.

echoes.text: But now thus says Yahweh who created you, Jacob, and he who formed you, Israel: “Don’t be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine. When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they will not overflow you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be burned, and flame will not scorch you.
echoes.note: 'Fear not... when you pass through the waters I will be with you' pairs the precise reassurance ('Don't be afraid') with passage through threatening waters. Coherence with the disciples' deliverance; the chapter's I-AM resonates with Isaiah 43:10 below.

echoes.text: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me.
echoes.note: 'that you may... believe me and understand that I am he (ani hu / ego eimi)' supplies the LXX 'I am' that stands behind Jesus' words on the sea. Strengthens the case that v.20's ego eimi is theophanic rather than mere identification.

echoes.text: Those who go down to the sea in ships, who do business in great waters; These see Yahweh’s works, and his wonders in the deep. For he commands, and raises the stormy wind, which lifts up its waves. They mount up to the sky; they go down again to the depths. Their soul melts away because of trouble. They reel back and forth, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits’ end. Then they cry to Yahweh in their trouble, and he brings them out of their […]
echoes.note: Seafarers in a wind-tossed storm cry out and God 'made the storm a calm' and 'brought them to their desired haven' — strikingly close to the boat reaching land 'immediately' (v.21). Good Coherence though John gives stilling-by-arrival rather than rebuke of the storm.

echoes.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and Yahweh caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all the night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. The children of Israel went into the midst of the sea on the dry ground, and the waters were a wall to them on their right hand, and on their left. The Egyptians pursued, and went in after them into the midst of the sea: all of Pharaoh’s horses, his chariots, and his horsemen. In the […]
echoes.note: Under the Passover frame, a nighttime deliverance over/through the sea recalls the Red Sea crossing where Israel 'feared' then was saved. Typological rather than verbal; coheres with the exodus pattern saturating the chapter.

pericopes.text: On the next day, the multitude that stood on the other side of the sea saw that there was no other boat there, except the one in which his disciples had embarked, and that Jesus hadn’t entered with his disciples into the boat, but his disciples had gone away alone. However boats from Tiberias came near to the place where they ate the bread after the Lord had given thanks. When the multitude therefore saw that Jesus wasn’t there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the boats, and came to Capernaum, seeking Jesus. When they found him on the other side of the sea, they asked him, “Rabbi, when did you come here?” Jesus answered them, “Most certainly I tell you, you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves, and were filled. Don’t work for the food which perishes, but for the food which remains to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For God the Father has sealed him.” They said therefore to him, “What must we do, that we may work the works of God?” Jesus answered them, “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.” They said therefore to him, “What then do you do for a sign, that we may see, and believe you? What work do you do? Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness. As it is written, ‘He gave them bread out of heaven to eat.’” Jesus therefore said to them, “Most certainly, I tell you, it wasn’t Moses who gave you the bread out of heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread out of heaven. For the bread of God is that which comes down out of heaven, and gives life to the world.” They said therefore to him, “Lord, always give us this bread.”

echoes.text: He rained down manna on them to eat, and gave them food from the sky.
echoes.note: 'He gave them bread out of heaven to eat' (v.31) is a formal citation ('as it is written') closest in wording to LXX Psalm 78:24 ('arton ouranou edoken autois'). The chapter's hermeneutical hinge; maximal Volume.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not.
echoes.note: 'I am about to rain bread from heaven for you' is the originating text behind the v.31 citation; Jesus directly contests its meaning ('it was not Moses who gave...'). The quotation conflates Exodus 16 with Psalm 78, so both are primary sources.

echoes.text: and gave them bread from the sky for their hunger, and brought water out of the rock for them for their thirst, and commanded them that they should go in to possess the land which you had sworn to give them.
echoes.note: 'You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger' is a third witness to the formula the crowd cites, showing the manna-from-heaven line was a fixed liturgical commonplace (Recurrence) rather than a single text.

echoes.text: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. Why do you spend money for that which is not bread? and your labor for that which doesn’t satisfy? listen diligently to me, and eat you that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness. Turn your ear, and come to me; hear, and your soul shall live: and I will make an everlasting covenant with […]
echoes.note: 'Why spend money for that which is not bread... eat what is good... that your soul may live' undergirds Jesus' contrast between 'food which perishes' and 'food which remains to eternal life' (v.27). Coherent invitation-to-true-nourishment background.

echoes.text: Moses said to them, “Let no one leave of it until the morning.” Notwithstanding they didn’t listen to Moses, but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and became foul: and Moses was angry with them. They gathered it morning by morning, everyone according to his eating. When the sun grew hot, it melted.
echoes.note: The manna that bred worms and stank when hoarded overnight gives concrete force to 'the food which perishes' (v.27). A plausible but faint verbal-conceptual link within the active manna matrix; contested as deliberate.

pericopes.text: Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life. He who comes to me will not be hungry, and he who believes in me will never be thirsty. But I told you that you have seen me, and yet you don’t believe. All those whom the Father gives me will come to me. He who comes to me I will in no way throw out. For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me. This is the will of my Father who sent me, that of all he has given to me I should lose nothing, but should raise him up at the last day. This is the will of the one who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son, and believes in him, should have eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day.”

echoes.text: “Come, eat some of my bread, Drink some of the wine which I have mixed!
echoes.note: Wisdom's invitation 'Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed' stands behind 'I am the bread of life. He who comes to me will not hunger.' Strong Coherence: Jesus speaks as personified Wisdom hosting a banquet that confers life.

echoes.text: Come to me, you that are desirous of me, And be you filled with my produce. For my memorial is sweeter than honey, And my inheritance than the honeycomb. They that eat me will yet be hungry; And those who drink me will yet be thirsty.
echoes.note: Wisdom says 'Come to me... those who eat me will hunger for more, those who drink me will thirst for more.' John inverts it ('will never hunger... never thirst'), a deliberate transformation signalling Jesus surpasses Wisdom/Torah. High Availability and Coherence; the inversion is the point.

echoes.text: They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun strike them: for he who has mercy on them will lead them, even by springs of water he will guide them.
echoes.note: 'They shall not hunger or thirst... he who has pity will lead them' supplies the hunger-and-thirst-abolished promise of the eschatological return. Coheres tightly with v.35's double negation; an exilic-restoration backdrop to the bread of life.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: The repeated 'I will raise him up at the last day' (vv.39-40) draws on the clearest OT resurrection text, 'many who sleep in the dust shall awake... to everlasting life.' Provides the Availability for John's last-day raising; recurs across the discourse.

pericopes.text: The Jews therefore murmured concerning him, because he said, “I am the bread which came down out of heaven.” They said, “Isn’t this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then does he say, ‘I have come down out of heaven?’” Therefore Jesus answered them, “Don’t murmur among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I will raise him up in the last day. It is written in the prophets, ‘They will all be taught by God.’ Therefore everyone who hears from the Father, and has learned, comes to me. Not that anyone has seen the Father, except he who is from God. He has seen the Father. Most certainly, I tell you, he who believes in me has eternal life. I am the bread of life. Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread which comes down out of heaven, that anyone may eat of it and not die. I am the living bread which came down out of heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. Yes, the bread which I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.”

echoes.text: The whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron in the wilderness; and the children of Israel said to them, “We wish that we had died by the hand of Yahweh in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots, when we ate our fill of bread, for you have brought us out into this wilderness, to kill this whole assembly with hunger.” Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the […]
echoes.note: 'The Jews therefore murmured concerning him' (v.41,43) deliberately casts the audience as the wilderness generation that 'murmured against Moses and Aaron' over bread. High Volume and Coherence: the same verb-of-grumbling against the same gift (bread from heaven).

echoes.text: All your children shall be taught of Yahweh; and great shall be the peace of your children.
echoes.note: 'It is written in the prophets, They will all be taught by God' (v.45) formally cites Isaiah 54:13 ('all your children shall be taught by the LORD'). A second explicit citation in the chapter; high Volume.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people: and they shall teach no more every man his neighbor, and every man his brother, saying, Know Yahweh; for they shall all know me, from their least to their greatest, says Yahweh: for I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin […]
echoes.note: 'They shall all know me, from the least to the greatest' (new-covenant interiority of divine teaching) reinforces the 'taught by God' citation and the drawing/learning that brings one to Jesus (vv.44-45). Strong Coherence as a secondary new-covenant source.

echoes.text: The mixed multitude that was among them lusted exceedingly: and the children of Israel also wept again, and said, “Who will give us flesh to eat? We remember the fish, which we ate in Egypt for nothing; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlic; but now we have lost our appetite. There is nothing at all except this manna to look at.” The manna was like coriander seed, and its appearance like the appearance of bdellium. […]
echoes.note: 'Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died' (v.49) recalls the wilderness generation that craved, ate, and perished. The manna's described provision (Num 11:7-9) plus the death of that generation give Volume to Jesus' contrast with bread that lets one 'not die.'

echoes.text: He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.”
echoes.note: 'Not that anyone has seen the Father, except he who is from God' (v.46) reprises the Mosaic axiom 'no one shall see me and live.' Coheres with John's recurring claim that the Son alone has seen God (cf. 1:18); moderate Volume here.

echoes.text: and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month; and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it at evening. They shall take some of the blood, and put it on the two door posts and on the lintel, on the houses in which they shall eat it. They shall eat the flesh in that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread. They shall eat it with bitter herbs. Don’t eat it raw, nor boiled at all with water, but roasted with […]
echoes.note: 'The bread which I will give for the life of the world is my flesh' (v.51), under the Passover frame, fuses bread with the slain paschal lamb whose flesh is eaten and whose blood saves. Typological Coherence prepares the eat-flesh scandal of the next pericope.

pericopes.text: The Jews therefore contended with one another, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” Jesus therefore said to them, “Most certainly I tell you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you don’t have life in yourselves. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day. For my flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood lives in me, and I in him. As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father; so he who feeds on me, he will also live because of me. This is the bread which came down out of heaven—not as our fathers ate the manna, and died. He who eats this bread will live forever.” He said these things in the synagogue, as he taught in Capernaum.

echoes.text: “‘Any man of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who live as foreigners among them, who eats any kind of blood, I will set my face against that soul who eats blood, and will cut him off from among his people. For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life. Therefore I have said to the children of Israel, “No person […]
echoes.note: 'Drink his blood' (v.53) collides head-on with the absolute Levitical prohibition: 'I will set my face against any who eats blood... the life is in the blood.' The scandal of vv.52-53 is unintelligible without this law; high Volume and Coherence as the offense John exploits.

echoes.text: They shall eat the flesh in that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread. They shall eat it with bitter herbs.
echoes.note: 'They shall eat the flesh that night' — the paschal lamb whose flesh is consumed. Jesus' demand to eat his flesh, set 'at Passover,' identifies him as the lamb; high typological Coherence binding the discourse to the chapter's opening note (v.4).

echoes.text: But flesh with its life, that is, its blood, you shall not eat.
echoes.note: 'You shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood' is the primal Noachic blood prohibition predating Sinai, broadening the scandal of v.53 beyond Israel to a universal taboo. Adds Recurrence to the blood-prohibition background.

echoes.text: Only be sure that you don’t eat the blood; for the blood is the life. You shall not eat the life with the flesh.
echoes.note: 'Only be sure that you do not eat the blood, for the blood is the life' restates the prohibition with the life-in-the-blood rationale that John ironically affirms (the blood gives life). Reinforces the contested commandment behind the discourse.

echoes.text: They that eat me will yet be hungry; And those who drink me will yet be thirsty.
echoes.note: Wisdom's 'those who eat me... those who drink me' returns here with literal eating and drinking, deepening the Wisdom-banquet identification of Jesus. Coheres with v.35; the eat/drink pairing strengthens the Sirach link.

echoes.text: “Come, eat some of my bread, Drink some of the wine which I have mixed!
echoes.note: 'Eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed' — Wisdom's bread-and-wine banquet underlies the flesh-as-food/blood-as-drink doubling of vv.53-56. Lower distinctiveness than the Leviticus collision but adds the sapiential meal frame.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not.
echoes.note: 'Not as our fathers ate the manna, and died' (v.58) closes the discourse by again invoking the heaven-bread of Exodus 16, now surpassed. Recurrence of the governing manna text rather than a fresh allusion.

pericopes.text: Therefore many of his disciples, when they heard this, said, “This is a hard saying! Who can listen to it?” But Jesus knowing in himself that his disciples murmured at this, said to them, “Does this cause you to stumble? Then what if you would see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? It is the spirit who gives life. The flesh profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life.
