But there are some of you who don’t believe.” For Jesus knew from the beginning who they were who didn’t believe, and who it was who would betray him. He said, “For this cause have I said to you that no one can come to me, unless it is given to him by my Father.” At this, many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. Jesus said therefore to the twelve, “You don’t also want to go away, do you?” Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life. We have come to believe and know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Jesus answered them, “Didn’t I choose you, the twelve, and one of you is a devil?” Now he spoke of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot, for it was he who would betray him, being one of the twelve.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: 'What if you would see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?' (v.62) trades on the Danielic Son of Man who comes with the clouds before the Ancient of Days; John reverses the vector to ascent. Provides the title's apocalyptic Availability.

echoes.text: Thus says the Lord Yahweh to these bones: Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and you shall live. I will lay sinews on you, and will bring up flesh on you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you, and you shall live; and you shall know that I am Yahweh. So I prophesied as I was commanded: and as I prophesied, there was a noise, and behold, an earthquake; and the bones came together, bone to its bone. I saw, and, behold, there were sinews […]
echoes.note: 'It is the spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing' (v.63) echoes the valley-of-bones promise 'I will put my spirit within you, and you shall live.' Coherent spirit-gives-life theology; the dry-bones spirit animates dead flesh.

echoes.text: Now the Egyptians are men, and not God; and their horses flesh, and not spirit. When Yahweh stretches out his hand, both he who helps shall stumble, and he who is helped shall fall, and they all shall be consumed together.
echoes.note: 'The Egyptians are flesh and not spirit' supplies the flesh/spirit antithesis behind 'the flesh profits nothing' (v.63), where flesh is the weak human plane and spirit the divine. Conceptual Coherence; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: 'The spirit who gives life' (v.63) may glance at the breath of life by which the LORD made the man a living being. Foundational but diffuse; offered as a faint creational backdrop to life-giving Spirit.

echoes.text: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.
echoes.note: Peter's 'you are the Holy One of God' (v.69) resonates with 'you will not let your Holy One see corruption,' a key resurrection/messianic title. Coheres with the chapter's raising-on-the-last-day refrain; the holy-one designation is OT-rooted.

echoes.text: They envied Moses also in the camp, and Aaron, Yahweh’s saint.
echoes.note: Aaron is 'the holy one of the LORD' — the only OT figure given nearly this exact title, offering a priestly alternative background to Peter's confession (v.69). Lower Volume than Psalm 16; contested as the operative source.

echoes.text: For it is no vain thing for you; because it is your life, and through this thing you shall prolong your days in the land, where you go over the Jordan to possess it.”
echoes.note: 'You have the words of eternal life' (v.68) faintly recalls Moses' 'it is no empty word for you, but your very life.' The word-as-life motif suits John's Mosaic typology; diffuse and contested.

pericopes.text: After these things, Jesus was walking in Galilee, for he wouldn’t walk in Judea, because the Jews sought to kill him. Now the feast of the Jews, the Feast of Booths, was at hand. His brothers therefore said to him, “Depart from here, and go into Judea, that your disciples also may see your works which you do. For no one does anything in secret, and himself seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, reveal yourself to the world.” For even his brothers didn’t believe in him. Jesus therefore said to them, “My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready. The world can’t hate you, but it hates me, because I testify about it, that its works are evil. You go up to the feast. I am not yet going up to this feast, because my time is not yet fulfilled.” Having said these things to them, he stayed in Galilee.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Speak to the children of Israel, and say, ‘On the fifteenth day of this seventh month is the feast of tents for seven days to Yahweh. On the first day shall be a holy convocation: you shall do no regular work. Seven days you shall offer an offering made by fire to Yahweh. On the eighth day shall be a holy convocation to you; and you shall offer an offering made by fire to Yahweh. It is a solemn assembly; you shall do no […]
echoes.note: The whole chapter is framed by 'the Feast of the Jews, the Feast of Booths' (v.2), the pilgrimage festival Leviticus institutes with its seven days of dwelling in booths and rejoicing 'before the LORD your God.' Availability and volume are high: the named feast supplies the liturgical theater (water-libation, temple lights) that every subsequent saying exploits. John deliberately stages Jesus' self-disclosure against this Mosaic ordinance.

echoes.text: You shall keep the feast of tents seven days, after you have gathered in from your threshing floor and from your wine press. You shall rejoice in your feast, you, your son, your daughter, your male servant, your female servant, the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, who are within your gates. You shall keep a feast to Yahweh your God seven days in the place which Yahweh chooses; because Yahweh your God will bless you in all your […]
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's parallel legislation makes Booths a mandatory pilgrimage to 'the place the LORD will choose' (Jerusalem/temple), explaining the pressure to 'go up to the feast' (vv.3,8,10). The Deuteronomic command to 'rejoice in your feast' undergirds the brothers' urging that Jesus 'reveal yourself to the world' at the festival. Coherence with the going-up-to-Judea motif is strong.

echoes.text: I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother’s children.
echoes.note: 'Even his brothers didn't believe in him' (v.5) coheres with the psalm of the righteous sufferer, 'I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother's children' — a psalm John cites elsewhere for Jesus' zeal and rejection. Recurrence of Psalm 69 in the Fourth Gospel raises the plausibility that the brothers' unbelief is read figurally through the estranged sufferer.

pericopes.text: But when his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly, but as it were in secret. The Jews therefore sought him at the feast, and said, “Where is he?” There was much murmuring among the multitudes concerning him. Some said, “He is a good man.” Others said, “Not so, but he leads the multitude astray.” Yet no one spoke openly of him for fear of the Jews.

echoes.text: Three times in a year all of your shall males appear before Yahweh your God in the place which he chooses: in the feast of unleavened bread, in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tents. They shall not appear before Yahweh empty.
echoes.note: 'When his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up' enacts the Deuteronomic requirement that every male 'appear before the LORD' three times a year, Booths being one. The going-up language and the search 'at the feast' (v.11) presuppose the pilgrim crowds the law gathers. Coherence with the festival frame is strong though the verbal contact is general.

pericopes.text: But when it was now the midst of the feast, Jesus went up into the temple and taught. The Jews therefore marveled, saying, “How does this man know letters, having never been educated?” Jesus therefore answered them, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me. If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God, or if I am speaking from myself. He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory, but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and no unrighteousness is in him. Didn’t Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keeps the law? Why do you seek to kill me?” The multitude answered, “You have a demon! Who seeks to kill you?” Jesus answered them, “I did one work, and you all marvel because of it. Moses has given you circumcision (not that it is of Moses, but of the fathers), and on the Sabbath you circumcise a boy. If a boy receives circumcision on the Sabbath, that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me, because I made a man completely healthy on the Sabbath? Don’t judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment.”

echoes.text: I will raise them up a prophet from among their brothers, like you. I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I shall command him. It shall happen, that whoever will not listen to my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him.
echoes.note: 'My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me' (v.16) and 'he who sent me is true' echo the prophet-like-Moses who speaks only what God commands, into whose mouth God puts his words. The sending/speaking-not-from-self language is the diagnostic mark distinguishing the true prophet (Deut 18) from one who speaks presumptuously. Strong coherence with John's prophet-Christology, reinforced by v.40 ('truly the prophet').

echoes.text: Moses said, “Hereby you shall know that Yahweh has sent me to do all these works; for they are not from my own mind.
echoes.note: Moses' self-authentication, 'the LORD has sent me to do all these works, and I have not done them of my own accord,' supplies the precise idiom of vv.17-18 ('if I am speaking from myself... seeks his own glory'). The criterion of not seeking one's own glory but the sender's marks divine commission. Availability and verbal coherence are good even if the contact is unmarked.

echoes.text: Moses commanded us a law, an inheritance for the assembly of Jacob.
echoes.note: 'Didn't Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keeps the law?' (v.19) directly invokes the Mosaic Torah as a body, with the Pentateuch as availability. The argument turns on the law's own internal logic, and John names Moses three times in this unit. Quotation-strength reference to Torah as institution rather than a single verse.

echoes.text: In the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.
echoes.note: 'On the Sabbath you circumcise a boy' (vv.22-23) rests on the law that a male child is circumcised 'on the eighth day,' which can fall on a Sabbath, overriding Sabbath rest. Leviticus 12:3 is the explicit eighth-day legislation Jesus reasons from a fortiori (if circumcision overrides Sabbath, how much more healing a whole man). High volume and coherence.

echoes.text: This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your seed after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin. It will be a token of the covenant between me and you. He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he who is born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your seed.
echoes.note: 'Moses has given you circumcision (not that it is of Moses, but of the fathers)' (v.22) corrects the attribution to the Abrahamic covenant, where God commands circumcision on the eighth day as the sign 'between me and you.' The patriarchal origin ('of the fathers') points precisely to Genesis 17, prior to Moses. Direct conceptual citation.

echoes.text: “‘You shall do no injustice in judgment. You shall not be partial to the poor, nor show favoritism to the great; but you shall judge your neighbor in righteousness.
echoes.note: 'Don't judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment' (v.24) echoes the Holiness Code's command, 'you shall do no injustice in judgment... in righteousness you shall judge your neighbor.' The pairing of forbidden partial judgment with commanded righteous judgment matches Leviticus closely. High coherence; the verse recurs as a juridical touchstone in this chapter (cf. vv.51).

echoes.text: I commanded your judges at that time, saying, “Hear cases between your brothers, and judge righteously between a man and his brother, and the foreigner who is living with him. You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall hear the small and the great alike. You shall not be afraid of the face of man, for the judgment is God’s. The case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me, and I will hear it.”
echoes.note: The charge to judges, 'judge righteously... you shall not be partial in judgment... you shall not be afraid of the face of man,' undergirds 'judge righteous judgment' (v.24) and anticipates Nicodemus' procedural appeal (v.51). Recurrence within the chapter strengthens the figural reading of impartial judgment. Verbal overlap is with the 'righteous judgment' idiom.

echoes.text: His delight will be in the fear of Yahweh. He will not judge by the sight of his eyes, neither decide by the hearing of his ears; but with righteousness he will judge the poor, and decide with equity for the humble of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth; and with the breath of his lips he will kill the wicked.
echoes.note: The messianic shoot 'shall not judge by what his eyes see... but with righteousness he shall judge' is the prophetic mirror of v.24's 'do not judge by appearance but judge righteous judgment.' Coherence with John's messianic theme (the crowd debating whether Jesus is the Christ) makes this more than coincidental, though John gives no citation formula. Contested as an unmarked echo.

echoes.text: “Thus has Yahweh of Armies spoken, saying, ‘Execute true judgment, and show kindness and compassion every man to his brother.
echoes.note: 'Render true judgment, show kindness and mercy' is one more prophetic locus for the impartial-justice ideal behind v.24. Volume is low and the contact is thematic rather than verbal, but Zechariah's prominence elsewhere in John 7 (rivers of living water) raises availability. Marked contested and low.

pericopes.text: Therefore some of them of Jerusalem said, “Isn’t this he whom they seek to kill? Behold, he speaks openly, and they say nothing to him. Can it be that the rulers indeed know that this is truly the Christ? However we know where this man comes from, but when the Christ comes, no one will know where he comes from.” Jesus therefore cried out in the temple, teaching and saying, “You both know me, and know where I am from. I have not come of myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you don’t know. I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me.” They sought therefore to take him; but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come. But of the multitude, many believed in him. They said, “When the Christ comes, he won’t do more signs than those which this man has done, will he?”

echoes.text: He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people?
echoes.note: 'When the Christ comes, no one will know where he comes from' (v.27) reflects a strand of expectation about the Messiah's hidden origin; Isaiah's 'as for his generation, who considered it?' was read in Second-Temple sources for the servant's obscure origin. The hiddenness motif coheres with John's irony that they know Jesus' earthly origin but not his heavenly one (vv.28-29). Contested and allusive.

echoes.text: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, being small among the clans of Judah, out of you one will come out to me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings out are from of old, from ancient times.
echoes.note: The popular belief about the Messiah's unknown origin (v.27) stands in tension with, and presupposes, the Bethlehem expectation made explicit at v.42. Micah's 'whose origins are from of old, from ancient days' could itself feed the 'no one will know where he comes from' tradition. Low volume here; the fuller Micah contact belongs to 7.6.

pericopes.text: The Pharisees heard the multitude murmuring these things concerning him, and the chief priests and the Pharisees sent officers to arrest him. Then Jesus said, “I will be with you a little while longer, then I go to him who sent me. You will seek me, and won’t find me; and where I am, you can’t come.” The Jews therefore said among themselves, “Where will this man go that we won’t find him? Will he go to the Dispersion among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks? What is this word that he said, ‘You will seek me, and won’t find me; and where I am, you can’t come’?”

echoes.text: But from there you shall seek Yahweh your God, and you shall find him, when you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul.
echoes.note: 'You will seek me, and won't find me' (v.34) inverts the Deuteronomic promise 'you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search with all your heart.' The reversal (seeking without finding) functions as covenantal judgment language. Volume and verbal contact are modest; marked contested.

echoes.text: Then will they call on me, but I will not answer. They will seek me diligently, but they will not find me;
echoes.note: 'They will seek me diligently but will not find me' is Wisdom's verdict on those who spurned her, closely matching 'you will seek me, and won't find me' (v.34). The Wisdom-Christology of John (incarnate Logos withdrawing) gives strong coherence, and the verbal parallel is tight. The unmarked allusion fits John's pattern of figural Wisdom motifs.

echoes.text: They will go with their flocks and with their herds to seek Yahweh; but they won’t find him. He has withdrawn himself from them.
echoes.note: 'They shall go to seek the LORD, but they will not find him; he has withdrawn from them' parallels the seek-but-not-find judgment of v.34. Hosea casts it as God hiding because of unfaithfulness, coherent with the crowd's unbelief. Low volume, offered as an alternate prophetic source.

echoes.text: He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
echoes.note: 'Will he go to the Dispersion among the Greeks?' (v.35) ironically gestures toward the prophetic ingathering of the scattered, where the messianic root 'gathers the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.' John's irony (the mission to the Greeks the speakers mock) coheres with the Diaspora-ingathering hope. Contested, thematic.

pericopes.text: Now on the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink! He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.” But he said this about the Spirit, which those believing in him were to receive. For the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus wasn’t yet glorified.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day, that living waters will go out from Jerusalem; half of them toward the eastern sea, and half of them toward the western sea; in summer and in winter will it be.
echoes.note: 'From within him will flow rivers of living water' (v.38), declared 'on the last and greatest day' of Booths, draws on Zechariah's eschatological vision read at the feast: 'living waters shall flow out from Jerusalem.' Zechariah 14 is the Tabernacles lectionary, explicitly naming the feast (14:16-19), giving maximal availability and coherence. This is the spine of John's water typology here.

echoes.text: He brought me back to the door of the house; and behold, waters issued out from under the threshold of the house eastward; (for the forefront of the house was toward the east;) and the waters came down from under, from the right side of the house, on the south of the altar. Then he brought me out by the way of the gate northward, and led me round by the way outside to the outer gate, by the way of the gate that looks toward the east; and behold, there ran […]
echoes.note: The temple-river vision, water flowing from beneath the threshold and swelling into a life-giving river, supplies the 'rivers of living water' imagery flowing from the new temple (Jesus/the believer). High volume and coherence: John casts Jesus' body as the eschatological temple source. The plural 'rivers' and life-giving flow match Ezekiel's swelling stream.

echoes.text: He split rocks in the wilderness, and gave them drink abundantly as out of the depths. He brought streams also out of the rock, and caused waters to run down like rivers.
echoes.note: 'He split the rocks in the wilderness... brought streams out of the rock and caused waters to run down like rivers' is the wilderness water-from-the-rock typology underlying 'rivers of living water' at the water-libation feast. Booths commemorated wilderness dwelling; the rock-water gift is the natural figural source. The verbal 'rivers' (potamous) coheres with John's plural.

echoes.text: Moses lifted up his hand, and struck the rock with his rod twice, and water came out abundantly. The congregation and their livestock drank.
echoes.note: Moses striking the rock so that 'water came out abundantly' is the foundational wilderness rock-water event behind v.38, tied to Booths' commemoration of the wilderness sojourn and its water-pouring rite. Coherence is strong; offered alongside Exodus 17:6 as the source-event for the rock typology. Medium because the contact is mediated through the Psalm/feast tradition.

echoes.text: and Yahweh will guide you continually, and satisfy your soul in dry places, and make strong your bones; and you shall be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters don’t fail.
echoes.note: 'You shall be like a watered garden, like a spring of water whose waters do not fail' supplies the image of the believer as an unfailing inward source ('from within him will flow'), matching the interiority of v.38. Isaiah's spring-that-fails-not coheres with the Spirit's permanence (v.39). A plausible component of John's composite scriptural citation.

echoes.text: For I will pour water on him who is thirsty, and streams on the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit on your seed, and my blessing on your offspring:
echoes.note: 'I will pour water on the thirsty land... I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring' directly joins water-outpouring to Spirit-giving, exactly the move John makes when he glosses the living water as 'the Spirit' (v.39). The water/Spirit equation gives strong coherence and supplies the interpretive key John attaches to the saying. High confidence as a Spirit-water source.

echoes.text: Therefore with joy you will draw water out of the wells of salvation.
echoes.note: 'With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation' was the text sung at the Tabernacles water-libation (the Hallel/water-drawing rite). The festal water-drawing ceremony is precisely the backdrop of Jesus' invitation 'if anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink' (v.37). Coherence with the liturgical setting is high; verbal contact moderate.

echoes.text: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
echoes.note: 'Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters' is the closest invitation-formula to v.37, 'if anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink.' The thirst-come-drink structure and free offer match. John re-voices the prophetic summons with Jesus as the water-giver; medium confidence as an unmarked but strongly parallel allusion.

echoes.text: The words of a man’s mouth are like deep waters. The fountain of wisdom is like a flowing brook.
echoes.note: 'The words of a man's mouth are deep waters; the fountain of wisdom is a flowing stream' may feed the 'rivers of living water... from within him' image, linking inner source to wisdom/teaching. Low volume, offered because John's living-water motif elsewhere blends Wisdom and Spirit. Contested.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.
echoes.note: 'I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh' grounds v.39's note that the Spirit 'was not yet given,' since the prophetic Spirit-outpouring awaited the eschaton. The pouring-out language coheres with the water imagery and explains the deferral until Jesus is glorified. Medium as background to the editorial Spirit comment.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day, that the mountains will drop down sweet wine, the hills will flow with milk, all the brooks of Judah will flow with waters, and a fountain will flow out from Yahweh’s house, and will water the valley of Shittim.
echoes.note: 'A fountain shall come forth from the house of the LORD' joins the Zechariah/Ezekiel temple-spring cluster behind the 'rivers of living water.' Joel's fountain from the temple coheres with Jesus as the eschatological temple-source on the feast day. Offered as a recurrent member of the temple-river tradition John draws on.

pericopes.text: Many of the multitude therefore, when they heard these words, said, “This is truly the prophet.” Others said, “This is the Christ.” But some said, “What, does the Christ come out of Galilee? Hasn’t the Scripture said that the Christ comes of the seed of David, and from Bethlehem, the village where David was?” So there arose a division in the multitude because of him. Some of them would have arrested him, but no one laid hands on him.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: 'This is truly the prophet' (v.40) names the eschatological prophet-like-Moses God promised to raise up, 'to him you shall listen.' Booths' Mosaic/wilderness setting and Jesus' Moses-discourse earlier (vv.19-23) make the Deuteronomic prophet the precise referent. High coherence and recurrence of the prophet motif in John (cf. 1:21, 6:14).

echoes.text: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, being small among the clans of Judah, out of you one will come out to me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings out are from of old, from ancient times.
echoes.note: 'The Christ comes... from Bethlehem, the village where David was' (v.42) reflects the scribal reading of Micah, 'But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah... from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel.' John presents the crowd citing Scripture ('Hasn't the Scripture said'), the nearest thing to a formal quotation in the chapter. Maximal volume and availability.

echoes.text: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom.
echoes.note: 'The Christ comes of the seed of David' (v.42) invokes the Davidic covenant, 'I will raise up your offspring after you... and I will establish his kingdom.' The 'seed of David' formula is the covenantal root of messianic expectation the crowd recites. Strong coherence with the Bethlehem-of-David clause and the whole is-this-the-Christ debate.

echoes.text: “I have made a covenant with my chosen one, I have sworn to David, my servant, ‘I will establish your seed forever, and build up your throne to all generations.’” Selah.
echoes.note: 'I have made a covenant with my chosen one... I will establish your offspring forever' restates the Davidic 'seed' promise behind v.42. The psalm's covenant-with-David vocabulary reinforces the 'seed of David' expectation; medium because 2 Samuel 7 is the more direct source. Recurrence of the Davidic-seed theme raises coherence.

echoes.text: Yahweh has sworn to David in truth. He will not turn from it: “I will set the fruit of your body on your throne.
echoes.note: 'The LORD swore to David... one of the fruit of your body I will set on your throne' is another locus of the Davidic-seed oath underlying 'the seed of David' (v.42). The Bethlehem/David pairing coheres with the throne-promise. Offered as a member of the Davidic-covenant cluster the crowd's scriptural objection presupposes.

pericopes.text: The officers therefore came to the chief priests and Pharisees, and they said to them, “Why didn’t you bring him?” The officers answered, “No man ever spoke like this man!” The Pharisees therefore answered them, “You aren’t also led astray, are you? Have any of the rulers believed in him, or of the Pharisees? But this multitude that doesn’t know the law is accursed.” Nicodemus (he who came to him by night, being one of them) said to them, “Does our law judge a man, unless it first hears from him personally and knows what he does?” They answered him, “Are you also from Galilee? Search, and see that no prophet has arisen out of Galilee.” Everyone went to his own house,

echoes.text: I commanded your judges at that time, saying, “Hear cases between your brothers, and judge righteously between a man and his brother, and the foreigner who is living with him. You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall hear the small and the great alike. You shall not be afraid of the face of man, for the judgment is God’s. The case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me, and I will hear it.”
echoes.note: Nicodemus' 'Does our law judge a man, unless it first hears from him personally?' (v.51) applies the Mosaic charge to judges, 'hear the cases between your brothers and judge righteously... you shall not be partial.' The duty to hear a party before condemning is the procedural core of the Deuteronomic judicial code. High coherence with the chapter's 'judge righteous judgment' (v.24).

echoes.text: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established. If an unrighteous witness rises up against any man to testify against him of wrongdoing, then both the men, between whom the controversy is, shall stand before Yahweh, before the priests and the judges who shall be in those days; and the judges shall make […]
echoes.note: Nicodemus' appeal to due process (v.51) reflects the law of inquiry and witnesses, where judges 'shall inquire diligently' and a matter is established only after examination. The insistence that the law not condemn without first hearing the accused matches the diligent-inquiry requirement. Strong verbal-conceptual contact and recurrence of the fair-hearing theme.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: 'No prophet has arisen out of Galilee' (v.52) is John's irony against the very prophet-like-Moses expectation (v.40); the Pharisees deny on geographical grounds what Scripture and Jonah (a Galilean prophet) would unsettle. The prophet motif from Deuteronomy frames the dismissal as mistaken. Medium; functions through dramatic irony rather than citation.

echoes.text: But there shall be no more gloom for her who was in anguish. In the former time, he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali; but in the latter time he has made it glorious, by the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.
echoes.note: 'Search, and see that no prophet has arisen out of Galilee' (v.52) is ironized by Isaiah's prophecy that 'Galilee of the nations' would see a great light — a messianic dawn from the despised region. John's reader hears the Pharisees contradicting Scripture's own honoring of Galilee. Low volume and unmarked; offered as the corrective subtext.

pericopes.text: but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. Now very early in the morning, he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him. He sat down, and taught them. The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman taken in adultery. Having set her in the midst, they told him, “Teacher, we found this woman in adultery, in the very act. Now in our law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. What then do you say about her?” They said this testing him, that they might have something to accuse him of. But Jesus stooped down, and wrote on the ground with his finger. But when they continued asking him, he looked up and said to them, “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her.” Again he stooped down, and with his finger wrote on the ground. They, when they heard it, being convicted by their conscience, went out one by one, beginning from the oldest, even to the last. Jesus was left alone with the woman where she was, in the middle. Jesus, standing up, saw her and said, “Woman, where are your accusers? Did no one condemn you?” She said, “No one, Lord.” Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.”

echoes.text: “‘The man who commits adultery with another man’s wife, even he who commits adultery with his neighbor’s wife, the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death.
echoes.note: The accusers' charge presupposes the Holiness Code's death sentence for adultery, which Leviticus prescribes for both parties. High Volume and Coherence: the scene is staged as a halakhic test about applying exactly this statute, and the conspicuous absence of the male partner exposes the accusers' selective use of the law.

echoes.text: If a man is found lying with a woman married to a husband, then they shall both die, the man who lay with the woman and the woman. So you shall remove the evil from Israel. If there is a young lady who is a virgin pledged to be married to a husband, and a man finds her in the city, and lies with her; then you shall bring them both out to the gate of that city, and you shall stone them to death with stones; the lady, because she didn’t cry, being in the […]
echoes.note: The specific penalty of stoning (rather than unspecified execution) for a betrothed woman taken in adultery supplies the legal frame the Pharisees invoke when they say Moses commanded stoning. High Coherence with their wording; the citation of 'Moses commanded us to stone' points to the Deuteronomic form of the law.

echoes.text: The hand of the witnesses shall be first on him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. So you shall remove the evil from your midst.
echoes.note: Jesus' 'let him who is without sin throw the first stone' reworks the rule that the hands of the witnesses shall be first against the condemned to put away evil. High Coherence: Jesus accepts the procedure but disqualifies the witnesses morally rather than legally, turning the witness-stone rule back on the accusers.

echoes.text: but you shall surely kill him. Your hand shall be first on him to put him to death, and afterwards the hands of all the people.
echoes.note: The parallel statute that the informer's hand shall be first to execute reinforces the witness-first-stone tradition behind v.7. Lower Volume than 17:7 but the same legal motif; Recurrence within Deuteronomy strengthens that the 'first stone' formula is the intended backdrop.

echoes.text: “You shall not spread a false report. Don’t join your hand with the wicked to be a malicious witness.
echoes.note: The prohibition of joining hands with a wicked man as a malicious witness illumines the narrator's note that they spoke 'testing him, that they might accuse him.' Moderate Coherence: the accusers function as the malicious witnesses the law forbids, an irony built on this statute.

echoes.text: “Keep far from a false charge, and don’t kill the innocent and righteous: for I will not justify the wicked.
echoes.note: 'Keep far from a false charge, and do not kill the innocent' coheres with Jesus' refusal to condemn and with exposing the accusers' bad faith. Contested because the verbal contact is thematic rather than lexical, but the coherence with the pericope's concern for unjust killing is strong.

echoes.text: A man lived in Babylon, and his name was Joakim: and he took a wife, whose name was Susanna, the daughter of Helkias, a very fair woman, and one that feared the Lord. Her parents also were righteous, and taught their daughter according to the law of Moses. Now Joakim was a great rich man, and had a fair garden joining to his house: and to him resorted the Jews; because he was more honorable than all others. And the same year there were appointed two of […]
echoes.note: The Susanna narrative (Greek Daniel) is the closest Second-Temple analogue: a wise judge intervenes in a capital adultery accusation, tests and discredits the accusers, and saves the accused. High Coherence and Availability; the figural pattern of a Daniel-like discerner overturning a rigged witness procedure plausibly shapes the scene, though direct dependence is debated.

echoes.text: Yahweh, the hope of Israel, all who forsake you shall be disappointed. Those who depart from me shall be written in the earth, because they have forsaken Yahweh, the spring of living waters.
echoes.note: Jesus' twice-noted writing on the ground may evoke 'those who turn away from you shall be written in the earth, for they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living water.' Coherence with John's living-water theme is suggestive, but the gesture is unexplained in the text and the link remains a classic patristic conjecture.

echoes.text: He gave to Moses, when he finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, stone tablets, written with God’s finger.
echoes.note: The detail that Jesus wrote 'with his finger' may recall the finger of God inscribing the tablets of the law, casting the lawgiver writing afresh over against those who wield Moses' law. Low Volume and contested; the verbal hook ('finger,' 'wrote') is real but the application is speculative.

echoes.text: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.
echoes.note: The two-or-three-witness requirement hovers over a scene where the accusers withdraw one by one until no valid witness remains to condemn. Faint here and developed explicitly in 8:17; flagged for Recurrence across the chapter rather than strong presence in this pericope.

pericopes.text: Again, therefore, Jesus spoke to them, saying, “I am the light of the world.He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.” The Pharisees therefore said to him, “You testify about yourself. Your testimony is not valid.” Jesus answered them, “Even if I testify about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I came from, and where I am going; but you don’t know where I came from, or where I am going. You judge according to the flesh. I judge no one. Even if I do judge, my judgment is true, for I am not alone, but I am with the Father who sent me. It’s also written in your law that the testimony of two people is valid. I am one who testifies about myself, and the Father who sent me testifies about me.” They said therefore to him, “Where is your Father?” Jesus answered, “You know neither me, nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also.” Jesus spoke these words in the treasury, as he taught in the temple. Yet no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come.

echoes.text: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.
echoes.note: 'I am the light of the world... will have the light of life' draws on the people who walked in darkness seeing a great light. High Volume in the light/darkness antithesis and strong Coherence with John's prologue light theme; Isaiah's dawning light on those in the land of deep darkness is a primary source for Johannine light Christology.

echoes.text: “I, Yahweh, have called you in righteousness, and will hold your hand, and will keep you, and make you a covenant for the people, as a light for the nations; to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.
echoes.note: The Servant given as 'a light to the nations' to open blind eyes underwrites the universal scope of 'light of the world.' High Coherence: John repeatedly casts Jesus in Servant terms, and the worldwide reach of the light matches Isaiah's covenant-to-the-peoples commission.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: 'I will give you as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth' supplies the 'of the world' scope of Jesus' claim. High Recurrence with 42:6 and strong Coherence with John's mission to gather scattered children of God.

echoes.text: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.
echoes.note: 'Arise, shine, for your light has come... nations shall come to your light' frames the eschatological light to which peoples are drawn. High Coherence with the Tabernacles setting and with Jesus as the light that the world follows; the procession-to-the-light image matches 'he who follows me.'

echoes.text: Yahweh went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, to lead them on their way, and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light, that they might go by day and by night:
echoes.note: The pillar of fire that led Israel by night so they could walk is the exodus type behind 'he who follows me will not walk in darkness but have the light of life.' High Coherence given the Tabernacles temple-lamp ceremony commemorating wilderness guidance; Jesus presents himself as the guiding light-presence for a new exodus.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? Yahweh is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid?
echoes.note: 'The LORD is my light and my salvation' lends the divine self-designation Jesus appropriates. Moderate Volume; Coherence is strong because John's 'I am' light-claim takes up a predicate Scripture reserves for the LORD, reinforcing the chapter's high Christology.

echoes.text: For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, And an unspotted mirror of the working of God, And an image of his goodness.
echoes.note: Wisdom as 'a reflection of eternal light' and unspotted mirror of God supplies Second-Temple Wisdom-light language close to John's incarnate Logos-light. Good Availability and Coherence with Johannine Wisdom Christology, though the link is conceptual rather than verbal.

echoes.text: It will be a unique day which is known to Yahweh; not day, and not night; but it will come to pass, that at evening time there will be light.
echoes.note: Zechariah's Tabernacles-day vision of continuous light ('at evening time there shall be light'), read liturgically at the feast, situates Jesus' light-claim within the festival's eschatological imagery. Moderate Coherence with the temple setting of v.20.

echoes.text: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.
echoes.note: 'Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path' links walking, word, and light, themes that converge in the pericope. Low Volume and contested; offered for the walking-by-light motif rather than a distinct source.

echoes.text: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.
echoes.note: 'It is written in your law that the testimony of two people is true' explicitly cites the two-or-three-witness statute. High Volume (near-quotation) and total Coherence; Jesus appeals to this rule to count himself and the Father as the two valid witnesses.

echoes.text: At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, he who is to die shall be put to death. At the mouth of one witness he shall not be put to death.
echoes.note: The parallel formulation that a matter is established on the evidence of two or three witnesses reinforces the law Jesus cites in v.17. Recurrence within Deuteronomy strengthens the witness-law backdrop; slightly lower Volume than 19:15.

echoes.text: “‘Whoever kills any person, the murderer shall be slain at the mouth of witnesses; but one witness shall not testify against any person that he die.
echoes.note: The capital-case rule requiring multiple witnesses extends the legal field Jesus invokes. Low Volume; included for Recurrence of the witness statute across the Pentateuch rather than as a primary source.

pericopes.text: Jesus said therefore again to them, “I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sins. Where I go, you can’t come.” The Jews therefore said, “Will he kill himself, that he says, ‘Where I am going, you can’t come’?” He said to them, “You are from beneath. I am from above. You are of this world. I am not of this world. I said therefore to you that you will die in your sins; for unless you believe that I amhe, you will die in your sins.” They said therefore to him, “Who are you?” Jesus said to them, “Just what I have been saying to you from the beginning. I have many things to speak and to judge concerning you. However he who sent me is true; and the things which I heard from him, these I say to the world.” They didn’t understand that he spoke to them about the Father. Jesus therefore said to them, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and I do nothing of myself, but as my Father taught me, I say these things. He who sent me is with me. The Father hasn’t left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him.” As he spoke these things, many believed in him.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”
echoes.note: 'Unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins' and 'then you will know that I am he' deploy the absolute egō eimi rooted in God's self-revelation 'I AM WHO I AM.' High Coherence with the chapter's climactic I AM in v.58; Jesus appropriates the divine Name as the object of saving faith.

echoes.text: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me.
echoes.note: 'That you may know and believe me and understand that I am he' (LXX hina pisteusēte... hoti egō eimi) supplies the exact 'believe that I am he' construction of v.24,28. High Volume and Coherence; Isaiah's courtroom of witnesses for the one God matches John's witness theme and 'I am he' formula.

echoes.text: Who has worked and done it, calling the generations from the beginning? I, Yahweh, the first, and with the last, I am he.”
echoes.note: 'I, the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he' (egō eimi) furnishes the same self-predication tied to God's sovereignty over the generations. Recurrence with 43:10 strengthens the case that John draws the absolute 'I am he' from Deutero-Isaiah's monotheistic self-declarations.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
echoes.note: 'My servant shall be exalted and lifted up' undergirds 'when you have lifted up the Son of Man.' John's double-meaning of hypsoō (crucifixion/exaltation) coheres tightly with Isaiah's Servant who is lifted up; moderate Volume but high thematic Coherence.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Make a fiery serpent, and set it on a pole. It shall happen, that everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live.” Moses made a serpent of brass, and set it on the pole. If a serpent had bitten any man, when he looked at the serpent of brass, he lived.
echoes.note: The bronze serpent lifted on a pole so that those who look live is the lifting-up type John established in 3:14 and recalls here with 'lifted up the Son of Man.' Recurrence across John and Coherence of the look-and-live/lift-and-know pattern support a figural reading.

echoes.text: When I tell the wicked, You shall surely die; and you give him no warning, nor speak to warn the wicked from his wicked way, to save his life; the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at your hand.
echoes.note: 'You will die in your sins' echoes Ezekiel's watchman warning that the wicked 'shall die in his iniquity' if unwarned. Moderate Coherence: John uses the prophetic death-in-sin formula for those who reject the light, and Ezekiel is its densest source.

echoes.text: As for his father, because he cruelly oppressed, robbed his brother, and did that which is not good among his people, behold, he shall die in his iniquity.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's repeated 'he shall die in his iniquity' for the unrepentant strengthens the prophetic background of 'die in your sins.' Lower Volume than 3:18; included for Recurrence of the formula within Ezekiel.

echoes.text: Then will they call on me, but I will not answer. They will seek me diligently, but they will not find me;
echoes.note: 'You will seek me and not find me; where I am going you cannot come' resonates with Wisdom's warning that those who refused her 'will seek me diligently but will not find me.' Faint and contested, but the seek-but-not-find judgment pattern coheres with Johannine Wisdom Christology.

pericopes.text: Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him, “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” They answered him, “We are Abraham’s seed, and have never been in bondage to anyone. How do you say, ‘You will be made free’?” Jesus answered them, “Most certainly I tell you, everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin. A bondservant doesn’t live in the house forever. A son remains forever. If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed. I know that you are Abraham’s seed, yet you seek to kill me, because my word finds no place in you. I say the things which I have seen with my Father; and you also do the things which you have seen with your father.” They answered him, “Our father is Abraham.” Jesus said to them, “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth, which I heard from God. Abraham didn’t do this. You do the works of your father.” They said to him, “We were not born of sexual immorality. We have one Father, God.” Therefore Jesus said to them, “If God were your father, you would love me, for I came out and have come from God. For I haven’t come of myself, but he sent me. Why don’t you understand my speech? Because you can’t hear my word. You are of your father, the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning, and doesn’t stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks on his own; for he is a liar, and its father. But because I tell the truth, you don’t believe me. Which of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me? He who is of God hears the words of God. For this cause you don’t hear, because you are not of God.”

echoes.text: that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your seed greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore. Your seed will possess the gate of his enemies.
echoes.note: The dispute turns on being 'Abraham's seed,' invoking the patriarchal promise that Abraham's offspring would be multiplied. High Coherence: Jesus concedes physical descent (sperma) but redefines true sonship by deeds, pressing the gap between biological seed and genuine children of Abraham.

echoes.text: Therefore she said to Abraham, “Cast out this handmaid and her son! For the son of this handmaid will not be heir with my son, Isaac.”
echoes.note: 'A slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever' alludes to Sarah's demand that the slave woman's son not inherit with the free son, the Isaac/Ishmael household division. High Coherence; the slave-vs-son contrast that grounds Jesus' freedom argument is drawn from this Genesis scene of casting out the bondservant.

echoes.text: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you. All of the families of the earth will be blessed in you.”
echoes.note: The Abrahamic blessing-to-the-nations promise underlies the claim to do 'the works of Abraham,' i.e., faith-hospitality toward God's messenger rather than murder. Moderate Coherence; Abraham's welcome of divine visitors stands behind 'you would do the works of Abraham.'

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]
echoes.note: Abraham's hospitable reception of the LORD and his angels at Mamre exemplifies 'the works of Abraham' that the hostile interlocutors fail to imitate by seeking to kill Jesus. Coherence is good in Jewish exegesis that paired Abraham's welcome with his descendants' murderous rejection of prophets.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely […]
echoes.note: 'You are of your father the devil... a liar and the father of lies' reads the Eden serpent's deceit as the devil's primal lie that brought death. High Coherence: the murderer-from-the-beginning and liar-from-the-beginning charges fuse the serpent's deception with the death it caused, the dominant Second-Temple reading of Genesis 3.

echoes.text: Cain said to Abel, his brother, “Let’s go into the field.” While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him.
echoes.note: 'A murderer from the beginning' likely also evokes Cain's killing of Abel, the first human murder, traditionally traced to the devil's influence (cf. 1 John 3:12, but the OT base is Genesis 4). Moderate Coherence with 'you seek to kill me,' aligning the accusers with the archetypal fratricide.

echoes.text: But by the envy of the devil death entered into the world, And those who are of his portion make trial thereof.
echoes.note: 'Through the devil's envy death entered the world' is the clearest Second-Temple bridge interpreting Genesis 3 as the devil being a murderer from the beginning. High Availability and Coherence; this verse supplies precisely the devil-as-death-bringer logic John's charge presupposes.

echoes.text: When Yahweh spoke at first by Hosea, Yahweh said to Hosea, “Go, take for yourself a wife of prostitution and children of unfaithfulness; for the land commits great adultery, forsaking Yahweh.”
echoes.note: 'We were not born of sexual immorality' (porneia) may carry the prophetic charge that idolatrous Israel was born of harlotry; the interlocutors deny the very status the prophets assigned faithless Israel. Faint and contested, offered for the figural irony of the porneia denial.

pericopes.text: Then the Jews answered him, “Don’t we say well that you are a Samaritan, and have a demon?” Jesus answered, “I don’t have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me. But I don’t seek my own glory. There is one who seeks and judges. Most certainly, I tell you, if a person keeps my word, he will never see death.” Then the Jews said to him, “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and the prophets; and you say, ‘If a man keeps my word, he will never taste of death.’ Are you greater than our father, Abraham, who died? The prophets died. Who do you make yourself out to be?” Jesus answered, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say that he is our God. You have not known him, but I know him. If I said, ‘I don’t know him,’ I would be like you, a liar. But I know him, and keep his word. Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day. He saw it, and was glad.” The Jews therefore said to him, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” Jesus said to them, “Most certainly, I tell you, before Abraham came into existence, I AM.” Therefore they took up stones to throw at him, but Jesus was hidden, and went out of the temple, having gone through their midst, and so passed by.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”
echoes.note: 'Before Abraham came into existence, I AM' (egō eimi) climactically claims the divine Name revealed at the burning bush, asserting timeless self-existence over against Abraham's createdness. Highest Volume of the chapter and total Coherence; the immediate attempt to stone him for blasphemy confirms the hearers grasped a divine self-identification.

echoes.text: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me. I myself am Yahweh; and besides me there is no savior. I have declared, I have saved, and I have shown; and there was no strange god among you. Therefore you are my witnesses”, says Yahweh, “and I am God. Yes, since the day was I am he; and there is no […]
echoes.note: Deutero-Isaiah's 'I am he... before me no god was formed... I am God, and also henceforth I am he' provides the absolute, eternal egō eimi that v.58 enacts. High Coherence and Recurrence (also behind 8:24,28); John draws the unqualified I AM from Isaiah's monotheistic self-declarations.

echoes.text: Who has worked and done it, calling the generations from the beginning? I, Yahweh, the first, and with the last, I am he.”
echoes.note: 'Who has performed this... calling the generations from the beginning? I, the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he' supplies the over-the-generations claim implicit in standing before Abraham. Moderate Volume; reinforces the Isaianic I AM backdrop.

echoes.text: Then Abraham fell on his face, and laughed, and said in his heart, “Will a child be born to him who is one hundred years old? Will Sarah, who is ninety years old, give birth?”
echoes.note: 'Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day' connects to Abraham's laughter/rejoicing at the promise of Isaac, read in Jewish tradition as joy over the messianic future. Moderate Coherence; the verb of rejoicing and the forward-looking 'day' are anchored in the covenant-promise scenes of Abraham.

echoes.text: After these things, God tested Abraham, and said to him, “Abraham!” He said, “Here I am.” He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.” Abraham rose early in the morning, and saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son. He split the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and […]
echoes.note: The Aqedah, where Abraham 'saw the place afar off' and named the mount 'the LORD will provide/be seen,' was widely read as Abraham foreseeing the day of deliverance, illuminating 'he saw it and was glad.' Good Availability in Second-Temple Abraham traditions and Coherence with Abraham's prophetic sight.

echoes.text: He who blasphemes Yahweh’s name, he shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall certainly stone him. The foreigner as well as the native-born, when he blasphemes the Name, shall be put to death.
echoes.note: 'They took up stones to throw at him' enacts the statute that one who blasphemes the Name shall be stoned by all the congregation. High Coherence: the stoning response directly judges Jesus' I AM as blasphemous use of the divine Name, so the law of Leviticus 24 is the operative legal backdrop.

echoes.text: Before the mountains were born, before you had formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, you are God.
echoes.note: 'Before the mountains were brought forth... from everlasting to everlasting you are God' parallels the pre-Abrahamic eternity asserted in v.58. Low Volume and verbal contact, but coheres with the claim to existence prior to creation/patriarch.

echoes.text: What man is he who shall live and not see death, who shall deliver his soul from the power of Sheol? Selah.
echoes.note: 'What man can live and never see death?' frames the dispute over Jesus' promise that one who keeps his word 'will never see death,' which the hearers measure against Abraham's death. Faint; offered for the see/taste-death motif rather than as a primary source.

echoes.text: “Look among the nations, watch, and wonder marvelously; for I am working a work in your days, which you will not believe though it is told you.
echoes.note: The prophets dying yet the patriarch's hope of seeing God's 'day' resonates faintly with prophetic 'in your days' announcements of a work to be marveled at. Highly contested and low Volume; included only for maximal coverage of the 'see my day' language.
echoes.lxxText: Behold, ye despisers, and look, and wonder marvelously, and vanish: for I work a work in your days, which ye will in no wise believe, though a man declare it to you.

pericopes.text: As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. His disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” Jesus answered, “Neither did this man sin, nor his parents; but, that the works of God might be revealed in him. I must work the works of him who sent me, while it is day. The night is coming, when no one can work. While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.”

echoes.text: you shall not bow yourself down to them, nor serve them, for I, Yahweh your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, on the third and on the fourth generation of those who hate me,
echoes.note: The disciples' question 'who sinned, this man or his parents' presupposes the Decalogue principle of God visiting the iniquity of fathers upon children. The transgenerational logic is precisely what is at issue; Volume is moderate and Coherence high, since Johannine sin-theology engages the retribution framework only to overturn it.

echoes.text: The soul who sins, he shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be on him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be on him.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's countervailing principle that 'the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father' frames the very debate the disciples raise. Jesus' answer ('neither did this man sin, nor his parents') aligns with Ezekiel's repudiation of inherited guilt, making this a coherent and available Second-Temple intertext.

echoes.text: “Remember, now, whoever perished, being innocent? Or where were the upright cut off?
echoes.note: The friends' assumption that suffering proves prior sin (Eliphaz: 'who ever perished, being innocent?') is the wisdom-debate background to the disciples' question. Job as a whole resists the suffering-equals-sin calculus; the echo is thematic and diffuse rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to him, “Who made man’s mouth? Or who makes one mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Isn’t it I, Yahweh?
echoes.note: YHWH to Moses: 'Who makes a man dumb or deaf, or seeing or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?' This grounds blindness in God's sovereign purpose, exactly Jesus' reframing ('that the works of God might be revealed'). Coherence is high since the giver of sight here becomes incarnate as the light-bringer.

echoes.text: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.
echoes.note: 'I am the light of the world' resonates with Zion's eschatological illumination where YHWH's light shines on a darkened earth. The light-of-the-nations motif is available and coherent with John's worldwide scope, though no verbal citation links them.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? Yahweh is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid?
echoes.note: 'The LORD is my light and my salvation' supplies a scriptural backdrop for Jesus' self-identification as light, especially apposite as a blind man is about to receive sight/salvation. The echo is conceptual; Volume is low and many candidates compete.

pericopes.text: When he had said this, he spat on the ground, made mud with the saliva, anointed the blind man’s eyes with the mud, and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means “Sent”). So he went away, washed, and came back seeing.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: Jesus forms mud from spittle and the ground and applies it to make eyes whole, evoking the Creator forming the man from the dust of the ground. The clay-and-creation figure casts the healing as a new-creation act by the agent of Genesis 1's 'let there be light'; Coherence with the light-of-the-world saying is strong.

echoes.text: By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”
echoes.note: The 'ground/dust' material of the healing recalls the adamic dust to which humanity belongs. The reversal — dust here restores rather than condemns — supports a new-creation reading, though the link rides on the same Genesis 2-3 imagery as the stronger 2:7 echo.

echoes.text: “Because this people have refused the waters of Shiloah that go softly, and rejoice in Rezin and Remaliah’s son;
echoes.note: John glosses Siloam as 'Sent,' and the pool's name derives from the gently-flowing 'waters of Shiloah' that Judah despised in Isaiah 8:6. The deliberate etymological note signals figural intent: the rejected waters become the means of sight, and 'Sent' identifies Jesus as the one sent by the Father. High Volume via the explicit gloss.

echoes.text: The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs. To him will the obedience of the peoples be.
echoes.note: The Hebrew 'Shiloh' ('until Shiloh comes') was read messianically in Second-Temple tradition and shares the consonantal root behind Siloam/'Sent.' John's 'Sent One' Christology may exploit this resonance, but the linguistic bridge is contested and the gloss more naturally targets Isaiah's Shiloah.

echoes.text: Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying, “Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh shall come again to you, and you shall be clean.”
echoes.note: 'Go, wash' in a specific body of water and be made whole closely patterns Elisha's command to Naaman to wash in the Jordan and be cleansed. The prophetic-healing-by-washing type, with obedience producing restoration, is coherent and the man's later confession that Jesus is 'a prophet' reinforces the Elijah/Elisha matrix.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.
echoes.note: 'Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened' is the eschatological sign of God's coming; the actual opening of a blind man's eyes enacts it. The healing is a programmatic fulfillment-sign, and John repeatedly frames Jesus' works as the dawning of the promised age. High Coherence and Recurrence across Isaiah's sight oracles.

pericopes.text: The neighbors therefore, and those who saw that he was blind before, said, “Isn’t this he who sat and begged?” Others were saying, “It is he.” Still others were saying, “He looks like him.” He said, “I am he.” They therefore were asking him, “How were your eyes opened?” He answered, “A man called Jesus made mud, anointed my eyes, and said to me, ‘Go to the pool of Siloam, and wash.’ So I went away and washed, and I received sight.” Then they asked him, “Where is he?” He said, “I don’t know.”

echoes.text: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.
echoes.note: 'In that day...the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity' supplies the eschatological frame as neighbors marvel that the beggar now sees. The pericope is largely narrative dialogue, so the echo is ambient rather than pointed, carried over from the healing itself.

pericopes.text: They brought him who had been blind to the Pharisees. It was a Sabbath when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes. Again therefore the Pharisees also asked him how he received his sight. He said to them, “He put mud on my eyes, I washed, and I see.” Some therefore of the Pharisees said, “This man is not from God, because he doesn’t keep the Sabbath.” Others said, “How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?” There was division among them. Therefore they asked the blind man again, “What do you say about him, because he opened your eyes?” He said, “He is a prophet.”

echoes.text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
echoes.note: The conflict turns on Jesus 'making mud' and healing on the Sabbath, engaging the Decalogue's Sabbath command and its later halakhic elaborations (kneading clay was forbidden work). The Sabbath statute is the legal axis of the Pharisees' charge that Jesus is 'not from God.'

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: The healed man's verdict 'He is a prophet' invokes the Mosaic promise of a prophet like Moses whom Israel must heed. John develops the prophet-like-Moses Christology, and the sign-working healer fits the criterion of the true prophet; Coherence with John's wider Moses typology is strong.

pericopes.text: The Jews therefore did not believe concerning him, that he had been blind, and had received his sight, until they called the parents of him who had received his sight, and asked them, “Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? How then does he now see?” His parents answered them, “We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind; but how he now sees, we don’t know; or who opened his eyes, we don’t know. He is of age. Ask him. He will speak for himself.” His parents said these things because they feared the Jews; for the Jews had already agreed that if any man would confess him as Christ, he would be put out of the synagogue. Therefore his parents said, “He is of age. Ask him.”

echoes.text: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.
echoes.note: The interrogation of the parents to corroborate the son's testimony reflects the Torah's two-or-three-witnesses requirement that governs Johannine 'witness' motifs. The link is structural/legal rather than verbal, and the courtroom framing is broadly Deuteronomic.

pericopes.text: So they called the man who was blind a second time, and said to him, “Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.” He therefore answered, “I don’t know if he is a sinner. One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see.” They said to him again, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?” He answered them, “I told you already, and you didn’t listen. Why do you want to hear it again? You don’t also want to become his disciples, do you?” They insulted him and said, “You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God has spoken to Moses. But as for this man, we don’t know where he comes from.” The man answered them, “How amazing! You don’t know where he comes from, yet he opened my eyes. We know that God doesn’t listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God, and does his will, he listens to him. Since the world began it has never been heard of that anyone opened the eyes of someone born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.” They answered him, “You were altogether born in sins, and do you teach us?” They threw him out.

echoes.text: Joshua said to Achan, “My son, please give glory to Yahweh, the God of Israel, and make confession to him. Tell me now what you have done! Don’t hide it from me!”
echoes.note: 'Give glory to God' is a near-verbatim adjuration formula: Joshua so charges Achan to confess before God in a judicial setting. The Pharisees use the identical oath-formula to pressure the man to recant, marking his testimony as sworn courtroom speech. High Volume via the fixed idiom.

echoes.text: Therefore you shall make images of your tumors, and images of your mice that mar the land; and you shall give glory to the God of Israel: perhaps he will lighten his hand from off you, and from off your gods, and from off your land.
echoes.note: 'Give glory to the God of Israel' as a confessional demand recurs in the Philistine episode, reinforcing the formula behind 9:24. It is a secondary witness to the same idiom rather than an independent source; Joshua 7:19 is the closer judicial parallel.

echoes.text: Since then, there has not arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom Yahweh knew face to face,
echoes.note: 'We are disciples of Moses... God has spoken to Moses' echoes the Torah's claim that no prophet arose like Moses, whom YHWH knew face to face. The Pharisees stake authority on Mosaic revelation, the very framework John uses to argue Jesus surpasses Moses. Coherence high within the chapter's Moses polemic.

echoes.text: With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”
echoes.note: 'With him I speak mouth to mouth' grounds the unique standing of Moses claimed by 'God has spoken to Moses.' The Pharisees' 'we know God has spoken to Moses, but we don't know where this man is from' trades on this Mosaic-speech privilege. Available and coherent with the disciples-of-Moses boast.

echoes.text: If I cherished sin in my heart, the Lord wouldn’t have listened.
echoes.note: 'If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me' is closely paraphrased by 'God does not listen to sinners, but to the worshiper who does his will.' The man invokes a wisdom-psalm axiom about answered prayer to argue Jesus is from God. High Coherence and near-propositional match.

echoes.text: Yahweh is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous.
echoes.note: 'The LORD is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous' is the proverbial doublet behind 9:31's 'God does not listen to sinners but to the worshiper who does his will.' Recurrence with Psalm 66:18 strengthens both as the wisdom substrate of the man's argument.

echoes.text: When you spread out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you. Yes, when you make many prayers, I will not hear. Your hands are full of blood.
echoes.note: 'When you spread out your hands I will hide my eyes... I will not hear' supplies the prophetic version of God refusing to hear sinners. It reinforces 9:31 alongside the psalm and proverb, broadening the 'God hears the righteous' axiom across Torah-Prophets-Writings.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s eyes are toward the righteous. His ears listen to their cry.
echoes.note: 'The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous, and his ears toward their cry' is a further wisdom witness to the principle that God hears the God-fearing but not the wicked. It coheres with 9:31 and adds Recurrence, though the man's wording is closest to Psalm 66:18 and Proverbs 15:29.

echoes.text: He will not accept any person against a poor man; And he will listen to the prayer of him that is wronged. He will in no wise despise the supplication of the fatherless; Nor the widow, when she pours out her tale. Do not the tears of the widow run down her cheek? And is not her cry against him that has caused them to fall? He that serves God according to his good pleasure shall be accepted, And his supplication shall reach to the clouds.
echoes.note: Ben Sira affirms that God hears the prayer of the humble and the one who serves him with his whole heart, a deuterocanonical articulation of the doctrine in 9:31. Available within Second-Temple piety and coherent, though the canonical psalm/proverb are the nearer sources.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.
echoes.note: 'Since the world began it was never heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind' frames the sign as unprecedented — only God can do the eschatological eye-opening of Isaiah 35:5. The man's argument turns the prophetic sign-act into proof of divine origin. Coherence with the chapter's controlling Isaianic motif.

echoes.text: Yahweh opens the eyes of the blind. Yahweh raises up those who are bowed down. Yahweh loves the righteous.
echoes.note: 'The LORD opens the eyes of the blind' names eye-opening as a distinctly divine work, undergirding 'if this man were not from God he could do nothing.' The man reasons exactly along the psalm's lines, attributing a God-only act to Jesus. Strong Coherence with John's high Christology.

pericopes.text: Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, and finding him, he said, “Do you believe in the Son of God?” He answered, “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?” Jesus said to him, “You have both seen him, and it is he who speaks with you.” He said, “Lord, I believe!” and he worshiped him.
