Jesus said, “I came into this world for judgment, that those who don’t see may see; and that those who see may become blind.” Those of the Pharisees who were with him heard these things, and said to him, “Are we also blind?” Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now you say, ‘We see.’ Therefore your sin remains.

echoes.text: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: 'I came for judgment, that those who don't see may see, and those who see may become blind' inverts and fulfills Isaiah's commission to blind the seeing and deafen the hearing. John elsewhere cites Isaiah 6:10 explicitly (12:40), making this the controlling intertext for the chapter's sight/blindness-as-judgment theme. High Recurrence and Coherence.

echoes.text: “Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see. Who is blind, but my servant? Or who is as deaf as my messenger whom I send? Who is as blind as he who is at peace, and as blind as Yahweh’s servant? You see many things, but don’t observe. His ears are open, but he doesn’t listen.
echoes.note: 'Who is blind but my servant... seeing many things, but you do not observe' supplies the prophetic paradox of those who possess sight yet remain blind, mirroring the Pharisees who 'see' yet have sin remaining. Coherent with the judicial blinding motif and available within the Isaianic servant oracles.

echoes.text: Bring out the blind people who have eyes, and the deaf who have ears.
echoes.note: 'Bring forth the people who are blind, yet have eyes, and the deaf who have ears' reinforces the sighted-yet-blind paradox applied to the Pharisees. Secondary to Isaiah 6 and 42; adds Recurrence to the Isaianic blindness cluster but contributes little independently.

echoes.text: Pause and wonder! Blind yourselves and be blind! They are drunken, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink. For Yahweh has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes, the prophets; and he has covered your heads, the seers.
echoes.note: Isaiah's stupefied, blinded leaders ('they are blind... the LORD has poured on you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes') parallel the self-confident Pharisees judged blind. The judicial-blinding theme coheres, though the verbal contact is faint amid the stronger Isaiah 6 link.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: 'Do you believe in the Son of Man?' (a strong textual variant for 'Son of God') invokes the Danielic Son of Man before whom worship is rendered, fitting the man's response of belief and worship in 9:38. The link depends on the variant reading, so confidence is low though the title is Danielic.

echoes.text: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.
echoes.note: 'In that day the deaf shall hear... and the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity and darkness' frames the chapter's resolution: a blind man comes to physical and spiritual sight while the seeing are darkened. The double movement realizes Isaiah's reversal-of-perception oracle and coheres with the light/darkness frame.

pericopes.text: “Most certainly, I tell you, one who doesn’t enter by the door into the sheep fold, but climbs up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber. But one who enters in by the door is the shepherd of the sheep. The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, and the sheep listen to his voice. He calls his own sheep by name, and leads them out. Whenever he brings out his own sheep, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice. They will by no means follow a stranger, but will flee from him; for they don’t know the voice of strangers.” Jesus spoke this parable to them, but they didn’t understand what he was telling them.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and tell them, even to the shepherds, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves! Shouldn’t the shepherds feed the sheep? You eat the fat, and you clothe yourself with the wool, you kill the fatlings; but you don’t feed the sheep. You haven’t strengthened the diseased, neither have you healed that which was sick, neither […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel 34 is the controlling subtext for the whole discourse: false shepherds who do not enter rightly and exploit the flock vs. the true shepherd. The thief/robber who climbs in 'some other way' answers Ezekiel's self-feeding shepherds, and the rightful shepherd entering by the door answers the LORD's own shepherding. High volume, recurrence across the chapter, and coherence with John's polemic against Israel's leaders.

echoes.text: “Let Yahweh, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation, who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: Moses asks the LORD to appoint a shepherd who leads Israel 'out' and brings them 'in,' so the congregation not be sheep without a shepherd. John's shepherd who 'leads them out' (v.3) and goes before them (v.4) echoes the leading-out/going-before language of the appointment of a shepherd over Israel.

echoes.text: for he is our God. We are the people of his pasture, and the sheep in his care. Today, oh that you would hear his voice!
echoes.note: 'The sheep listen to his voice' and refusal to follow strangers resonates with 'the sheep of his hand. Today, if you would hear his voice.' The motif of the flock recognizing and hearing the shepherd's voice is verbally and thematically coherent.

echoes.text: Know that Yahweh, he is God. It is he who has made us, and we are his. We are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.
echoes.note: 'We are his people, and the sheep of his pasture' supplies the flock-belonging frame behind the shepherd who knows his own and calls them by name. Faint; competes with Psalm 95 and the broader shepherd-of-Israel topos.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh my God: “Feed the flock of slaughter. Their buyers slaughter them, and go unpunished. Those who sell them say, ‘Blessed be Yahweh, for I am rich;’ and their own shepherds don’t pity them. For I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land,” says Yahweh; “but, behold, I will deliver the men everyone into his neighbor’s hand, and into the hand of his king. They will strike the land, and out of their hand I will not deliver them.” So I fed […]
echoes.note: Zechariah's flock 'doomed to slaughter' under worthless shepherds who do not care for the sheep, and the breaking of the bond with the flock, anticipates John's thieves/robbers contrasted with the true shepherd. Recurs more strongly at vv.11-13, but the false-shepherd indictment colors the parable here.

pericopes.text: Jesus therefore said to them again, “Most certainly, I tell you, I am the sheep’s door. All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep didn’t listen to them. I am the door. If anyone enters in by me, he will be saved, and will go in and go out, and will find pasture. The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.

echoes.text: This is the gate of Yahweh; the righteous will enter into it.
echoes.note: 'This is the gate of the LORD; the righteous will enter into it' undergirds Jesus' self-identification as the door through which one 'enters in' and 'will be saved.' Psalm 118 is a major Johannine/Synoptic source and the entering-and-being-saved language coheres with the entrance-gate motif.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and tell them, even to the shepherds, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves! Shouldn’t the shepherds feed the sheep? You eat the fat, and you clothe yourself with the wool, you kill the fatlings; but you don’t feed the sheep. You haven’t strengthened the diseased, neither have you healed that which was sick, neither […]
echoes.note: 'All who came before me are thieves and robbers' continues the indictment of Israel's bad shepherds in Ezekiel 34, while 'find pasture' (v.9) directly echoes the LORD's promise to feed his flock in good pasture (Ezek 34:14). Strong recurrence and coherence with the governing subtext.

echoes.text: who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: 'Will go in and go out, and will find pasture' echoes the shepherd who leads Israel 'out' and brings them 'in' so they may be led to pasture. The go-in/go-out idiom for secure shepherded life is shared, though common in the OT.

echoes.text: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says Yahweh. Therefore thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, against the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them; behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings, says Yahweh. I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they […]
echoes.note: 'Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep' parallels the thief who 'comes to steal, kill, and destroy.' Jeremiah promises to set up shepherds who will feed the flock so none is lacking, coherent with John's life-giving shepherd over against destroyers.

pericopes.text: I am the good shepherd.The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He who is a hired hand, and not a shepherd, who doesn’t own the sheep, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees. The wolf snatches the sheep, and scatters them. The hired hand flees because he is a hired hand, and doesn’t care for the sheep. I am the good shepherd. I know my own, and I’m known by my own; even as the Father knows me, and I know the Father. I lay down my life for the sheep. I have other sheep, which are not of this fold.I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice. They will become one flock with one shepherd. Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it again. No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. I received this commandment from my Father.”

echoes.text: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out. As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land; and I […]
echoes.note: The LORD himself seeks, gathers, and feeds the scattered sheep, rescuing them from where they were scattered in the day of clouds. Jesus as the good shepherd who knows his own enacts the LORD's own pastoral self-commitment, making the divine claim of Ezekiel 34 the load-bearing subtext.

echoes.text: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd. I, Yahweh, will be their God, and my servant David prince among them; I, Yahweh, have spoken it.
echoes.note: 'I will set up one shepherd over them, my servant David... and I the LORD will be their God.' This is the source of the singular good shepherd and converges with v.16's 'one flock, one shepherd.' High volume and exact thematic match to the Davidic-messianic single shepherd.

echoes.text: My servant David shall be king over them; and they all shall have one shepherd: they shall also walk in my ordinances, and observe my statutes, and do them.
echoes.note: 'David my servant shall be king over them; and they all shall have one shepherd' is the closest verbal antecedent to 'one flock, one shepherd' (v.16). Recurs with Ezek 34:23 and reinforces the reunification of a divided flock under one Davidic shepherd.

echoes.text: He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.
echoes.note: 'He will feed his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arm' supplies the tender LORD-as-shepherd image behind the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. Coherent with John's identification of Jesus with the LORD's own shepherding care.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.
echoes.note: 'The LORD is my shepherd... though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death.' The good shepherd who lays down his life and faces the wolf evokes the shepherd who protects through death's shadow. Strong cultural availability, though the laying-down-of-life motif goes beyond Psalm 23.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to me, “Take for yourself yet again the equipment of a foolish shepherd. For, behold, I will raise up a shepherd in the land, who will not visit those who are cut off, neither will seek those who are scattered, nor heal that which is broken, nor feed that which is sound; but he will eat the flesh of the fat sheep, and will tear their hoofs in pieces. Woe to the worthless shepherd who leaves the flock! The sword will be on his arm, and on his […]
echoes.note: The 'worthless shepherd' who deserts the flock, does not care for the perishing, and abandons them to be devoured is the negative counterpart to John's hired hand who flees the wolf and does not care for the sheep. Verbal and thematic coherence in the abandonment/devouring imagery.

echoes.text: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered. My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and on every high hill: yes, my sheep were scattered on all the surface of the earth; and there was no one who searched or sought.
echoes.note: Without a shepherd the flock 'became food for all the beasts of the field, and were scattered.' The wolf that snatches and scatters the sheep (v.12) replays Ezekiel's scattering and devouring of the unshepherded flock.

echoes.text: The Lord Yahweh, who gathers the outcasts of Israel, says, “Yet will I gather others to him, besides his own who are gathered.”
echoes.note: 'The Lord GOD, who gathers the outcasts of Israel, says, Yet others will I gather besides his own that are gathered.' This is the strongest antecedent for the 'other sheep... not of this fold' whom the shepherd must also bring (v.16), grounding the Gentile ingathering.

echoes.text: I will surely assemble, Jacob, all of you; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as a flock in the midst of their pasture; they will swarm with people.
echoes.note: 'I will surely gather all of you, Jacob... I will put them together like the sheep of Bozrah... they will swarm with people.' Supplies the regathering-into-one-flock image behind the 'one flock' formed from other sheep. Coherent but competes with Ezekiel/Isaiah gathering texts.

echoes.text: He shall stand, and shall shepherd in the strength of Yahweh, in the majesty of the name of Yahweh his God: and they will live, for then he will be great to the ends of the earth.
echoes.note: 'He shall stand and shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD' offers the messianic ruler-as-shepherd whose flock dwells securely 'to the ends of the earth,' faintly behind the universal one-flock vision. Lower volume than the Ezekiel cluster.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth. He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and […]
echoes.note: 'All we like sheep have gone astray... the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all,' and the servant who 'poured out his soul to death.' The shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep may fuse the suffering servant with the shepherd. Contested and faint in John, which rarely cites Isaiah 53 explicitly.

pericopes.text: Therefore a division arose again among the Jews because of these words. Many of them said, “He has a demon, and is insane! Why do you listen to him?” Others said, “These are not the sayings of one possessed by a demon. It isn’t possible for a demon to open the eyes of the blind, is it?”

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.
echoes.note: 'Then the eyes of the blind will be opened' lies behind the crowd's argument that a demoniac cannot open the eyes of the blind (v.21), recalling ch.9 and the messianic sign. Faint here; carried over from the healing narrative rather than newly invoked.

pericopes.text: It was the Feast of the Dedication at Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s porch. The Jews therefore came around him and said to him, “How long will you hold us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.” Jesus answered them, “I told you, and you don’t believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name, these testify about me. But you don’t believe, because you are not of my sheep, as I told you. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all. No one is able to snatch them out of my Father’s hand. I and the Father are one.”

echoes.text: But Judas and his kindred said, Behold, our enemies are discomfited: let us go up to cleanse the holy place, and to dedicate it afresh. And all the army was gathered together, and they went up to mount Sion. And they saw the sanctuary laid desolate, and the altar profaned, and the gates burned up, and shrubs growing in the courts as in a forest or as on one of the mountains, and the priests’ chambers pulled down; and they tore their clothes, and made […]
echoes.note: The Feast of the Dedication (Hanukkah) commemorates Judas Maccabeus' cleansing and rededication of the temple altar, the festival's institution. John's explicit setting at this feast (v.22) frames Jesus, the one whom the Father 'consecrated' (v.36), as the true dedicated/sanctified one. High availability as Second-Temple background.

echoes.text: And Maccabaeus and those who were with him, the Lord leading them on, recovered the temple and the city; and they pulled down the altars that had been built in the marketplace by the aliens, and also the walls of sacred inclosures. And having cleansed the sanctuary they made another altar of sacrifice; and striking stones and taking fire out of them, they offered sacrifices, after they had ceased for two years, and burned incense, and lighted lamps, and […]
echoes.note: Parallel account of the purification and rededication of the temple and the eight-day festival 'in the manner of Tabernacles,' establishing the Dedication setting. Reinforces 1 Macc 4 as the festival's narrative grounding for John's winter feast.

echoes.text: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out. As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land; and I […]
echoes.note: 'My sheep hear my voice... and they follow me' (v.27) restates the LORD's own knowing and gathering of his flock from Ezekiel 34, now claimed by Jesus. The sustained shepherd theme links the Dedication confrontation back to the discourse's governing subtext.

echoes.text: Yes, since the day was I am he; and there is no one who can deliver out of my hand. I will work, and who can hinder it?”
echoes.note: 'There is no one who can deliver out of my hand' undergirds 'no one will snatch them out of my hand' (v.28) and 'out of my Father's hand' (v.29). The security-in-the-divine-hand idiom is a deliberate divine self-claim applied to Jesus.

echoes.text: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.
echoes.note: 'There is no one who can deliver out of my hand' (the same idiom) with 'I kill and I make alive' stands behind Jesus giving eternal life and holding the sheep inviolably. Reinforces the divine-hand security motif alongside Isaiah.

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.
echoes.note: 'Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one' resonates behind 'I and the Father are one' (v.30). The Shema's oneness language is reframed christologically; coherent with the blasphemy charge that follows, though the unity claimed is functional/relational.

pericopes.text: Therefore Jews took up stones again to stone him. Jesus answered them, “I have shown you many good works from my Father. For which of those works do you stone me?” The Jews answered him, “We don’t stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy: because you, being a man, make yourself God.” Jesus answered them, “Isn’t it written in your law, ‘I said, you are gods?’ If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came (and the Scripture can’t be broken), do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God?’ If I don’t do the works of my Father, don’t believe me. But if I do them, though you don’t believe me, believe the works; that you may know and believe that the Father is in me, and I in the Father.” They sought again to seize him, and he went out of their hand.

echoes.text: I said, “You are gods, all of you are sons of the Most High.
echoes.note: Jesus cites verbatim 'I said, you are gods' (v.34) from the law to defend calling himself Son of God. This is the only formal OT citation in the chapter, introduced with 'Isn't it written in your law,' and the argument turns on the precise wording. Highest volume and clarity.

echoes.text: God presides in the great assembly. He judges among the gods. “How long will you judge unjustly, and show partiality to the wicked?” Selah. “Defend the weak, the poor, and the fatherless. Maintain the rights of the poor and oppressed. Rescue the weak and needy. Deliver them out of the hand of the wicked.” They don’t know, neither do they understand. They walk back and forth in darkness. All the foundations of the earth are shaken. I said, “You are gods, […]
echoes.note: Beyond the quoted v.6, the whole psalm frames those 'to whom the word of God came' (v.35) as the divine council/judges called 'gods,' supplying the a-fortiori logic for the one the Father consecrated. The surrounding context, not just the citation, drives the defense.

echoes.text: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
echoes.note: 'Before you came forth out of the womb I sanctified you; I appointed you a prophet' parallels 'the one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world' (v.36). The consecrate-and-send pattern of prophetic commissioning is closely echoed.

echoes.text: You shall put them on Aaron your brother, and on his sons with him, and shall anoint them, and consecrate them, and sanctify them, that they may minister to me in the priest’s office.
echoes.note: The consecration of Aaron and his sons to serve the LORD provides cultic resonance for the Father's 'sanctifying' of Jesus, fitting the Dedication setting where the altar itself is consecrated. Faint and competes with the prophetic-commission sense of Jer 1:5.

echoes.text: He who blasphemes Yahweh’s name, he shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall certainly stone him. The foreigner as well as the native-born, when he blasphemes the Name, shall be put to death.
echoes.note: 'He who blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death... shall stone him' grounds the crowd's move to stone Jesus 'for blasphemy' (vv.31-33). The stoning-for-blasphemy procedure is the legal backdrop the narrative presupposes.

pericopes.text: He went away again beyond the Jordan into the place where John was baptizing at first, and there he stayed. Many came to him. They said, “John indeed did no sign, but everything that John said about this man is true.” Many believed in him there.

Now a certain man was sick, Lazarus from Bethany, of the village of Mary and her sister, Martha. It was that Mary who had anointed the Lord with ointment, and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother, Lazarus, was sick. The sisters therefore sent to him, saying, “Lord, behold, he for whom you have great affection is sick.” But when Jesus heard it, he said, “This sickness is not to death, but for the glory of God, that God’s Son may be glorified by it.” Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus. When therefore he heard that he was sick, he stayed two days in the place where he was. Then after this he said to the disciples, “Let’s go into Judea again.” The disciples told him, “Rabbi, the Jews were just trying to stone you, and are you going there again?” Jesus answered, “Aren’t there twelve hours of daylight? If a man walks in the day, he doesn’t stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if a man walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light isn’t in him.” He said these things, and after that, he said to them, “Our friend, Lazarus, has fallen asleep, but I am going so that I may awake him out of sleep.” The disciples therefore said, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.” Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he spoke of taking rest in sleep. So Jesus said to them plainly then, “Lazarus is dead. I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, so that you may believe. Nevertheless, let’s go to him.” Thomas therefore, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples, “Let’s go also, that we may die with him.”

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: The 'sickness not unto death but for the glory of God' frames Lazarus' death as a stage on which divine life-giving will be displayed, echoing the Creator who breathes life into dust. Faint, but coheres with John's creation theology (1:1-4) and the breath-of-life motif that undergirds resurrection texts. Contested.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: Jesus' euphemism that Lazarus 'has fallen asleep' and will be awakened maps onto Daniel's 'many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake,' the classic OT idiom for resurrection as awakening from sleep. Volume is moderate (shared sleep/awaken vocabulary) and coheres with the chapter's resurrection program. Availability secure as the seminal resurrection text.

echoes.text: so man lies down and doesn’t rise. Until the heavens are no more, they shall not awake, nor be roused out of their sleep.
echoes.note: Job's 'man lies down and rises not till the heavens are no more; they will not awake nor be roused from their sleep' supplies the sleep-of-death idiom that Jesus inverts by awakening Lazarus. Coherence is good but volume is faint and the idiom is widely diffused. Contested as a specific source.

echoes.text: Behold, and answer me, Yahweh, my God. Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death;
echoes.note: 'Lighten my eyes lest I sleep the sleep of death' associates sleep with death and divine light, resonating with both the 'fallen asleep' euphemism and Jesus' day/night light saying (vv.9-10). Faint and idiomatic; offered honestly as low-confidence.

echoes.text: Give glory to Yahweh your God, before he causes darkness, and before your feet stumble on the dark mountains, and, while you look for light, he turns it into the shadow of death, and makes it gross darkness.
echoes.note: Jesus' walking-in-the-day-versus-stumbling-in-the-dark saying echoes the prophetic 'give glory to the LORD before he brings darkness, before your feet stumble on the twilight mountains.' Shared stumble/light/darkness imagery; coherence with Johannine light theme but low volume. Contested.

pericopes.text: So when Jesus came, he found that he had been in the tomb four days already. Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away. Many of the Jews had joined the women around Martha and Mary, to console them concerning their brother. Then when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary stayed in the house. Therefore Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died. Even now I know that, whatever you ask of God, God will give you.” Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.” Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.” Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies. Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?” She said to him, “Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Christ, God’s Son, he who comes into the world.”

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: Martha's confession 'I know he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day' is precisely the Danielic doctrine of bodily resurrection at the end, the only OT text giving it explicit shape. High volume and recurrence; Jesus then collapses 'the last day' into his own person ('I am the resurrection'). Availability and coherence are strong.

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]
echoes.note: The whole Lazarus episode enacts Ezekiel's vision: God opens graves, raises the dead, and gives life by his Spirit/word so that 'you shall know that I am the LORD.' 'I am the resurrection and the life' figurally fulfills Yahweh's promise to raise the dead from their tombs. High volume of shared grave/raising imagery and strong coherence with the sign's purpose (that they may believe / know).

echoes.text: I will ransom them from the power of Sheol. I will redeem them from death! Death, where are your plagues? Sheol, where is your destruction? “Compassion will be hidden from my eyes.
echoes.note: 'Shall I ransom them from the power of Sheol? Shall I redeem them from Death?' grounds the hope that death is not final, the hope Martha voices. Jesus as 'the resurrection and the life' answers Hosea's rhetorical challenge to Death. Moderate volume; coheres with the chapter's victory-over-death theme.

echoes.text: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
echoes.note: 'Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust!' is the Isaianic resurrection promise underlying both Martha's last-day hope and the literal raising of Lazarus. Strong volume (dead-shall-live, awake-from-dust) and coherence with Daniel 12:2 cluster.

echoes.text: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.
echoes.note: 'I kill and I make alive' is the foundational divine self-claim that only God gives and takes life; Jesus' 'I am the resurrection and the life' assumes this prerogative in the first person. The 'I am' form coheres with the Johannine egō eimi sayings rooted in Deuteronomy/Isaiah self-declarations. Moderate volume.

echoes.text: “Yahweh kills, and makes alive. He brings down to Sheol, and brings up.
echoes.note: Hannah's 'The LORD kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up' parallels Deuteronomy 32:39 as the OT confession of God's resurrection power that Jesus now wields. Coheres with the life-giving claim; moderate volume via the kill/make-alive pairing.

echoes.text: I will not die, but live, and declare Yah’s works.
echoes.note: 'I shall not die, but live, and recount the deeds of the LORD' resonates with Jesus' promise that the believer 'shall never die.' Faint verbal contact; offered as low-confidence given the Psalm's broader Passion-week use. Contested.

pericopes.text: When she had said this, she went away, and called Mary, her sister, secretly, saying, “The Teacher is here, and is calling you.” When she heard this, she arose quickly, and went to him. Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was in the place where Martha met him. Then the Jews who were with her in the house, and were consoling her, when they saw Mary, that she rose up quickly and went out, followed her, saying, “She is going to the tomb to weep there.” Therefore when Mary came to where Jesus was, and saw him, she fell down at his feet, saying to him, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died.” When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews weeping who came with her, he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled, and said, “Where have you laid him?” They told him, “Lord, come and see.” Jesus wept. The Jews therefore said, “See how much affection he had for him!” Some of them said, “Couldn’t this man, who opened the eyes of him who was blind, have also kept this man from dying?”

echoes.text: You number my wanderings. You put my tears into your bottle. Aren’t they in your book?
echoes.note: 'You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle' frames divine attentiveness to human weeping, resonating with Jesus weeping and being deeply moved at the tomb. Faint and thematic rather than verbal; coherence with the compassion motif but low volume. Contested.

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
echoes.note: Jesus 'troubled in spirit' and weeping, 'a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief,' figures the Servant who bears human sorrow. Coheres with the chapter's later substitution theme (Caiaphas, vv.50-52) and John's Servant Christology. Moderate volume via the grief/sorrow correspondence.

echoes.text: Joseph fell on his father’s face, wept on him, and kissed him.
echoes.note: Joseph weeping over and mourning his dead father supplies a patriarchal precedent for righteous weeping over the dead, ambient behind 'Jesus wept.' Very faint, generic mourning topos; honestly low-confidence. Contested.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.
echoes.note: The bystanders' 'this man who opened the eyes of the blind' recalls Isaiah's eschatological sign that 'the eyes of the blind shall be opened,' which John applies to Jesus' ch.9 sign. The cross-reference here invokes that Isaianic frame as proof of life-giving power. Low volume in this pericope; contested as a direct echo.

pericopes.text: Jesus therefore, again groaning in himself, came to the tomb. Now it was a cave, and a stone lay against it. Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of him who was dead, said to him, “Lord, by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days.” Jesus said to her, “Didn’t I tell you that if you believed, you would see God’s glory?” So they took away the stone from the place where the dead man was lying. Jesus lifted up his eyes, and said, “Father, I thank you that you listened to me. I know that you always listen to me, but because of the multitude that stands around I said this, that they may believe that you sent me.” When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!” He who was dead came out, bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Free him, and let him go.”

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]
echoes.note: The command 'Lazarus, come out!' and the dead man emerging from the cave-tomb enact Ezekiel's 'I will open your graves and raise you from your graves' brought to life by the word. The grave-clothes/loosing imagery and the loud summoning voice are strongly coherent with the dry-bones vivification by God's word. Highest-volume figural anchor of the chapter.

echoes.text: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]
echoes.note: Elijah raising the widow of Zarephath's son is the foundational prophet-raises-the-dead type that Jesus surpasses; cf. the 'four days' to magnify the miracle. Strong recurrence (paired with Elisha) and coherence: a prophet's word/prayer restores a dead son to life. Availability secure.

echoes.text: When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and laid on his bed. He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh. He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then […]
echoes.note: Elisha raising the Shunammite's son completes the prophetic resurrection pattern behind the Lazarus sign; the restored child and Jesus' restored friend share the dead-son-revived type. High recurrence with 1 Kings 17; coherence with John's portrayal of Jesus as the prophet greater than Elijah/Elisha.

echoes.text: God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
echoes.note: Jesus' creative summons by 'a loud voice' that calls the dead into life echoes the divine word that calls being out of nothing ('Let there be light'), consistent with John's prologue identifying Jesus as the creative Word. Moderate volume; strong coherence with Johannine creation/word theology.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: The bodily emergence of one who slept in the dust anticipates Daniel's awakening of those who sleep in the dust; Lazarus is a proleptic enactment of the last-day resurrection Martha named (v.24). Moderate volume here, reinforcing the chapter-wide Danielic frame.

echoes.text: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
echoes.note: 'Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; your dead shall live' is enacted as Lazarus is summoned from the dust of the tomb. The literal raising performs Isaiah's promise; moderate volume reinforcing the resurrection-promise cluster of the chapter.

pericopes.text: Therefore many of the Jews, who came to Mary and saw what Jesus did, believed in him. But some of them went away to the Pharisees, and told them the things which Jesus had done. The chief priests therefore and the Pharisees gathered a council, and said, “What are we doing? For this man does many signs. If we leave him alone like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.” But a certain one of them, Caiaphas, being high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all, nor do you consider that it is advantageous for us that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish.” Now he didn’t say this of himself, but being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but that he might also gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad. So from that day forward they took counsel that they might put him to death.

echoes.text: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t […]
echoes.note: Caiaphas' 'it is better that one man die for the people' unwittingly states the Servant's vicarious substitution: 'he was cut off from the land of the living for the transgression of my people.' John flags it as prophecy, making the one-dies-for-the-many a deliberate Isaianic atonement type. High volume and coherence.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: That Jesus would die 'not for the nation only but to gather the scattered children of God into one' echoes the Servant's commission to be 'a light to the nations' and to restore the dispersed of Israel, widening salvation beyond the nation. Moderate volume; coheres with John's universalizing of the death's scope.

echoes.text: As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land; and I will feed them on the mountains of Israel, by the watercourses, and in all the inhabited places of the […]
echoes.note: 'Gather together into one the children of God who are scattered' enacts the shepherd-God's promise to 'seek out my scattered sheep and gather them from where they were scattered.' Strong volume on the gather/scatter vocabulary and coherence with John 10's shepherd theme. Availability secure.

echoes.text: Say to them, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I will take the children of Israel from among the nations, where they are gone, and will gather them on every side, and bring them into their own land: and I will make them one nation in the land, on the mountains of Israel; and one king shall be king to them all; and they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all;
echoes.note: Following the dry-bones grave-opening, Ezekiel 37 promises to 'gather' the scattered Israelites 'and make them one nation' — precisely the gathering-into-one of v.52. The same chapter that grounds the resurrection sign grounds the ingathering, a tight intra-Ezekielian coherence. High volume.

echoes.text: that then Yahweh your God will release you from captivity, have compassion on you, and will return and gather you from all the peoples where Yahweh your God has scattered you. If your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of the heavens, from there Yahweh your God will gather you, and from there he will bring you back.
echoes.note: 'He will gather you again from all the peoples where the LORD scattered you... from there he will gather you' is the covenantal ingathering-of-the-dispersed promise behind 'gather into one the scattered children of God.' Moderate-to-high volume on the scatter/gather diaspora language; coherence with the universal scope.

echoes.text: He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
echoes.note: 'He will assemble the banished of Israel and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth' supplies the eschatological-ingathering idiom for gathering the scattered children of God. Moderate volume; recurs with Deuteronomy 30 and Ezekiel 34/37 in the dispersion-gathering cluster.

echoes.text: I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they shall be fruitful and multiply.
echoes.note: 'I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them' parallels Ezekiel 34 in the shepherd-gathers-the-scattered motif behind v.52. Moderate volume, reinforcing the gathering theme; coheres with John's flock/shepherd imagery.

echoes.text: I will signal for them, and gather them; for I have redeemed them; and they will increase as they have increased. I will sow them among the peoples; and they will remember me in far countries; and they will live with their children, and will return.
echoes.note: 'I will gather them in... though I scattered them among the nations, yet in far countries they shall remember me' echoes the scatter/gather pattern of v.52. Faint relative to the stronger Ezekiel/Deuteronomy parallels; offered as low-confidence. Contested.

echoes.text: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save many people alive.
echoes.note: Caiaphas' malicious counsel that providentially saves many enacts Joseph's 'you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to keep many people alive.' The dramatic irony of unwitting prophecy producing salvation is strongly coherent; moderate volume via the evil-counsel-turned-deliverance pattern.

echoes.text: “‘So you shall not pollute the land in which you are; for blood pollutes the land. No atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, but by the blood of him who shed it.
echoes.note: The notion that the land/nation is preserved by a death ('no expiation for the land for blood except by the blood of him who shed it') faintly underlies Caiaphas' calculus that one death spares the nation. Low volume and contested as a deliberate echo.

pericopes.text: Jesus therefore walked no more openly among the Jews, but departed from there into the country near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim. He stayed there with his disciples. Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand. Many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover, to purify themselves. Then they sought for Jesus and spoke one with another, as they stood in the temple, “What do you think—that he isn’t coming to the feast at all?” Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had commanded that if anyone knew where he was, he should report it, that they might seize him.

echoes.text: There were certain men, who were unclean because of the dead body of a man, so that they could not keep the Passover on that day, and they came before Moses and before Aaron on that day. Those men said to him, “We are unclean because of the dead body of a man. Why are we kept back, that we may not offer the offering of Yahweh in its appointed season among the children of Israel?” Moses answered them, “Wait, that I may hear what Yahweh will command […]
echoes.note: The pilgrims going up 'to purify themselves' before Passover reflects the Mosaic requirement of ritual purity to keep the feast (Num 9 provides for the unclean). Moderate volume on the Passover-purification linkage; coheres with John's framing of Jesus' death at Passover. Availability secure as the Passover-law text.

echoes.text: For there were many in the assembly who had not sanctified themselves: therefore the Levites were in charge of killing the Passovers for everyone who was not clean, to sanctify them to Yahweh. For a multitude of the people, even many of Ephraim and Manasseh, Issachar and Zebulun, had not cleansed themselves, yet they ate the Passover otherwise than it is written. For Hezekiah had prayed for them, saying, “May the good Yahweh pardon everyone who sets his […]
echoes.note: Hezekiah's Passover, where many who had not purified themselves needed cleansing to eat the Passover, supplies the concrete precedent for pilgrims purifying themselves before the feast (v.55). Moderate volume; coheres with the purification-for-Passover theme. Contested only as to which purification text is primary.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]
echoes.note: 'The Passover of the Jews was at hand' sets the death-plot against the Passover-lamb backdrop that John develops (cf. 1:29; 19:14), figuring Jesus as the Passover lamb slain for the people — tying back to Caiaphas' one-dies-for-many. Moderate volume here but high coherence with John's Passover Christology.

echoes.text: “He who touches the dead body of any man shall be unclean seven days. He shall purify himself with water on the third day, and on the seventh day he shall be clean; but if he doesn’t purify himself the third day, then the seventh day he shall not be clean.
echoes.note: Purification before the feast also evokes the corpse-uncleanness law requiring cleansing — pointed given the chapter's tombs and a four-days-dead body. Faint and inferential; offered as low-confidence. Contested.

echoes.text: When he saw that, he arose, and went for his life, and came to Beersheba, which belongs to Judah, and left his servant there. But he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness, and came and sat down under a juniper tree: and he requested for himself that he might die, and said, “It is enough. Now, O Yahweh, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.”
echoes.note: Jesus withdrawing to the wilderness region near Ephraim to avoid the murder-plot faintly mirrors prophets (Elijah, David) fleeing to the wilderness when sought to be killed. Generic flight-to-wilderness topos, low volume. Contested.

pericopes.text: Then six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, who had been dead, whom he raised from the dead. So they made him a supper there. Martha served, but Lazarus was one of those who sat at the table with him. Mary, therefore, took a pound of ointment of pure nard, very precious, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment. Then Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, one of his disciples, who would betray him, said, “Why wasn’t this ointment sold for three hundred denarii, and given to the poor?” Now he said this, not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief, and having the money box, used to steal what was put into it. But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. She has kept this for the day of my burial. For you always have the poor with you, but you don’t always have me.”

echoes.text: While the king sat at his table, my perfume spread its fragrance.
echoes.note: Mary's pure nard whose fragrance fills the house echoes the Song's 'while the king was on his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance.' The shared lexeme nardos (LXX) plus the banquet-couch setting and the diffusing scent give real Volume and Coherence; John frames the anointing of the messianic 'king' (the next pericope's title) in the idiom of the Bride's love-gift.

echoes.text: Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates, with precious fruits: henna with spikenard plants, spikenard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with every kind of incense tree; myrrh and aloes, with all the best spices,
echoes.note: The catalogue of spices 'nard and saffron... with all chief spices' supplies the only other biblical concentration of nard as a costly love-perfume, reinforcing the Songs register behind Mary's extravagant anointing. Low confidence: thematic resonance without verbal anchor beyond the shared spice.

echoes.text: Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the midst of his brothers: and the Spirit of Yahweh came mightily on David from that day forward. So Samuel rose up, and went to Ramah.
echoes.note: Anointing with oil is the act that makes a king/Messiah (christos); Mary's anointing of Jesus figurally enacts the royal-messianic identity the crowd will acclaim in v.13. Faint and contested, since John explicitly redirects the act toward burial rather than coronation.

echoes.text: For the poor will never cease out of the land. Therefore I command you to surely open your hand to your brother, to your needy, and to your poor, in your land.
echoes.note: Jesus' 'you always have the poor with you' directly invokes Deut 15:11, 'the poor will never cease out of the land,' the Torah charge that grounds open-handed giving. High Volume by near-quotation and clear Availability; the allusion turns the verse's perpetual-poverty clause to relativize almsgiving against the unrepeatable burial of Messiah.

echoes.text: They buried him in his own tombs, which he had dug out for himself in the city of David, and laid him in the bed which was filled with sweet odors and various kinds of spices prepared by the perfumers’ art: and they made a very great burning for him.
echoes.note: Burial anointing with spices for a king (Asa) provides OT precedent for Jesus' reading of the nard as 'for the day of my burial.' Faint; the practice is generic enough that the link rests on theme rather than verbal contact.

pericopes.text: A large crowd therefore of the Jews learned that he was there, and they came, not for Jesus’ sake only, but that they might see Lazarus also, whom he had raised from the dead. But the chief priests conspired to put Lazarus to death also, because on account of him many of the Jews went away and believed in Jesus.

On the next day a great multitude had come to the feast. When they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, they took the branches of the palm trees, and went out to meet him, and cried out, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!” Jesus, having found a young donkey, sat on it. As it is written, “Don’t be afraid, daughter of Zion. Behold, your King comes, sitting on a donkey’s colt.” His disciples didn’t understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things were written about him, and that they had done these things to him. The multitude therefore that was with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb, and raised him from the dead, was testifying about it. For this cause also the multitude went and met him, because they heard that he had done this sign. The Pharisees therefore said among themselves, “See how you accomplish nothing. Behold, the world has gone after him.”

echoes.text: Save us now, we beg you, Yahweh! Yahweh, we beg you, send prosperity now. Blessed is he who comes in Yahweh’s name! We have blessed you out of Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: 'Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord' quotes Ps 118:25-26 verbatim (hosanna = hoshia-na, 'save now'). Maximal Volume and Recurrence (a Hallel pilgrim-psalm sung at the feasts), with John adding 'the King of Israel' to make the messianic coherence explicit.

echoes.text: You shall take on the first day the fruit of goodly trees, branches of palm trees, and boughs of thick trees, and willows of the brook; and you shall rejoice before Yahweh your God seven days.
echoes.note: The crowd's palm branches (ta baia ton phoinikon) echo the festal foliage commanded for Booths, 'branches of palm trees,' carried in cultic rejoicing before the Lord. Coherence is strong since palms had become a nationalist-liturgical symbol of deliverance; the gesture frames Jesus' entry as covenant-festival acclamation.

echoes.text: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your King comes to you! He is righteous, and having salvation; lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
echoes.note: 'Don't be afraid, daughter of Zion. Behold, your King comes, sitting on a donkey's colt' is a formula-cited fulfillment of Zech 9:9 (John conflates its opening with Isa/Zeph 'fear not'). Highest Volume and explicit 'as it is written'; the humble-king-on-a-colt image is the controlling typology of the whole entry.

echoes.text: Yahweh has taken away your judgments. He has thrown out your enemy. The King of Israel, Yahweh, is in your midst. You will not be afraid of evil any more. In that day, it will be said to Jerusalem, “Don’t be afraid, Zion. Don’t let your hands be weak.”
echoes.note: John's 'Don't be afraid, daughter of Zion' more exactly matches Zeph 3:16 ('Do not fear, O Zion') and 3:15 ('the King of Israel, the Lord, is in your midst') than Zech 9:9's 'rejoice greatly.' The 'King of Israel' acclaim (v.13) and the 'fear not' opening suggest a deliberate Zephaniah blend; medium for the conflation.

echoes.text: Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine; he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.
echoes.note: Jacob's blessing of Judah 'binding his colt (polos) to the vine' is the classic messianic donkey text read alongside Zech 9:9; the shared polos and royal-Judah expectation give faint background support to the colt motif. Low and contested: no verbal citation in John.

echoes.text: And he entered into it on the three and twentieth day of the second month, in the hundred and seventy and first year, with praise and palm branches, and with harps, and with cymbals, and with viols, and with hymns, and with songs: because a great enemy was destroyed out of Israel.
echoes.note: Simon's triumphal entry into Jerusalem 'with praise and palm branches' (also 2 Macc 10:7) shows palms as the established Second-Temple sign of liberation-procession into the holy city. Availability and Coherence make this the nearest cultural template for John's palm-waving crowd; echo, not citation.

pericopes.text: Now there were certain Greeks among those that went up to worship at the feast. These, therefore, came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and asked him, saying, “Sir, we want to see Jesus.” Philip came and told Andrew, and in turn, Andrew came with Philip, and they told Jesus. Jesus answered them, “The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit. He who loves his life will lose it. He who hates his life in this world will keep it to eternal life. If anyone serves me, let him follow me. Where I am, there will my servant also be. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him.

echoes.text: It shall happen in the latter days, that the mountain of Yahweh’s house shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it. Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For out of Zion the law shall go out, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.
echoes.note: The Greeks who 'went up to worship' and seek Jesus faintly enact the pilgrimage of the nations to Zion in the last days. Coherence with John's universalizing 'I will draw all people' (v.32) gives the motif some weight; low because no verbal contact.

echoes.text: In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening don’t withhold your hand; for you don’t know which will prosper, whether this or that, or whether they both will be equally good.
echoes.note: The seed-sowing wisdom of 'in the morning sow your seed... you do not know which will prosper' lies behind the grain-of-wheat agricultural maxim, though Jesus inverts it: the seed must die to bear fruit. Faint and generic; sowing imagery was broadly available.

echoes.text: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.
echoes.note: 'Those who sow in tears... goes out weeping, bearing the seed... comes home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves' offers a death-to-harvest pattern resonant with the grain that dies to bear much fruit. Thematic Coherence only; no lexical anchor, hence low.

pericopes.text: “Now my soul is troubled. What shall I say? ‘Father, save me from this time?’ But for this cause I came to this time. Father, glorify your name!” Then there came a voice out of the sky, saying, “I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again.” The multitude therefore, who stood by and heard it, said that it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.” Jesus answered, “This voice hasn’t come for my sake, but for your sakes. Now is the judgment of this world. Now the prince of this world will be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” But he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die.

echoes.text: My soul is also in great anguish. But you, Yahweh—how long? Return, Yahweh. Deliver my soul, and save me for your loving kindness’ sake.
echoes.note: 'Now my soul is troubled... save me from this time?' echoes the lament psalter, esp. Ps 6:3-4 'my soul is greatly troubled... save my life,' the Johannine analogue to the Synoptic Gethsemane. Coherence with the psalmist's troubled-soul-then-deliverance pattern is strong; medium since John gives no citation formula.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Make a fiery serpent, and set it on a pole. It shall happen, that everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live.” Moses made a serpent of brass, and set it on the pole. If a serpent had bitten any man, when he looked at the serpent of brass, he lived.
echoes.note: 'If I am lifted up from the earth' (hypsotho) reactivates the bronze-serpent type John named in 3:14: the lifted-up serpent that gives life when looked upon prefigures the crucified-glorified Son of Man. High Coherence and Recurrence across John; the verb 'lifted up' is the load-bearing link to Moses' standard.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
echoes.note: John's distinctive fusion of 'lifted up' with 'glorified' tracks the LXX of the Servant Song: 'my servant shall be exalted (hypsothesetai) and glorified (doxasthesetai) exceedingly.' The pairing hypsoo + doxazo is rare and precise, giving strong Volume; John reads crucifixion as the Servant's exaltation.

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
echoes.note: 'Now the prince of this world will be cast out' faintly resonates with the protevangelium's defeat of the serpent. Low and contested; the casting-out of the ruler is more cosmic/apocalyptic than tied to any single verse.

pericopes.text: The multitude answered him, “We have heard out of the law that the Christ remains forever. How do you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up?’ Who is this Son of Man?” Jesus therefore said to them, “Yet a little while the light is with you. Walk while you have the light, that darkness doesn’t overtake you. He who walks in the darkness doesn’t know where he is going. While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become children of light.” Jesus said these things, and he departed and hid himself from them.

echoes.text: His seed will endure forever, his throne like the sun before me. It will be established forever like the moon, the faithful witness in the sky.” Selah.
echoes.note: The crowd's 'we have heard out of the law that the Christ remains forever' rests on the Davidic-covenant promise that his offspring/throne 'shall endure forever.' Coherence with messianic exegesis is strong; medium because John cites 'the law' generically rather than a fixed text.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'Who is this Son of Man?' and the claim that the Christ 'remains forever' invoke Daniel's heavenly Son of Man given everlasting dominion. The crowd's puzzlement over an eternal yet 'lifted up' Son of Man trades on Dan 7's title; medium for the conceptual rather than verbal link.

echoes.text: Of the increase of his government and of peace there shall be no end, on the throne of David, and on his kingdom, to establish it, and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from that time on, even forever. The zeal of Yahweh of Armies will perform this.
echoes.note: The notion of the messianic king whose government and reign have 'no end' supports the crowd's 'remains forever.' Faint background to the eternal-Messiah expectation; low, with no verbal contact.

echoes.text: House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Walk while you have the light... that you may become children of light' draws on the prophetic 'walk in the light of the Lord' and the wider light/darkness covenant motif. Coherence with Isaiah's light-walking and John's pervasive light theme gives medium weight; an idiom rather than a citation.

pericopes.text: But though he had done so many signs before them, yet they didn’t believe in him, that the word of Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, which he spoke, “Lord, who has believed our report? To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” For this cause they couldn’t believe, for Isaiah said again, “He has blinded their eyes and he hardened their heart, lest they should see with their eyes, and perceive with their heart, and would turn, and I would heal them.” Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory, and spoke of him. Nevertheless even of the rulers many believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they didn’t confess it, so that they wouldn’t be put out of the synagogue, for they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise.

echoes.text: Who has believed our message? To whom has the arm of Yahweh been revealed?
echoes.note: 'Lord, who has believed our report? To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?' is a formula-cited quotation ('that the word of Isaiah... might be fulfilled') of Isa 53:1 LXX verbatim. Maximal Volume; John reads Israel's unbelief at the signs through the Servant Song's lament over a rejected revelation.

echoes.text: Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: 'He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they should see... and turn, and I would heal them' quotes Isa 6:10, the commission-text of judicial hardening (cf. its NT recurrence). High Volume and explicit attribution to Isaiah; the divine blinding explains the unbelief just described.

echoes.text: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple.
echoes.note: 'Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory, and spoke of him' alludes to the throne-vision of Isa 6:1, 'I saw the Lord... high and lifted up,' identifying the glory Isaiah beheld with Christ's. Strong Coherence: John binds the 'lifted up' (hypsoo) Servant to the 'high and lifted up' enthroned Lord of the call narrative.

pericopes.text: Jesus cried out and said, “Whoever believes in me, believes not in me, but in him who sent me. He who sees me sees him who sent me. I have come as a light into the world, that whoever believes in me may not remain in the darkness. If anyone listens to my sayings, and doesn’t believe, I don’t judge him. For I came not to judge the world, but to save the world. He who rejects me, and doesn’t receive my sayings, has one who judges him. The word that I spoke, the same will judge him in the last day. For I spoke not from myself, but the Father who sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak. I know that his commandment is eternal life. The things therefore which I speak, even as the Father has said to me, so I speak.”

echoes.text: I will raise them up a prophet from among their brothers, like you. I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I shall command him. It shall happen, that whoever will not listen to my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him.
echoes.note: 'I spoke not from myself, but the Father... gave me a commandment what I should say' and the warning that the rejected 'word' will judge in the last day echo the prophet-like-Moses who speaks only the words God commands, and whom God will hold men accountable to hear. Coherence with John's prophet christology is strong; medium absent a citation formula.

echoes.text: He said to them, “Set your heart to all the words which I testify to you this day, which you shall command your children to observe to do, all the words of this law. For it is no vain thing for you; because it is your life, and through this thing you shall prolong your days in the land, where you go over the Jordan to possess it.”
echoes.note: 'I know that his commandment is eternal life... this word is your life' resonates with Moses' charge that the law-word 'is no trifle for you, but your very life.' Faint thematic link between commandment and life; low, with only conceptual contact.

echoes.text: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.
echoes.note: 'I have come as a light into the world, that whoever believes... may not remain in the darkness' continues the light-to-the-nations motif of Isaiah's eschatological dawn. Coherence with John's universal-light christology gives faint support; low, idiomatic rather than cited.

pericopes.text: Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him, Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God, and was going to God,

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]
echoes.note: John frames the entire farewell on the eve of 'the feast of the Passover,' deliberately situating Jesus' self-giving against the exodus deliverance. Volume and coherence are high in John, which has already cast Jesus as the lamb (1:29) and dates the crucifixion to Passover. The footwashing supper thus becomes the new Passover meal of departure.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'The Father had given all things into his hands' echoes the giving of universal dominion to the one like a son of man. The handing-over language coheres with John's repeated Son-of-Man glorification motif and prepares for 13:31. Coherence is strong though the wording is general.

echoes.text: You make him ruler over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet:
echoes.note: 'All things into his hands' may echo the psalmist's 'you put all things under his feet/gave him dominion.' The thought-rhyme of universal subjection is present but the verbal overlap is faint and the motif is widely diffused.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared of old to me, saying, Yes, I have loved you with an everlasting love: therefore with loving kindness have I drawn you.
echoes.note: 'Having loved his own... he loved them to the end' resonates with the LORD's everlasting love and faithful hesed toward his own people. The covenant-love register fits, but the wording is too common to claim a deliberate citation.

pericopes.text: During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him,

echoes.text: Satan stood up against Israel, and moved David to number Israel.
echoes.note: 'The devil having already put into the heart of Judas to betray him' echoes the Satan who 'stood up against Israel and incited David.' The pattern of the adversary inciting a human agent to a destructive deed coheres with the fuller 'Satan entered into him' of 13:27. Availability and recurrence in Second-Temple Satan-tradition support the link.

echoes.text: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” Then Satan […]
echoes.note: The accuser figure who provokes harm against the righteous undergirds the Johannine 'devil.' The connection is thematic rather than verbal and the Job satan is a heavenly prosecutor, so the echo is faint.

pericopes.text: arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel, and wrapped a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet, and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him. Then he came to Simon Peter. He said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?” Jesus answered him, “You don’t know what I am doing now, but you will understand later.” Peter said to him, “You will never wash my feet!” Jesus answered him, “If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me.” Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!” Jesus said to him, “Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed, but is completely clean. You are clean, but not all of you.” For he knew him who would betray him, therefore he said, “You are not all clean.”

echoes.text: Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.
echoes.note: Abraham's 'let a little water be brought and wash your feet' establishes footwashing as the host's act of hospitality, here inverted so the Lord performs the servant's task. The image is the closest patriarchal antecedent and coheres with John's reversal of status. Recurrence of the motif across Genesis strengthens availability.

echoes.text: She arose, and bowed herself with her face to the earth, and said, “Behold, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.”
echoes.note: Abigail's 'a servant to wash the feet of my lord's servants' marks footwashing as the lowliest slave duty. Jesus assuming exactly this office dramatizes 13:16 (the servant not greater than his lord). The status-coherence is strong.

echoes.text: Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet in it. When they go into the Tent of Meeting, they shall wash with water, that they not die; or when they come near to the altar to minister, to burn an offering made by fire to Yahweh. So they shall wash their hands and their feet, that they not die: and it shall be a statute forever to them, even to him and to his descendants throughout their generations.”
echoes.note: The priestly laver where Aaron and his sons wash hands and feet to be clean for service frames footwashing as cultic purification for ministry. Jesus' 'if I don't wash you, you have no part with me' reads the act as priestly consecration. Coherence with the cleansing language is high.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, “This is the statute of the law which Yahweh has commanded. Tell the children of Israel to bring you a red heifer without spot, in which is no defect, and which was never yoked. You shall give her to Eleazar the priest, and he shall bring her outside of the camp, and one shall kill her before his face. Eleazar the priest shall take some of her blood with his finger, and sprinkle her blood toward the front of the […]
