echoes.note: The water of purification that cleanses defilement supplies the conceptual background for 'completely clean.' The transfer from ritual to christological cleansing fits John's pattern of fulfilling purification rites. The link is conceptual, not verbal.

echoes.text: Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean. Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow.
echoes.note: 'Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow' supplies the imagery of moral cleansing behind 'you are clean.' The penitential washing register coheres with Jesus distinguishing the bathed-and-clean from the betrayer. Wording overlaps in the wash/clean pairing.

echoes.text: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you.
echoes.note: 'I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean' is the eschatological cleansing promise most verbally aligned with 'you are clean.' Its new-covenant context coheres with the new commandment of 13:34. Volume of the clean-water motif raises confidence.

echoes.text: “In that day there will be a spring opened to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for sin and for uncleanness.
echoes.note: The fountain opened 'for sin and for impurity' supplies an eschatological cleansing backdrop. The connection is thematic and the wording does not closely match. Marked faint.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: The 'beautiful feet' of the herald is sometimes invoked behind footwashing, but the link is associative only and the volume is negligible. Listed for completeness and marked contested.

pericopes.text: So when he had washed their feet, put his outer garment back on, and sat down again, he said to them, “Do you know what I have done to you? You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am. If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that you also should do as I have done to you. Most certainly I tell you, a servant is not greater than his lord, neither one who is sent greater than he who sent him. If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.

echoes.text: She arose, and bowed herself with her face to the earth, and said, “Behold, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.”
echoes.note: 'A servant is not greater than his lord' restates the lord/servant hierarchy that Abigail's footwashing self-description presumes, now made the basis for mutual service. The status logic coheres tightly with the preceding act. Recurrence of the master/servant ordering across the OT supports availability.

echoes.text: Abraham said to his servant, the elder of his house, who ruled over all that he had, “Please put your hand under my thigh.
echoes.note: 'One who is sent is not greater than he who sent him' reflects the shaliach principle dramatized by Abraham's commissioned servant who acts with his master's authority. The agency concept is Second-Temple and pervasive, so the echo is conceptual and faint.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;
echoes.note: 'Blessed are you if you do them' adopts the OT beatitude form that ties blessing to doing the will/law. The macarism cadence is biblical but generic, so the link is to a form rather than a text.

pericopes.text: I don’t speak concerning all of you. I know whom I have chosen. But that the Scripture may be fulfilled, ‘He who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me.’ From now on, I tell you before it happens, that when it happens, you may believe that I am he. Most certainly I tell you, he who receives whomever I send, receives me; and he who receives me, receives him who sent me.”

echoes.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
echoes.note: Explicitly introduced 'that the Scripture may be fulfilled,' Jesus cites 'He who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me.' This is a formal quotation, John's clearest OT citation in the chapter, applying the lament of the betrayed righteous sufferer to Judas. Volume, recurrence in the Passion tradition, and coherence are all maximal.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”
echoes.note: 'That when it happens, you may believe that I am he' (ego eimi) draws on the divine self-naming 'I AM.' The absolute ego eimi pervades John's Christology and here is tied to prediction-and-fulfillment as proof of identity. Coherence with the Johannine I-AM sayings is very high.

echoes.text: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me.
echoes.note: 'That you may know and believe me... that I am he' supplies the exact pattern of foretelling-so-you-may-believe-I-am-he that John reproduces in 13:19. The Deutero-Isaian 'I am he' (ani hu) is the immediate scriptural matrix for the Johannine ego eimi. Verbal and structural overlap are strong.

echoes.text: Remember the former things of old: for I am God, and there is no one else; I am God, and there is none like me; declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times things that are not yet done; saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure;
echoes.note: 'Declaring the end from the beginning... before it happens' grounds Jesus' 'I tell you before it happens' as the divine prerogative of predictive sovereignty. The link reinforces the I-am theme and coheres with Isaiah 43. Recurrence of this announce-beforehand motif in Isaiah raises confidence.

echoes.text: therefore I have declared it to you from of old; before it came to pass I showed it to you; lest you should say, ‘My idol has done them, and my engraved image, and my molten image, has commanded them.’
echoes.note: 'I declared them to you from of old, before they came to pass... lest you say my idol did them' parallels Jesus telling them beforehand so they will believe. The fore-announcement-for-faith logic matches closely. A near-doublet of Isaiah 46, strengthening the cluster.

echoes.text: For it was not an enemy who insulted me, then I could have endured it. Neither was it he who hated me who raised himself up against me, then I would have hidden myself from him. But it was you, a man like me, my companion, and my familiar friend. We took sweet fellowship together. We walked in God’s house with company.
echoes.note: The betrayal by 'my equal, my companion, my familiar friend' with whom 'we took sweet counsel together' reinforces the table-companion betrayal of Psalm 41 applied to Judas. It is a coherent secondary lament of intimate treachery. Offered as an alternate/reinforcing source.

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
echoes.note: The 'heel' of the lifted-heel quotation can evoke the protoevangelium's heel-bruising enmity, given Satan's role in the betrayal. The catchword link is suggestive but the underlying Hebrew terms differ and the connection is interpretive. Marked contested.

echoes.text: Someone told David, saying, “Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom.” David said, “Yahweh, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness.”
echoes.note: Ahithophel, David's trusted counselor turned conspirator (and traditionally linked to Psalm 41/55), is a typological forerunner of the intimate betrayer. The echo is mediated through the psalm rather than direct. Faint, marked contested.

pericopes.text: When Jesus had said this, he was troubled in spirit, and testified, “Most certainly I tell you that one of you will betray me.” The disciples looked at one another, perplexed about whom he spoke. One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was at the table, leaning against Jesus’ breast. Simon Peter therefore beckoned to him, and said to him, “Tell us who it is of whom he speaks.” He, leaning back, as he was, on Jesus’ breast, asked him, “Lord, who is it?” Jesus therefore answered, “It is he to whom I will give this piece of bread when I have dipped it.” So when he had dipped the piece of bread, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot. After the piece of bread, then Satan entered into him. Then Jesus said to him, “What you do, do quickly.” Now no man at the table knew why he said this to him. For some thought, because Judas had the money box, that Jesus said to him, “Buy what things we need for the feast,” or that he should give something to the poor. Therefore having received that morsel, he went out immediately. It was night.

echoes.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
echoes.note: The dipped morsel handed to the betrayer at table enacts the just-quoted 'he who eats bread with me,' so the narrative dramatizes the scripture already cited. Coherence with 13:18 is exact. The shared-bread treachery is the controlling image.

echoes.text: Satan stood up against Israel, and moved David to number Israel.
echoes.note: 'Satan entered into him' completes the inciting-adversary pattern begun in 13:2, recalling the Satan who moved a man to a ruinous act. The intensification from 'put into the heart' to 'entered' tracks Second-Temple demonological development. Coherence is strong.

echoes.text: At meal time Boaz said to her, “Come here, and eat of the bread, and dip your morsel in the vinegar.” She sat beside the reapers, and they reached her parched grain, and she ate, and was satisfied, and left some of it.
echoes.note: 'Dip your morsel in the wine' is the only OT scene of a dipped morsel offered at a meal, providing possible verbal coloring for the dipped piece of bread. The setting is benevolent, not treacherous, so the link is lexical and faint. Marked contested.

echoes.text: “These are of those who rebel against the light. They don’t know its ways, nor stay in its paths. The murderer rises with the light. He kills the poor and needy. In the night he is like a thief. The eye also of the adulterer waits for the twilight, saying, ‘No eye shall see me.’ He disguises his face. In the dark they dig through houses. They shut themselves up in the daytime. They don’t know the light. For the morning is to all of them like thick […]
echoes.note: 'It was night' fits the OT topos of evildoers as those who rebel against the light and work in darkness. John's pervasive light/darkness dualism makes the closing clause symbolically charged. The echo is to a motif rather than a specific text.

echoes.text: For the poor will never cease out of the land. Therefore I command you to surely open your hand to your brother, to your needy, and to your poor, in your land.
echoes.note: The disciples' guess that Judas should 'give something to the poor' reflects the Deuteronomic almsgiving duty toward the poor at the feast. The connection is to ordinary festal piety and only incidental to the narrative. Faint.

pericopes.text: When he had gone out, Jesus said, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him. If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and he will glorify him immediately. Little children, I will be with you a little while longer. You will seek me, and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you can’t come,’ so now I tell you. A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another, just like I have loved you; that you also love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'Now the Son of Man has been glorified' draws on the one like a son of man who receives glory and dominion. John transposes the apocalyptic enthronement onto the hour of the cross, his signature reading of Daniel's glorification. Volume, recurrence, and coherence across John are maximal.

echoes.text: and he said to me, “You are my servant; Israel, in whom I will be glorified.”
echoes.note: 'You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified' provides the servant-glorification pattern behind 'God has been glorified in him... God will glorify him.' The mutual glorifying of God and his agent coheres with John's Servant Christology. The verbal overlap on 'glorified in' is notable.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Love one another' restates 'you shall love your neighbor as yourself,' the OT love command Jesus calls 'new' by christological measure ('as I have loved you'). Availability and recurrence are high; the command is the explicit scriptural substrate of the new commandment. Coherence with the footwashing example is strong.

echoes.text: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah: not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which my covenant they broke, although I was a husband to them, says Yahweh. But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in […]
echoes.note: Calling the love command 'new' evokes the new covenant with the law written on the heart, fitting the Passover/farewell setting. John presents internalized covenant love as the mark of the disciples. The conceptual coherence is strong though the wording is not quoted.

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: The Shema's 'love the LORD your God' stands behind the love command, here redirected to mutual love as the visible sign of belonging to Jesus. Pairing neighbor-love (Lev 19:18) with covenant love is a standard Second-Temple combination. Echo is conceptual.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: The promise of a new heart and spirit enabling obedience underlies the capacity to keep the 'new' commandment of love. The link is thematic to the new-covenant cluster and not verbally explicit. Faint, marked contested.

pericopes.text: Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered, “Where I am going, you can’t follow now, but you will follow afterwards.” Peter said to him, “Lord, why can’t I follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.” Jesus answered him, “Will you lay down your life for me? Most certainly I tell you, the rooster won’t crow until you have denied me three times.

echoes.text: Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.
echoes.note: Peter's confident boast 'I will lay down my life for you,' answered by the prediction of a threefold denial, fits the wisdom pattern that pride precedes a fall. The connection is to a proverbial topos rather than a cited text. Faint and marked contested.

echoes.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
echoes.note: The chapter's frame of intimate failure (betrayal by Judas, denial by Peter) extends the trusted-companion turning-away motif of the cited psalm to the inner circle. The link is structural across the pericopes rather than to the wording here. Faint.

pericopes.text: “Don’t let your heart be troubled. Believe in God. Believe also in me. In my Father’s house are many homes. If it weren’t so, I would have told you. I am going to prepare a place for you. If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and will receive you to myself; that where I am, you may be there also. Where I go, you know, and you know the way.”

echoes.text: Surely goodness and loving kindness shall follow me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in Yahweh’s house forever.
echoes.note: Jesus' promise to receive disciples into the 'Father's house' where they will dwell forever figurally fulfills the psalmist's hope to 'dwell in the house of the LORD forever.' Coherence is strong: John repeatedly reads the temple/house of God Christologically (2:16-21), and the eternal abode (monai) recasts the psalm's permanent residence in God's house. Volume rests on the shared house-dwelling motif rather than a verbal quotation.

echoes.text: One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after, that I may dwell in Yahweh’s house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh’s beauty, and to inquire in his temple.
echoes.note: 'One thing I have asked... to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life' supplies the prototypical longing for permanent residence in God's house that 14:2-3 grants the disciples. Recurrence of the 'house of the LORD as abode' topos in the Psalter strengthens the case; the contestation is that John gives no verbal cue, only the dwelling theme.

echoes.text: How lovely are your dwellings, Yahweh of Armies! My soul longs, and even faints for the courts of Yahweh. My heart and my flesh cry out for the living God. Yes, the sparrow has found a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may have her young, near your altars, Yahweh of Armies, my King, and my God. Blessed are those who dwell in your house. They are always praising you. Selah.
echoes.note: 'How lovely is your dwelling place... blessed are those who dwell in your house' frames the temple as the place of beatitude, the same register behind the 'many rooms' in the Father's house. Low confidence: thematically apt but adds no distinctive lexeme beyond the shared house/dwelling idea, and competes with the other Psalter echoes.

echoes.text: Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them. According to all that I show you, the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all of its furniture, even so you shall make it.
echoes.note: 'Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them' establishes the tabernacle as God's dwelling, the OT substrate John reworks when Jesus prepares an eternal dwelling-place and elsewhere reads his own body as the temple. Figural rather than verbal; the connection runs through John's larger temple Christology more than through 14:2 itself.

echoes.text: They set forward from the Mount of Yahweh three days’ journey. The ark of the covenant of Yahweh went before them three days’ journey, to seek out a resting place for them. The cloud of Yahweh was over them by day, when they set forward from the camp.
echoes.note: The ark going ahead 'to seek out a resting place' for Israel offers a faint Exodus-journey backdrop to Jesus going ahead to 'prepare a place' for his followers. Volume is weak and the lexical overlap thin; flagged low and contested as a possible wilderness-itinerary resonance rather than a deliberate citation.

pericopes.text: Thomas said to him, “Lord, we don’t know where you are going. How can we know the way?” Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me. If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on, you know him, and have seen him.”

echoes.text: Show me your ways, Yahweh. Teach me your paths. Guide me in your truth, and teach me, For you are the God of my salvation, I wait for you all day long.
echoes.note: 'Make me to know your ways, O LORD... lead me in your truth' fuses 'way' and 'truth' in a prayer for divine guidance, the very pairing Jesus claims to embody as 'the way and the truth.' Coherence is high with the Psalter's 'way of the LORD' theology; John transfers the divine path/truth that leads to God onto Jesus himself, who is now the access to the Father.

echoes.text: Teach me your way, Yahweh. I will walk in your truth. Make my heart undivided to fear your name.
echoes.note: 'Teach me your way, O LORD, that I may walk in your truth' again binds 'way' and 'truth' as the route to communion with God, paralleling 14:6's claim that the way and truth lead to the Father. Recurrence of this way/truth collocation across the Psalter raises Volume; the contestation is that John offers no formula-citation, only the absorbed idiom.

echoes.text: A highway will be there, a road, and it will be called The Holy Way. The unclean shall not pass over it, but it will be for those who walk in the Way. Wicked fools will not go there.
echoes.note: The 'Holy Way' on which the redeemed travel to Zion provides a prophetic 'way' that leads God's people home, figurally fulfilled when Jesus is the exclusive 'way' to the Father's house. Coherence with John's homecoming theme (14:2-3) is strong; the singular eschatological highway resonates with Jesus as the one road of return.

echoes.text: Behold, I have set before you this day life and prosperity, and death and evil. For I command you this day to love Yahweh your God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his ordinances, that you may live and multiply, and that Yahweh your God may bless you in the land where you go in to possess it. But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them; I denounce to […]
echoes.note: Moses sets before Israel 'life' and 'the way' of obeying the LORD, the choice that is itself 'your life' and the means to dwell in the land. Jesus' self-identification as 'the way... and the life' recasts this Deuteronomic life-through-the-way into a person; Coherence is reinforced by 14:15's love-and-keep-commandments idiom drawn from the same book.

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
echoes.note: The LORD proclaims himself 'abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (emet/aletheia),' the covenant 'truth' that John's prologue already applied to the incarnate Word (1:14, 'full of grace and truth'). Jesus' claim to be 'the truth' thus draws on the Sinai self-revelation of God's faithfulness; medium confidence given the strong Johannine recurrence of 'truth' language.

echoes.text: “Now therefore, my sons, listen to me, for blessed are those who keep my ways. Hear instruction, and be wise. Don’t refuse it. Blessed is the man who hears me, watching daily at my gates, waiting at my door posts. For whoever finds me, finds life, and will obtain favor from Yahweh.
echoes.note: Wisdom declares 'whoever finds me finds life' and blesses those who keep her 'ways,' supplying a way/life nexus mediated by a personified divine figure. Jesus as 'the way... and the life' through whom one reaches the Father parallels the Wisdom-mediator pattern; low confidence because the verbal links are diffuse and the Wisdom backdrop is more securely felt in John 1.

echoes.text: I have chosen the way of truth. I have set your ordinances before me.
echoes.note: 'I have chosen the way of faithfulness (truth)' once more couples 'way' and 'truth' as the path of covenant fidelity. It adds Recurrence to the way/truth motif behind 14:6 but is too generic on its own; flagged low and contested as cumulative support rather than a discrete source.

pericopes.text: Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us.” Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you such a long time, and do you not know me, Philip? He who has seen me has seen the Father. How do you say, ‘Show us the Father?’ Don’t you believe that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? The words that I tell you, I speak not from myself; but the Father who lives in me does his works. Believe me that I am in the Father, and the Father in me; or else believe me for the very works’ sake.

echoes.text: He said, “Please show me your glory.” He said, “I will make all my goodness pass before you, and will proclaim Yahweh’s name before you. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy.” He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.” Yahweh also said, “Behold, there is a place by me, and you shall stand on the rock. It will happen, while my glory passes by, that I will put you in a cleft of […]
echoes.note: Philip's 'show us the Father' directly replays Moses' 'show me your glory,' to which God replies that no one can see his face and live. John inverts the denial: the one who has seen Jesus has seen the Father, fulfilling the Sinai longing to behold God. High Volume and Coherence given the explicit 'show us'/'show me' request and John's programmatic 'no one has ever seen God; the only Son has made him known' (1:18).

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. He turned again into the camp, but his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, didn’t depart from the Tent.
echoes.note: The LORD spoke to Moses 'face to face, as a man speaks to his friend,' yet 33:20 forbids seeing God's face directly; this tension is exactly what 14:9 resolves by locating the Father's visible presence in Jesus. Coherence with the surrounding Exodus 33 theophany strengthens the medium rating beyond the headline 33:18-23 allusion.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to you out of the midst of the fire: you heard the voice of words, but you saw no form; you only heard a voice.
echoes.note: At Horeb Israel 'heard the sound of words but saw no form,' codifying that God is heard, not seen. Jesus' claim that his words are the Father's and that seeing him is seeing the Father answers this aniconic tradition. Low confidence: thematic counterpoint rather than verbal echo, supporting the 'unseen God' frame behind the pericope.

echoes.text: I will raise them up a prophet from among their brothers, like you. I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I shall command him.
echoes.note: God promises a prophet 'in whose mouth I will put my words... he shall speak all that I command him,' the pattern Jesus claims in 14:10: 'the words I speak are not from myself; the Father does his works.' The prophet-like-Moses speech-formula gives modest Coherence with John's sent-one Christology; low because John does not cite the prophet text here.

echoes.text: With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”
echoes.note: Moses uniquely beholds 'the form of the LORD' and speaks with him 'mouth to mouth,' a near-vision that 14:9 surpasses by granting the disciples the Father in the Son. Faint, contested support for the seeing-God motif; the lexical overlap is limited to the shared theophanic register.

pericopes.text: Most certainly I tell you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father. Whatever you will ask in my name, that will I do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you will ask anything in my name, I will do it.

echoes.text: but your eyes have seen all of Yahweh’s great work which he did.
echoes.note: Israel had 'seen all the great work of the LORD that he did,' framing God's redemptive deeds as 'works' the people witness; Jesus speaks of 'the works that I do' continuing in his followers. Low confidence: 'works of the LORD' is a broad Deuteronomic idiom rather than a targeted source, offering only thematic coloring to 14:12.

echoes.text: Israel served Yahweh all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, and had known all the work of Yahweh, that he had worked for Israel.
echoes.note: Israel served the LORD all the days that the elders 'had known all the work of the LORD that he did for Israel,' another instance of redemptive deeds as 'works.' It reinforces the OT 'works of God' register behind Jesus' 'greater works,' but is too generic to credit as a specific allusion; flagged low and contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh, you will ordain peace for us, for you have also worked all our works for us.
echoes.note: 'You have indeed done all our works for us,' confessing that human works are wrought by God, resonates faintly with 14:12's promise that believers will do the works Jesus does because he goes to the Father. Low and contested: a thematic affinity about divinely-empowered works rather than a deliberate citation.

echoes.text: Yahweh is near to all those who call on him, to all who call on him in truth. He will fulfill the desire of those who fear him. He also will hear their cry, and will save them.
echoes.note: 'The LORD is near to all who call on him... he fulfills the desire of those who fear him' undergirds the answered-petition promise of 14:13-14 ('whatever you ask in my name'). The granting-of-requests motif is widespread in the Psalter; low confidence because no single verse is verbally anchored, though it situates Jesus in the role of the request-granting LORD.

pericopes.text: If you love me, keep my commandments. I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever,— the Spirit of truth, whom the world can’t receive; for it doesn’t see him, neither knows him. You know him, for he lives with you, and will be in you.

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: The Shema's command to 'love the LORD your God' grounds the love-of-God demanded in 14:15, now reoriented to Jesus: 'if you love me, keep my commandments.' Coherence is strong because John fuses love and obedience in the Deuteronomic manner; medium rather than high since the wording is paraphrased and reattributed to Jesus.

echoes.text: Know therefore that Yahweh your God himself is God, the faithful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with them who love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations,
echoes.note: God keeps covenant 'with those who love him and keep his commandments,' the precise love+keep-commandments pairing echoed in 14:15 and 14:21. Recurrence of this formula across Deuteronomy raises Volume; the contestation is that John supplies the idiom without a citation marker.

echoes.text: and showing loving kindness to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.
echoes.note: The Decalogue promises steadfast love 'to those who love me and keep my commandments,' the foundational love-and-obey formula behind 14:15. Strong Coherence with John's repeated linkage of loving Jesus and keeping his word; medium because it is one of several overlapping Pentateuchal sources for the same idiom.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: 'I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes' supplies the new-covenant gift of an indwelling Spirit that produces obedience, exactly the logic of 14:15-17 where loving-and-obeying flows into the Paraclete who 'will be in you.' High Coherence: the Spirit given to dwell within and to enable commandment-keeping is Ezekiel's signature promise.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'The Spirit of the LORD shall rest on him, the Spirit of wisdom... and of knowledge' anchors the messianic 'Spirit of truth' the Father gives in 14:17. Coherence is good because Isaiah's endowing Spirit is a Spirit of knowledge/truth resting permanently; medium given the conceptual rather than verbal link to 'Spirit of truth.'

echoes.text: But they rebelled, and grieved his holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and he himself fought against them. Then he remembered the days of old, Moses and his people, saying, Where is he who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherds of his flock? where is he who put his holy Spirit in their midst?
echoes.note: Israel 'grieved his Holy Spirit,' yet God 'put in the midst of them his Holy Spirit,' one of the rare OT uses of 'his Holy Spirit' that the Paraclete passages presuppose. The motif of God placing his Spirit among the people undergirds 14:16-17's abiding Counselor; medium for the shared 'Holy Spirit' terminology with the wider Isaianic-Spirit complex.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: 'I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh' is the eschatological Spirit-bestowal that 14:16-17 promises in personalized form as the indwelling Paraclete. Coherence is solid within John's realized-eschatology of the Spirit's coming; medium because John individualizes the corporate outpouring and offers no verbal quotation.

echoes.text: This is the word that I covenanted with you when you came out of Egypt, and my Spirit lived among you. ‘Don’t be afraid.’
echoes.note: 'My Spirit remains in your midst; do not fear' couples the abiding Spirit with the dismissal of fear, paralleling the Paraclete who abides 'forever' alongside 14:27's 'let not your heart be afraid.' Low confidence: a suggestive thematic pairing of abiding-Spirit and courage rather than a demonstrable citation.

echoes.text: Yahweh came down in the cloud, and spoke to him, and took of the Spirit that was on him, and put it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, but they did so no more. But two men remained in the camp. The name of one was Eldad, and the name of the other Medad: and the Spirit rested on them; and they were of those who were written, but had not gone out to the Tent; and they prophesied in the camp. A young man ran, and told […]
echoes.note: The LORD takes the Spirit on Moses and places it on the seventy, with Moses wishing all the LORD's people were prophets endowed with the Spirit. This distribution of the Spirit to the community prefigures the Paraclete given to all the disciples; low and contested because the link is conceptual, lacking the 'Spirit of truth' vocabulary.

echoes.text: For a holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit. And will start away from thoughts that are without understanding, And will be put to confusion when unrighteousness has come in.
echoes.note: 'A holy and disciplined spirit will flee from deceit' and (1:7) 'the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world' offer a Second-Temple 'spirit of truth/wisdom that the deceitful world cannot hold,' resonant with 14:17's Spirit 'whom the world cannot receive.' Low confidence: deuterocanonical mood-music supporting the truth-vs-world contrast rather than a direct source.

pericopes.text: I will not leave you orphans. I will come to you. Yet a little while, and the world will see me no more; but you will see me. Because I live, you will live also. In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you. One who has my commandments, and keeps them, that person is one who loves me. One who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and will reveal myself to him.”

echoes.text: You shall no more be termed Forsaken; neither shall your land any more be termed Desolate: but you shall be called Hephzibah, and your land Beulah; for Yahweh delights in you, and your land shall be married.
echoes.note: 'You shall no more be termed Forsaken (Azubah)... for the LORD delights in you' counters abandonment with renewed presence, faintly behind 'I will not leave you orphans (orphanous); I will come to you.' Low confidence: the not-forsaking promise is thematically apt but lacks the orphan lexeme; flagged contested as ambient consolation language.

echoes.text: Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid or scared of them; for Yahweh your God himself is who goes with you. He will not fail you nor forsake you.”
echoes.note: 'He will not leave you or forsake you' is the classic divine-presence assurance, recast in 14:18 as Jesus' pledge not to abandon his own. The not-forsake formula gives modest Coherence with the consolation here; low because John uses the distinctive 'orphans' image rather than the Deuteronomic wording.

echoes.text: No man will be able to stand before you all the days of your life. As I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not fail you nor forsake you.
echoes.note: 'I will not leave you or forsake you,' God's commissioning promise to Joshua, contributes to the OT not-forsake topos standing behind 'I will not leave you orphans.' Recurrence of this formula (Deut/Josh) raises its cumulative Volume slightly, but the link to 14:18 remains thematic; low and contested.

echoes.text: A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.
echoes.note: God as 'father of the fatherless (orphans)' supplies the one strong OT orphan-care motif behind Jesus' refusal to leave the disciples 'orphans.' Figural and contested: the shared orphan vocabulary is suggestive, but John applies it to bereaved disciples rather than to literal orphans, so the connection is allusive at best.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him. Let us acknowledge Yahweh. Let us press on to know Yahweh. As surely as the sun rises, Yahweh will appear. He will come to us like the rain, like the spring rain that waters the earth.”
echoes.note: 'After two days he will revive us... that we may live before him,' a revival-after-a-little-while hope, lightly resonates with 14:19, 'because I live, you also will live,' and 'yet a little while.' Low confidence: the life-after-interval pattern is genuinely parallel but verbally diffuse, and the resurrection-on-the-third-day reading is contested.

pericopes.text: Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, “Lord, what has happened that you are about to reveal yourself to us, and not to the world?” Jesus answered him, “If a man loves me, he will keep my word. My Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our home with him. He who doesn’t love me doesn’t keep my words. The word which you hear isn’t mine, but the Father’s who sent me.

echoes.text: I will set my tent among you, and my soul won’t abhor you. I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you will be my people.
echoes.note: 'I will make my dwelling among you... and I will walk among you and be your God' is the covenant indwelling formula that 14:23 personalizes: 'we will come to him and make our home (monen) with him.' High Coherence because John reuses the same divine-dwelling-with-the-people promise, now realized as Father and Son abiding with the believer.

echoes.text: My tent also shall be with them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
echoes.note: 'My dwelling place shall be with them, and I will be their God,' the new-covenant restatement of God dwelling among his people, reinforces the indwelling promise of 14:23. Recurrence of the 'dwelling with them' formula (Lev/Ezek) strengthens Volume; medium because John gives the topos individual rather than national scope.

echoes.text: Sing and rejoice, daughter of Zion; for, behold, I come, and I will dwell in your midst,’ says Yahweh. Many nations shall join themselves to Yahweh in that day, and shall be my people; and I will dwell in your midst, and you shall know that Yahweh of Armies has sent me to you.
echoes.note: 'I will dwell in your midst... and many nations shall join themselves to the LORD... and shall be my people,' an eschatological in-dwelling promise resonant with the Father and Son making their home with the one who loves Jesus. Low confidence: it adds Recurrence to the divine-indwelling motif but contributes no distinctive wording to 14:23.

echoes.text: These words, which I command you this day, shall be on your heart;
echoes.note: 'These words that I command you... shall be on your heart,' the Shema's call to internalize God's word, undergirds 14:23-24's 'keep my word'/'the word you hear is the Father's.' Low and contested: the keep-the-word idiom is broadly Deuteronomic and not anchored to a single verse here.

pericopes.text: I have said these things to you, while still living with you. But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you. Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, give I to you. Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.

echoes.text: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The Aaronic blessing climaxes 'the LORD... give you peace (shalom),' the priestly bestowal of divine peace that Jesus reissues as 'Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you.' High Coherence: Jesus speaks the priestly gift-of-peace formula directly, distinguishing his giving from the world's, just as the blessing conveys God's own peace.

echoes.text: You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.
echoes.note: 'You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you,' linking peace with an untroubled, trusting heart, parallels 14:27's 'my peace I give... let not your heart be troubled.' Coherence is strong between the peace-and-undisturbed-heart pairing; medium because the connection is thematic rather than a verbal citation.

echoes.text: I create the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace, to him who is far off and to him who is near,” says Yahweh; “and I will heal them.”
echoes.note: 'Peace, peace, to the far and to the near, says the LORD; and I will heal him' is God's gift of peace to his people, the prophetic backdrop to Jesus bestowing his own peace. Medium for the shared divine-gift-of-peace motif; John heightens it by contrasting Jesus' peace with the world's hollow giving.

echoes.text: ‘The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former,’ says Yahweh of Armies; ‘and in this place will I give peace,’ says Yahweh of Armies.”
echoes.note: 'In this place I will give peace, declares the LORD of hosts,' tying peace to the eschatological house/temple, resonates with the farewell peace given amid the 'Father's house' discourse. Low confidence: a thematic temple-peace link rather than a verbal one, supplementing the stronger Aaronic and Isaianic echoes.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: The resting 'Spirit of wisdom and understanding' that teaches and counsels stands behind the Paraclete who 'will teach you all things' (14:26). Low and contested here because the teaching-Spirit link is better located at 14:17; included for the instructive-Spirit motif that the reminder-and-teaching function of the Counselor presupposes.

echoes.text: You gave also your good Spirit to instruct them, and didn’t withhold your manna from their mouth, and gave them water for their thirst.
echoes.note: 'You gave your good Spirit to instruct them,' a rare OT statement of the Spirit as teacher of God's people, parallels the Paraclete who 'will teach you all things.' Low confidence: genuine conceptual match for the teaching-Spirit, but verbally remote and not signaled as a source by John.

pericopes.text: You heard how I told you, ‘I go away, and I come to you.’ If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I said ‘I am going to my Father;’ for the Father is greater than I. Now I have told you before it happens so that, when it happens, you may believe. I will no more speak much with you, for the prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me. But that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father commanded me, even so I do. Arise, let us go from here.

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: 'You shall love the LORD your God' lies behind 14:28's 'if you loved me' and 14:31's 'that the world may know that I love the Father,' transposing the Shema's love onto the Father-Son relation. Low and contested: it reiterates the Deuteronomic love idiom already credited at 14:15, here governing Jesus' own filial love.

echoes.text: Now this is the commandment, the statutes, and the ordinances, which Yahweh your God commanded to teach you, that you might do them in the land where you go over to possess it;
echoes.note: 'The commandment... that the LORD commanded me to teach you' models the obedient mediator who does only as God commanded, the pattern Jesus claims in 14:31, 'as the Father commanded me, so I do.' Low confidence: the as-commanded obedience motif is generically Deuteronomic, supplying coloring rather than a specific source.

echoes.text: He laid his hands on him, and commissioned him, as Yahweh spoke by Moses.
echoes.note: Moses commissions Joshua 'as the LORD directed... so he did,' the do-as-commanded formula echoed in Jesus' 'as the Father commanded me, even so I do.' Low and contested: a faint obedient-agent parallel without verbal anchoring; one of several Pentateuchal 'as commanded, so he did' instances.

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
echoes.note: The protoevangelium's enmity between the serpent and the woman's seed faintly underlies 'the ruler of this world comes, and he has nothing in me,' where the satanic adversary advances but holds no claim on Jesus. Figural and contested: John's 'ruler of this world' draws on a Second-Temple satanology more than on a single Genesis verse, so the link is thematic.

echoes.text: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” Then Satan […]
echoes.note: The Adversary (ha-satan) who roams the earth and is granted limited power over the righteous supplies an OT antecedent for 'the ruler of this world' who comes but 'has nothing in' Jesus. Low confidence: it grounds the accusing-adversary figure conceptually, but John's title and the 'no claim on me' idea outrun anything verbal in Job.

pericopes.text: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer. Every branch in me that doesn’t bear fruit, he takes away. Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit. You are already pruned clean because of the word which I have spoken to you. Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch can’t bear fruit by itself, unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me. I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me, and I in him, the same bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. If a man doesn’t remain in me, he is thrown out as a branch, and is withered; and they gather them, throw them into the fire, and they are burned. If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you desire, and it will be done for you. “In this is my Father glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples.

echoes.text: You brought a vine out of Egypt. You drove out the nations, and planted it. You cleared the ground for it. It took deep root, and filled the land. The mountains were covered with its shadow. Its boughs were like God’s cedars. It sent out its branches to the sea, Its shoots to the River. Why have you broken down its walls, so that all those who pass by the way pluck it? The boar out of the wood ravages it. The wild animals of the field feed on it. Turn […]
echoes.note: The vine 'brought out of Egypt' that God planted and tended is the controlling image Jesus reworks: Israel-as-vine becomes Jesus the true vine. High volume and coherence — Ps 80 also has God's hand burning/cutting the vine (v.16), feeding the imagery of branches thrown into the fire in 15:6, and v.17 'the son of man' whom God strengthens.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The Song of the Vineyard: God's well-tended vineyard yields wild grapes and is judged. Jesus' 'true vine' answers Israel's failure to bear fruit; the Father as vinedresser (georgos) who prunes parallels the owner who tends and then strips Isaiah's vineyard. Strong thematic coherence on fruit-bearing and judgment.

echoes.text: Yet I had planted you a noble vine, wholly a right seed. How then have you turned into the degenerate branches of a foreign vine to me?
echoes.note: 'I planted you a choice vine... how then have you turned degenerate, a wild vine?' The contrast between the genuine (true) vine and the degenerate vine sharpens Jesus' 'I am the TRUE vine' — he is what planted Israel was meant to be. High coherence and availability.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, Son of man, what is the vine tree more than any tree, the vine-branch which is among the trees of the forest? Will wood be taken of it to make anything? Will men take a pin of it to hang any vessel on it? Behold, it is cast into the fire for fuel; the fire has devoured both its ends, and its midst is burned: is it profitable for any work? Behold, when it was whole, it was meet for no work: how much less, when the fire has […]
echoes.note: The vine-wood good for nothing but fuel, burned in the fire — directly underwrites 15:6, branches gathered, cast into fire, and burned. Ezekiel says the unfruitful vine is given to the fire for fuel; the verbal/conceptual link to the withered branch burned is strong.

echoes.text: He took also of the seed of the land, and planted it in a fruitful soil; he placed it beside many waters; he set it as a willow tree. It grew, and became a spreading vine of low stature, whose branches turned toward him, and its roots were under him: so it became a vine, and produced branches, and shot out sprigs. There was also another great eagle with great wings and many feathers: and behold, this vine bent its roots toward him, and shot out its […]
echoes.note: The vine planted and tended, which will or won't flourish and may wither, contributes to the cluster of prophetic vine imagery of planting, pruning and withering behind 15:1-6. Recurrence within the vine-of-Israel tradition strengthens it even though no single verbal quotation.

echoes.text: Your mother was like a vine, in your blood, planted by the waters: it was fruitful and full of branches by reason of many waters. It had strong rods for the scepters of those who bore rule, and their stature was exalted among the thick boughs, and they were seen in their height with the multitude of their branches. But it was plucked up in fury, it was cast down to the ground, and the east wind dried up its fruit: its strong rods were broken off and […]
echoes.note: Israel as a fruitful vine plucked up in fury, withered, and consumed by fire — same fruit/wither/fire complex as 15:2,6. Part of the recurrent Ezekiel vine-judgment tradition Jesus inverts as the true vine that abides.

echoes.text: Israel is a luxuriant vine that produces his fruit. According to the abundance of his fruit he has multiplied his altars. As their land has prospered, they have adorned their sacred stones.
echoes.note: 'Israel is a luxuriant vine that yields its fruit' yet turns to idolatry. Reinforces the vine-of-Israel topos of fruit that should but fails to glorify God, the backdrop for the true vine bearing 'much fruit' to the Father's glory (15:8).

echoes.text: He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.
echoes.note: The righteous as a tree planted by water 'that yields its fruit in its season' and does not wither frames the abiding/fruit-bearing/withering antithesis of 15:2-6. Coherence with the abide-and-bear-fruit motif; tree rather than vine, so a softer echo.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose trust Yahweh is. For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and shall not fear when heat comes, but its leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.
echoes.note: The one who trusts the Lord is like a tree planted by water that does not cease to bear fruit even in drought. Parallels remaining/abiding and continual fruit-bearing of the abiding branch (15:4-5); shares the 'not wither / bears fruit' contrast.

echoes.text: In that day, sing to her, “A pleasant vineyard! I, Yahweh, am its keeper. I will water it every moment. Lest anyone damage it, I will keep it night and day. Wrath is not in me, but if I should find briers and thorns, I would do battle! I would march on them and I would burn them together. Or else let him take hold of my strength, that he may make peace with me. Let him make peace with me.” In days to come, Jacob will take root. Israel will blossom and […]
echoes.note: The restored 'pleasant vineyard' that God keeps and waters night and day so Jacob 'shall fill the whole world with fruit' — the eschatological reversal of Isa 5. Jesus the true vine realizes this fruitful vineyard; coherence with 15:8's much fruit and the keeping/tending Father.

echoes.text: Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine; he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.
echoes.note: Judah's blessing binds the foal 'to the vine, his donkey's colt to the choice vine,' a messianic vine image read of the coming ruler. A faint contributory resonance to messianic 'true vine' typology rather than a direct source.

echoes.text: As the vine I put forth grace; And my flowers are the fruit of glory and riches.
echoes.note: Wisdom says 'I spread out my branches like a terebinth... like a vine I caused loveliness to bud, and my blossoms became glorious and abundant fruit.' Personified Wisdom as a fruitful vine offers a Second-Temple analogue to the 'I am the vine' self-predication, supporting the figural reading.

pericopes.text: Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love; even as I have kept my Father’s commandments, and remain in his love. I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full. “This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends, if you do whatever I command you. No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you. You didn’t choose me, but I chose you, and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain; that whatever you will ask of the Father in my name, he may give it to you. “I command these things to you, that you may love one another.

echoes.text: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. Yahweh your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth. Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, […]
echoes.note: 'You did not choose me, but I chose you' (15:16) echoes Israel's election: the Lord chose them not for their merit but in love. Strong coherence on divine election and love; covenantal keeping of commandments (15:10) belongs to the same Deuteronomic frame.

echoes.text: “But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend,
echoes.note: 'Abraham my friend' (lit. the one who loved me) — the title 'friend of God' Jesus confers, 'I have called you friends' (15:14-15). The friendship/election language ('Israel... whom I have chosen, offspring of Abraham my friend') gives high availability and coherence to the friend motif.

echoes.text: Didn’t you, our God, drive out the inhabitants of this land before your people Israel, and give it to the seed of Abraham your friend forever?
echoes.note: 'Abraham your friend' — second OT witness to the Abraham-as-friend-of-God title that 'you are my friends' (15:14) actualizes for the disciples. Recurrence with Isa 41:8 strengthens the friend-of-God tradition behind the saying.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. He turned again into the camp, but his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, didn’t depart from the Tent.
echoes.note: The Lord spoke to Moses 'as a man speaks to his friend' — the paradigm of intimate friendship with God in which the friend is told the divine purposes, matching 15:15: not servants but friends, 'for everything I heard from my Father I have made known to you.'

echoes.text: Yahweh said, “Will I hide from Abraham what I do, since Abraham has surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth will be blessed in him? For I have known him, to the end that he may command his children and his household after him, that they may keep the way of Yahweh, to do righteousness and justice; to the end that Yahweh may bring on Abraham that which he has spoken of him.”
echoes.note: 'Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?' — the friend of God is not kept ignorant of the master's plans, precisely the logic of 15:15 ('the servant doesn't know what his lord does... I have made known to you'). Coherence with the friend-vs-servant distinction.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Love your neighbor as yourself' underlies the new commandment to 'love one another' (15:12,17). Availability and thematic coherence are strong, though Jesus reframes the measure as 'as I have loved you.'

echoes.text: When he had made an end of speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul. Saul took him that day, and would let him go no more home to his father’s house. Then Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul.
echoes.note: Jonathan's covenant love for David, loving him 'as his own soul' and risking his life, is the paradigmatic OT instance of self-giving friendship behind 'greater love has no one than to lay down his life for his friends' (15:13). Faint but coherent.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The vineyard the Beloved tends out of love continues from 15:1-8 into the love/fruit language here (15:9-16); election to 'go and bear fruit that should remain' recalls God's purpose for his loved vineyard. Secondary recurrence of the chapter's controlling image.

pericopes.text: If the world hates you, you know that it has hated me before it hated you. If you were of the world, the world would love its own. But because you are not of the world, since I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you. Remember the word that I said to you: ‘A servant is not greater than his lord.’If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will keep yours also. But all these things will they do to you for my name’s sake, because they don’t know him who sent me. If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have had sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin. He who hates me, hates my Father also. If I hadn’t done among them the works which no one else did, they wouldn’t have had sin. But now have they seen and also hated both me and my Father. But this happened so that the word may be fulfilled which was written in their law, ‘They hated me without a cause.’

echoes.text: Don’t let those who are my enemies wrongfully rejoice over me; neither let those who hate me without a cause wink their eyes.
echoes.note: 'Let not those who hate me without cause wink the eye.' One of the two psalms behind the explicit citation 'They hated me without a cause' (15:25), introduced as 'written in their law.' Verbal correspondence to the hate-without-cause phrase is exact; a Davidic-righteous-sufferer text.

echoes.text: Those who hate me without a cause are more than the hairs of my head. Those who want to cut me off, being my enemies wrongfully, are mighty. I have to restore what I didn’t take away.
echoes.note: 'More than the hairs of my head are those who hate me without cause.' The other source of 15:25's formula; Ps 69 is heavily used of Jesus' passion elsewhere, raising its likelihood here. Exact verbal match to 'hated me without a cause.'

echoes.text: They have also surrounded me with words of hatred, and fought against me without a cause.
echoes.note: 'They... attack me without cause' — a further Davidic lament of causeless hatred in the same psalmic stream that supplies 15:25. A contributory background witness rather than the cited text.

echoes.text: But my enemies are vigorous and many. Those who hate me without reason are numerous.
echoes.note: 'Those who hate me wrongfully are mighty' — another lament-of-the-righteous text echoing causeless hatred of the innocent sufferer, coherent with the world's hatred theme (15:18-25) and the citation in 15:25.

echoes.text: Ahab said to Elijah, “Have you found me, my enemy?” He answered, “I have found you, because you have sold yourself to do that which is evil in the sight of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Have you found me, O my enemy?' / hating the prophet who confronts sin parallels 15:22-24: the world hates Jesus because his coming and works expose its sin, leaving it 'no excuse.' A faint resonance with the prophetic pattern of being hated for exposing guilt.

echoes.text: Hear Yahweh’s word, you who tremble at his word: “Your brothers who hate you, who cast you out for my name’s sake, have said, ‘Let Yahweh be glorified, that we may see your joy;’ but it is those who shall be disappointed.
echoes.note: 'Your brothers who hate you and cast you out for my name's sake' anticipates being persecuted 'for my name's sake' (15:21). The phrase about suffering on account of God's name gives coherence to the disciples' share in the world's hatred.

pericopes.text: “When the Counselorhas come, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will testify about me. You will also testify, because you have been with me from the beginning.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'The Spirit of the Lord shall rest on him, the Spirit of wisdom... and knowledge' grounds the title 'the Spirit of truth' (15:26) in the prophetic Spirit who imparts true knowledge of God. Coherence with the Spirit's testifying/witness role; medium volume.

echoes.text: Then he answered and spoke to me, saying, “This is Yahweh’s word to Zerubbabel, saying, ‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'Not by might... but by my Spirit, says the Lord' — divine action accomplished by the Spirit rather than human power, a backdrop to the Paraclete's empowering witness (15:26-27). A faint thematic echo rather than verbal.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: The promised outpouring of the Spirit on God's people stands behind Jesus' promise to 'send' the Spirit who, with the disciples, testifies (15:26-27). Availability of the eschatological Spirit-gift tradition; low verbal contact.

echoes.text: Yahweh came down in the cloud, and spoke to him, and took of the Spirit that was on him, and put it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, but they did so no more. But two men remained in the camp. The name of one was Eldad, and the name of the other Medad: and the Spirit rested on them; and they were of those who were written, but had not gone out to the Tent; and they prophesied in the camp. A young man ran, and told […]
echoes.note: The Spirit placed on the elders so they prophesy, and Moses' wish that all the Lord's people might have the Spirit, anticipates the Spirit given so the disciples 'also testify' (15:27). Faint coherence with Spirit-enabled witness.

pericopes.text: “These things have I spoken to you, so that you wouldn’t be caused to stumble. They will put you out of the synagogues. Yes, the time comes that whoever kills you will think that he offers service to God. They will do these thingsbecause they have not known the Father, nor me. But I have told you these things, so that when the time comes, you may remember that I told you about them. I didn’t tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you.

echoes.text: Behold, one of the children of Israel came and brought to his brothers a Midianite woman in the sight of Moses, and in the sight of all the congregation of the children of Israel, while they were weeping at the door of the Tent of Meeting. When Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, saw it, he rose up from the midst of the congregation, and took a spear in his hand. He went after the man of Israel into the pavilion, and thrust both of […]
echoes.note: 'Whoever kills you will think that he offers service to God' figurally invokes the Phinehas-zeal pattern, where killing in defense of God's honor is reckoned righteous and brings a covenant of priesthood. John frames synagogue persecution as misdirected cultic zeal; coherence with the prophet-killing motif is high, and Phinehas was the paradigmatic Second-Temple model of lethal zeal (1 Macc 2:26, 54).

echoes.text: Because for your sake, I have borne reproach. Shame has covered my face. I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother’s children. For the zeal of your house consumes me. The reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me.
echoes.note: Persecution 'for your sake' / zeal for God's house consuming the persecutor sits behind the idea that opponents act in supposed devotion. John 2:17 already cited this psalm, so recurrence within the Gospel supports a faint echo of the zeal-as-cover motif, but volume here is thin.

echoes.text: Hear Yahweh’s word, you who tremble at his word: “Your brothers who hate you, who cast you out for my name’s sake, have said, ‘Let Yahweh be glorified, that we may see your joy;’ but it is those who shall be disappointed.
echoes.note: Isaiah 66:5 speaks of brethren who hate and cast out the faithful 'for my name's sake,' claiming it is God who is glorified — strikingly close to expulsion from the synagogue done as service to God. Volume and coherence are strong; the verb of casting out the faithful from the cultic community matches John's aposynagogos.

echoes.text: The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’” They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house. Thus Joash the king didn’t remember the kindness which Jehoiada his […]
echoes.note: The killing of Zechariah the prophet in the temple court typifies prophets slain by the very people of God under pretense of fidelity. As a representative of the persecuted-prophets tradition it coheres with Jesus' warning that disciples will be killed by those who think they serve God.

pericopes.text: But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’ But because I have told you these things, sorrow has filled your heart. Nevertheless I tell you the truth: It is to your advantage that I go away, for if I don’t go away, the Counselor won’t come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you. When he has come, he will convict the world about sin, about righteousness, and about judgment; about sin, because they don’t believe in me; about righteousness, because I am going to my Father, and you won’t see me any more; about judgment, because the prince of this world has been judged.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh. His delight will be in the fear of Yahweh. He will not judge by the sight of his eyes, neither decide by the hearing of his ears; but with righteousness he will judge the poor, and decide with equity for the humble of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth; and with the […]
echoes.note: The Paraclete as 'Spirit of truth' who convicts the world recalls the Spirit of the LORD resting on the shoot of Jesse — wisdom, counsel, and judging with righteousness, reproving the earth. The convicting/judicial function of the Spirit (krinei, elenxei) coheres tightly with Isaiah's Spirit-endowed righteous judge.

echoes.text: Produce your cause,” says Yahweh. “Bring out your strong reasons,” says the King of Jacob. “Let them announce, and declare to us what shall happen. Declare the former things, what they are, that we may consider them, and know the latter end of them; or show us things to come. Declare the things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that you are gods. Yes, do good, or do evil, that we may be dismayed, and see it together. Behold, you are of nothing, […]
echoes.note: The Spirit convicting 'the world about sin, righteousness, and judgment' enacts the divine lawsuit (rib) of Deutero-Isaiah, where God prosecutes the nations and their idols, exposing their case as nothing. John's forensic vocabulary (elenchein, krisis, dikaiosyne) coheres with the Isaianic courtroom, supplying the conceptual matrix for the Paraclete's prosecutorial role.

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
echoes.note: 'The prince of this world has been judged' figurally evokes the protoevangelium's sentence on the serpent, read in Second-Temple tradition as the crushing of the adversary. The judgment of the ruler coheres with John's wider serpent/devil typology (8:44), though the verbal link is faint.

echoes.text: It shall happen in that day that Yahweh will punish the army of the high ones on high, and the kings of the earth on the earth. They shall be gathered together, as prisoners are gathered in the pit, and shall be shut up in the prison; and after many days shall they be visited.
echoes.note: Isaiah foretells the LORD punishing 'the host of the high ones' and the kings of the earth, shut up and visited after many days — a judgment of cosmic rulers that prefigures the 'prince of this world' being judged. The motif of a heavenly ruler subjected to verdict coheres with John 16:11.

echoes.text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”
echoes.note: The satan/accuser rebuked and condemned in the heavenly court anticipates the ruler of this world being judged. The forensic setting where the accuser is himself overruled coheres with the Paraclete (Advocate) replacing the prosecuting adversary.

pericopes.text: “I have yet many things to tell you, but you can’t bear them now. However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will declare to you things that are coming. He will glorify me, for he will take from what is mine, and will declare it to you. All things whatever the Father has are mine; therefore I said that he takesof mine, and will declare it to you.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: The 'Spirit of truth' who guides into all truth draws on the Spirit of wisdom and understanding; the leading/guiding function recalls the Spirit as teacher. Recurrence of the Spirit-of-truth title in John strengthens the Isaianic resonance.

echoes.text: Guide me in your truth, and teach me, For you are the God of my salvation, I wait for you all day long.
echoes.note: 'Guide me in your truth and teach me' supplies the precise idiom of being led/guided into truth (hodegein + aletheia in LXX), matching 'he will guide you into all truth.' Volume is notable because the verb and noun co-occur as in John 16:13.

echoes.text: Teach me to do your will, for you are my God. Your Spirit is good. Lead me in the land of uprightness.
echoes.note: 'Your good Spirit will lead me' pairs the divine Spirit with guidance into right paths, coherent with the Paraclete leading disciples. The conjunction of Spirit and leading reinforces the guidance motif though the wording is more distant than Psalm 25.

echoes.text: Surely the Lord Yahweh will do nothing, unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets.
echoes.note: 'The Lord GOD will do nothing but he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets' undergirds 'he will declare to you things that are coming' — the Spirit functioning as the prophetic revealer of God's hidden future. Coherence with the disclosure-of-the-future clause is good though the allusion is diffuse.

echoes.text: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these: as for you, O king, your thoughts came on your bed, what should happen hereafter; and he who reveals secrets has made known to you what shall happen.
echoes.note: 'There is a God in heaven who reveals secrets and has made known what shall come to pass' parallels the Spirit declaring 'things that are coming.' The apocalyptic disclosure of the future coheres with the Paraclete's revelatory role.

pericopes.text: A little while, and you will not see me. Again a little while, and you will see me.” Some of his disciples therefore said to one another, “What is this that he says to us, ‘A little while, and you won’t see me, and again a little while, and you will see me;’ and, ‘Because I go to the Father’?” They said therefore, “What is this that he says, ‘A little while’? We don’t know what he is saying.” Therefore Jesus perceived that they wanted to ask him, and he said to them, “Do you inquire among yourselves concerning this, that I said, ‘A little while, and you won’t see me, and again a little while, and you will see me?’ Most certainly I tell you, that you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy. A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow, because her time has come. But when she has delivered the child, she doesn’t remember the anguish any more, for the joy that a human being is born into the world. Therefore you now have sorrow, but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy away from you.

echoes.text: Like as a woman with child, who draws near the time of her delivery, is in pain and cries out in her pangs; so we have been before you, Yahweh. We have been with child. We have been in pain. We gave birth, it seems, only to wind. We have not worked any deliverance in the earth; neither have the inhabitants of the world fallen. Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of […]
echoes.note: The woman in labor whose anguish turns to deliverance, set beside resurrection ('your dead shall live'), is the controlling figure behind sorrow-turned-to-joy and 'I will see you again.' Volume is high (extended birth-pang image), recurrence strong in the prophets, and coherence with John's death-to-resurrection movement is exact.

echoes.text: “Before she travailed, she gave birth; before her pain came, she delivered a son. Who has heard such a thing? who has seen such things? Shall a land be born in one day? shall a nation be born at once? for as soon as Zion travailed, she gave birth to her children. Shall I bring to the birth, and not cause to be delivered?” says Yahweh: “shall I who cause to give birth shut the womb?” says your God. “Rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad for her, all you who […]
echoes.note: Zion's painless birth issuing in joy, comfort, and rejoicing hearts ('your heart shall rejoice') is closely echoed by 'your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy away.' The labor-to-joy reversal and the explicit heart-rejoicing give high volume and coherence.
