echoes.text: Now why do you cry out aloud? Is there no king in you? Has your counselor perished, that pains have taken hold of you as of a woman in travail? Be in pain, and labor to give birth, daughter of Zion, like a woman in travail; for now you will go out of the city, and will dwell in the field, and will come even to Babylon. There you will be rescued. There Yahweh will redeem you from the hand of your enemies.
echoes.note: Zion in labor 'like a woman in travail' who must groan before being delivered prefigures the disciples' pangs preceding deliverance. The eschatological birth-pang motif coheres with Jesus' 'her time has come' / 'a human being is born into the world.'

echoes.text: Ask now, and see whether a man does travail with child: why do I see every man with his hands on his waist, as a woman in travail, and all faces are turned into paleness? Alas! for that day is great, so that none is like it: it is even the time of Jacob’s trouble; but he shall be saved out of it.
echoes.note: The day of distress likened to a man in the pangs of a woman in labor — Jacob's trouble out of which he is saved — supplies the tribulation-then-salvation structure of 16:20-22. Coherence with the messianic 'birth-pangs' tradition is strong.

echoes.text: Come, my people, enter into your rooms, and shut your doors behind you. Hide yourself for a little moment, until the indignation is past.
echoes.note: 'Hide yourselves for a little while (mikron) until the indignation passes' is the closest LXX source for the repeated 'a little while' bracketing distress before vindication. The mikron-then-deliverance pattern coheres tightly with 16:16-19.

echoes.text: For this is what Yahweh of Armies says: ‘Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land;
echoes.note: 'Yet once, it is a little while (mikron), and I will shake the heavens' offers an eschatological 'little while' before God's decisive intervention. It supports the 'little while' time-marker, though the shaking-the-cosmos context is only loosely coherent.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him. Let us acknowledge Yahweh. Let us press on to know Yahweh. As surely as the sun rises, Yahweh will appear. He will come to us like the rain, like the spring rain that waters the earth.”
echoes.note: 'After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him' undergirds the short-interval-then-seeing-again pattern of 'a little while... and you will see me.' The revival-after-brief-interval coheres with the resurrection sense, though John does not cite it.

echoes.text: For his anger is but for a moment. His favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning.
echoes.note: 'Weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning' is a tight aphoristic match for 'you will weep and lament... but your sorrow will be turned into joy.' The night-weeping/morning-joy reversal coheres precisely with the sorrow-to-joy promise.

echoes.text: Then shall the virgin rejoice in the dance, and the young men and the old together; for I will turn their mourning into joy, and will comfort them, and make them rejoice from their sorrow.
echoes.note: 'I will turn their mourning into joy, and will comfort them, and make them rejoice from their sorrow' is verbally close to 'your sorrow will be turned into joy.' The turning-of-mourning-to-joy in the new-covenant restoration passage gives strong coherence.

pericopes.text: “In that day you will ask me no questions. Most certainly I tell you, whatever you may ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you. Until now, you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be made full. I have spoken these things to you in figures of speech. But the time is coming when I will no more speak to you in figures of speech, but will tell you plainly about the Father. In that day you will ask in my name; and I don’t say to you, that I will pray to the Father for you, for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me, and have believed that I came from God. I came from the Father, and have come into the world. Again, I leave the world, and go to the Father.”

echoes.text: Also delight yourself in Yahweh, and he will give you the desires of your heart.
echoes.note: 'Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart' resonates with 'whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it.' The granting-of-petitions motif coheres, though the link is generic to OT prayer theology.

echoes.text: It shall happen that, before they call, I will answer; and while they are yet speaking, I will hear.
echoes.note: 'Before they call, I will answer' frames the eschatological 'in that day' when asking yields immediate granting, coherent with 16:23-24's day of unhindered prayer. The new-creation setting matches John's 'in that day' marker.

echoes.text: With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”
echoes.note: God speaks to Moses 'mouth to mouth, clearly (plainly), and not in dark speeches' — the plain-speech vs. figures-of-speech contrast (16:25) echoes the riddle/plain-revelation distinction. Coherence with 'no more speak in figures but tell you plainly' is suggestive.

pericopes.text: His disciples said to him, “Behold, now you speak plainly, and speak no figures of speech. Now we know that you know all things, and don’t need for anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came from God.” Jesus answered them, “Do you now believe? Behold, the time is coming, yes, and has now come, that you will be scattered, everyone to his own place, and you will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me. I have told you these things, that in me you may have peace. In the world you have oppression; but cheer up! I have overcome the world.”

echoes.text: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is close to me,” says Yahweh of Armies. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; and I will turn my hand against the little ones.
echoes.note: 'Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered' lies behind 'you will be scattered, everyone to his own place, and you will leave me alone.' The scattering-of-the-flock-at-the-shepherd's-smiting is a recognized passion testimony; coherence is strong even without formal citation.

echoes.text: Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing? The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying, “Let’s break their bonds apart, and cast their cords from us.” He who sits in the heavens will laugh. The Lord will have them in derision. Then he will speak to them in his anger, and terrify them in his wrath: “Yet I have set my King on my holy hill of Zion.” I will tell […]
echoes.note: 'I have overcome the world' enacts the divine-warrior/royal-Son motif of Psalm 2, where the nations rage but the enthroned Son subdues them. The cosmic conquest coheres with John's 'ruler of this world' being judged and the Son's victory over a hostile world.

echoes.text: For to us a child is born. To us a son is given; and the government will be on his shoulders. His name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. Of the increase of his government and of peace there shall be no end, on the throne of David, and on his kingdom, to establish it, and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from that time on, even forever. The zeal of Yahweh of Armies will perform this.
echoes.note: 'That in me you may have peace' amid tribulation evokes the messianic 'Prince of Peace' whose government brings peace without end. The peace-in-the-Son motif coheres with John's farewell shalom (cf. 14:27), though volume here is low.

echoes.text: Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.
echoes.note: 'Fear not, for I am with you' undergirds 'cheer up!' and 'the Father is with me' as divine-presence reassurance against a hostile world. The do-not-fear / I-am-with-you formula coheres with Jesus' encouragement, though it is a widespread OT idiom.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The everlasting dominion given to the one like a son of man, that all should serve him, frames 'I have overcome the world' as the Son of Man's universal triumph over the nations. The cosmic victory coheres with Johannine exaltation, though the link is thematic.

pericopes.text: Jesus said these things, and lifting up his eyes to heaven, he said, “Father, the time has come. Glorify your Son, that your Son may also glorify you; even as you gave him authority over all flesh, he will give eternal life to all whom you have given him. This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ. I glorified you on the earth. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do. Now, Father, glorify me with your own self with the glory which I had with you before the world existed.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'You gave him authority over all flesh' (v2) reprises the one like a son of man to whom 'was given dominion... that all peoples should serve him.' High Volume in the verbal pairing of given-authority + universal scope; Recurrence is strong since Johannine and Synoptic Son of Man material draws steadily on Dan 7. Coherent with John's glorification-by-exaltation logic.

echoes.text: “Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed. When there were no depths, I was born, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains were settled in place, before the hills, I was born; while as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the beginning of the dust of the world. When he established the heavens, I was […]
echoes.note: 'The glory which I had with you before the world existed' (v5) figures the Son after personified Wisdom, who was beside God 'before the beginning of the earth' rejoicing in the inhabited world. Availability and Recurrence are high in Johannine Logos/Wisdom Christology (cf. John 1); the conceptual fit (preexistent agent of creation, delight/glory shared) is strong though the wording is not quoted.

echoes.text: Before the mountains were born, before you had formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, you are God.
echoes.note: 'Before the world existed' (v5) echoes 'before the mountains were brought forth, or ever you had formed the earth... from everlasting.' The temporal formula for divine pre-creation eternity coheres with the Son's claim to preexistent glory; Volume modest, supported by the same idiom in Wisdom traditions.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: 'Before the world existed' (v5) presupposes the creation account's absolute beginning, the backdrop against which the Son's pre-cosmic glory is asserted. Faint by itself but coherent with John 1:1's deliberate 'In the beginning' recasting of Genesis.

echoes.text: The heavens, the earth, and all their vast array were finished. On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done.
echoes.note: 'I have accomplished the work which you gave me to do' (v4) faintly mirrors God finishing the work of creation and resting. Possible figural completion-of-work motif, but the language is generic; marked contested for low Volume.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God' (v3) recasts 'let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD.' Knowing God as the supreme good is the load-bearing parallel; high Coherence with John's salvific epistemology and strong Recurrence of this Jeremianic theme in Second-Temple piety.

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: 'That they should know you' as life (v3) resonates with 'I desire... the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.' Knowledge of God as the heart of the covenant relationship supplies a coherent OT substratum, though John intensifies it to eternal life.

echoes.text: For to be acquainted with you is perfect righteousness, And to know your dominion is the root of immortality.
echoes.note: 'To know your power is the root of immortality' is a remarkably close conceptual antecedent to 'this is eternal life, that they should know you' (v3). Availability (deuterocanonical, pre-Johannine) and Coherence are high; the equation knowledge-of-God = immortality is nearly verbal, strengthening the case as a Second-Temple bridge.

echoes.text: For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of Yahweh’s glory, as the waters cover the sea.
echoes.note: 'They should know you' coupled with 'glorify' (vv1-3) faintly recalls 'the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD.' Knowledge-plus-glory cluster offers thematic coherence but Volume is low and diffuse.

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.
echoes.note: 'The only true God' (v3) presses the Shema's confession of the one LORD. Monotheistic exclusivity is the coherent backdrop, and John's 'only true' renders the Shema's uniqueness; modest Volume since the wording is interpretive rather than quoted.

echoes.text: He created me from the beginning before the world; And to the end I will not fail.
echoes.note: Personified Wisdom 'created before the ages' supplies a Second-Temple analogue to the Son's glory 'before the world existed' (v5). Reinforces the Wisdom-preexistence channel alongside Proverbs 8; low independent Volume.

pericopes.text: I revealed your name to the people whom you have given me out of the world. They were yours, and you have given them to me. They have kept your word. Now they have known that all things whatever you have given me are from you, for the words which you have given me I have given to them, and they received them, and knew for sure that I came from you, and they have believed that you sent me. I pray for them. I don’t pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours. All things that are mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’” God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.
echoes.note: 'I revealed your name to the people' (v6) figures Jesus' mission as the disclosure of the divine Name first given at the bush, where God names himself I AM and 'this is my name forever.' John's recurrent egō eimi sayings make this Name-revelation channel highly coherent and recurrent.

echoes.text: He said, “I will make all my goodness pass before you, and will proclaim Yahweh’s name before you. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy.”
echoes.note: 'I revealed your name' (v6) draws on the LORD's promise 'I will proclaim before you my name, the LORD.' The pattern of God making his Name known through a mediator coheres with the prayer's theology; Volume modest but the Name-proclamation motif recurs across the chapter (vv11,26).

echoes.text: Yahweh descended in the cloud, and stood with him there, and proclaimed Yahweh’s name. Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth, keeping loving kindness for thousands, forgiving iniquity and disobedience and sin; and that will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, and on the children’s children, on the […]
echoes.note: The Sinai theophany where the LORD 'proclaimed the name of the LORD' (grace, truth, steadfast love) underlies 'I revealed your name' (v6) and feeds John's grace-and-truth framework. Coherent and recurrent with John 1:14-17; the manifest-Name act is the shared structure.

echoes.text: Therefore my people shall know my name. Therefore they shall know in that day that I am he who speaks; behold, it is I.”
echoes.note: 'Therefore my people shall know my name' anticipates 'I revealed your name to the people... they have known' (vv6-7). The eschatological Name-knowledge promised to the elect people coheres tightly with Jesus' report to the Father; moderate Volume via the shared name/know pairing.

echoes.text: I will declare your name to my brothers. In the midst of the assembly, I will praise you.
echoes.note: 'I will tell of your name to my brothers' is the psalmist's vow that 'I revealed your name to the people whom you gave me' (v6) enacts. Recurrence is strong (Ps 22 pervades the Johannine passion); Coherence high since the speaker declares the Name to a given community.

echoes.text: He said of his father, and of his mother, ‘I have not seen him.’ He didn’t acknowledge his brothers, nor did he know his own children; for they have observed your word, and keep your covenant.
echoes.note: 'They have kept your word' (v6) echoes Levi who 'kept your word and held to your covenant.' The covenant-fidelity idiom for the consecrated supports the priestly coloring of the prayer; low Volume, generic phrasing.

echoes.text: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. Yahweh your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth.
echoes.note: 'The people whom you have given me out of the world... they were yours' (vv6,9) recasts Israel as God's own chosen possession 'out of all peoples.' Election-from-the-nations language is the coherent backdrop, though John substitutes 'world' for 'peoples'; low Volume.

pericopes.text: I am no more in the world, but these are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them through your name which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are. While I was with them in the world, I kept them in your name. Those whom you have given me I have kept. None of them is lost, except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.

echoes.text: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’ “So they shall put my name on the children of Israel; and I will bless them.”
echoes.note: 'Holy Father, keep them through your name' (v11) figures the Aaronic blessing where the LORD 'keep you' and 'so shall they put my name upon the people of Israel, and I will bless them.' The conjunction of keeping + the Name placed on the people is a strong, specific structural parallel to Jesus' priestly petition.

echoes.text: and join them for you one to another into one stick, that they may become one in your hand.
echoes.note: 'That they may be one, even as we are' (v11) figures the two sticks joined 'that they may become one in your hand,' Ezekiel's sign of regathered, unified Israel. The oneness-of-the-people motif is coherent with John's unity petitions (vv21-23) and recurs there, strengthening the figural reading.

echoes.text: For then I will purify the lips of the peoples, that they may all call on Yahweh’s name, to serve him shoulder to shoulder.
echoes.note: Keeping the people in the Name 'that they may be one' (v11) echoes the promise that purified peoples will 'call upon the name of the LORD and serve him with one accord' (lit. one shoulder). Name + unity cluster is coherent though the Volume is faint.

echoes.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
echoes.note: 'None of them is lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled' (v12) points to 'my close friend... who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me,' the betrayal text John explicitly cites at 13:18. High Coherence and Recurrence make this the leading scriptural referent for the fulfillment formula here.

echoes.text: Let his days be few. Let another take his office.
echoes.note: 'The son of destruction' whose loss fulfills Scripture (v12) is illumined by 'may his days be few; may another take his office,' the imprecation later applied to Judas in Acts. The betrayer-who-must-be-replaced motif coheres with the fulfillment claim; medium since John does not quote it here.

echoes.text: After this, Absalom prepared him a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him. Absalom rose up early, and stood beside the way of the gate. It was so, that when any man had a suit which should come to the king for judgment, then Absalom called to him, and said, “What city are you from?” He said, “Your servant is of one of the tribes of Israel.” Absalom said to him, “Behold, your matters are good and right; but there is no man deputized by the […]
echoes.note: The 'son of destruction' (v12) is typologically prefigured by Ahithophel, David's trusted counselor who betrays him, crosses with him over the brook, and hangs himself. The David/Jesus typology with a betraying intimate provides coherent, recurrent narrative substance behind Judas; figural rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Against whom do you sport yourselves? Against whom do you make a wide mouth, and stick out your tongue? Aren’t you children of disobedience, a seed of falsehood,
echoes.note: The Semitic idiom 'son of destruction/perdition' (v12) resembles prophetic 'children of transgression, offspring of deceit.' Supplies an OT pattern for the 'son of X' designation of the doomed, but the specific phrase is not borrowed; low Volume, contested.

pericopes.text: But now I come to you, and I say these things in the world, that they may have my joy made full in themselves. I have given them your word. The world hated them, because they are not of the world, even as I am not of the world. I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world even as I am not of the world.

echoes.text: You will show me the path of life. In your presence is fullness of joy. In your right hand there are pleasures forever more.
echoes.note: 'That they may have my joy made full in themselves' (v13) resonates with 'in your presence there is fullness of joy.' The eschatological-fullness-of-joy-before-God motif is coherent with Jesus' departure-to-the-Father context; moderate Volume on the shared joy/fullness pairing.

echoes.text: Those who hate me without a cause are more than the hairs of my head. Those who want to cut me off, being my enemies wrongfully, are mighty. I have to restore what I didn’t take away.
echoes.note: 'The world hated them' (v14) draws on 'those who hate me without cause are more than the hairs of my head,' a psalm John cites for groundless hatred (cf. 15:25 'they hated me without a cause'). Recurrence in the Johannine farewell makes the hatred-without-cause echo coherent here.

echoes.text: Yahweh will keep you from all evil. He will keep your soul.
echoes.note: 'Keep them from the evil one' (v15) parallels 'The LORD will keep you from all evil; he will keep your life.' The divine keeping/guarding-from-evil idiom is coherent with the prayer's repeated 'keep' language (vv11-12), though 'the evil one' personalizes it; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
echoes.note: 'Keep them from the evil one' (v15) faintly invokes the primeval serpent/adversary whose enmity God will overcome. Provides the figural source for a personal evil agent, but the connection is inferential; low Volume, contested.

echoes.text: For from the top of the rocks I see him. From the hills I see him. Behold, it is a people that dwells alone, and shall not be reckoned among the nations.
echoes.note: 'They are not of the world even as I am not of the world' (v16) echoes Israel 'a people dwelling alone, and not counting itself among the nations.' The set-apart, distinct-from-the-nations identity coheres with the disciples' otherworldly status; faint and generic.

pericopes.text: Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, even so I have sent them into the world. For their sakes I sanctify myself, that they themselves also may be sanctified in truth.

echoes.text: You shall put them on Aaron your brother, and on his sons with him, and shall anoint them, and consecrate them, and sanctify them, that they may minister to me in the priest’s office.
echoes.note: 'Sanctify them in your truth... for their sakes I sanctify myself' (vv17,19) figures the consecration of Aaron and his sons to priestly service ('anoint them, ordain them, and consecrate them'). The setting-apart-for-sacred-mission language gives the prayer its priestly architecture; coherent and recurrent across vv17-19.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Take Aaron and his sons with him, and the garments, and the anointing oil, and the bull of the sin offering, and the two rams, and the basket of unleavened bread; and assemble all the congregation at the door of the Tent of Meeting.” Moses did as Yahweh commanded him; and the congregation was assembled at the door of the Tent of Meeting. Moses said to the congregation, “This is the thing which Yahweh has commanded to be […]
echoes.note: The ordination rite consecrating Aaron underlies the double sanctification of disciples and self (vv17,19). Jesus as both consecrating priest and consecrated offering coheres with the chapter's high-priestly framing; figural Volume is substantial though no single verse is quoted.

echoes.text: You shall put on Aaron the holy garments; and you shall anoint him, and sanctify him, that he may minister to me in the priest’s office.
echoes.note: 'Sanctify them' (v17) recalls the command to clothe and 'consecrate' Aaron that he may serve as priest. Reinforces the consecration channel alongside Exod 28 and Lev 8; counted separately but lower independent Volume.

echoes.text: “Say to the people, ‘Sanctify yourselves against tomorrow, and you will eat flesh; for you have wept in the ears of Yahweh, saying, “Who will give us flesh to eat? For it was well with us in Egypt.” Therefore Yahweh will give you flesh, and you will eat.
echoes.note: 'Sanctify yourselves' as preparation to encounter the LORD offers an OT idiom behind 'sanctify them' (v17). Generic consecration language; supportive but faint, marked contested.

echoes.text: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
echoes.note: 'I sanctified you... and appointed you a prophet to the nations' parallels both 'sanctify them' and the sending 'into the world' (vv17-18). The set-apart-and-sent pattern for the prophetic commission coheres tightly with the disciples' consecration-for-mission; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: Your righteousness is an everlasting righteousness. Your law is truth.
echoes.note: 'Your word is truth' (v17) closely renders 'your law is truth' (Ps 119:142) and 'the sum of your word is truth' (119:160). Near-verbal correspondence gives high Volume; the equation of God's word with truth is the precise scriptural ground for the petition.

echoes.text: All of your words are truth. Every one of your righteous ordinances endures forever.
echoes.note: 'The sum of your word is truth, and every one of your righteous rules endures forever' is the most exact antecedent of 'your word is truth' (v17). High Volume and Coherence; listed alongside 119:142 as the twin source of the maxim.

echoes.text: “Now, O Lord Yahweh, you are God, and your words are truth, and you have promised this good thing to your servant.
echoes.note: 'Your words are truth' in David's prayer offers a second OT formulation behind 'your word is truth' (v17). Supports the maxim but with lower Volume than the Psalm 119 parallels; contested as the primary referent.

echoes.text: I heard the Lord’s voice, saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” Then I said, “Here I am. Send me!”
echoes.note: 'As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them' (v18) faintly recalls the prophetic sending 'Whom shall I send... Here I am, send me.' The divine commissioning-and-being-sent pattern is coherent though the wording is general; low Volume.

pericopes.text: Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who believe in me through their word, that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me. The glory which you have given me, I have given to them; that they may be one, even as we are one; I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one; that the world may know that you sent me, and loved them, even as you loved me.

echoes.text: and I will make them one nation in the land, on the mountains of Israel; and one king shall be king to them all; and they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all;
echoes.note: 'That they may all be one' / 'perfected into one' (vv21-23) figures Ezekiel's promise 'I will make them one nation... and one king shall be king over them all.' The unification of God's scattered people under one head is a coherent, recurrent figural backdrop for the Johannine unity petitions.

echoes.text: and join them for you one to another into one stick, that they may become one in your hand.
echoes.note: The two sticks 'joined... one in your hand' is the enacted sign behind repeated 'that they may be one' (vv21-22). Reinforces the Ezekiel reunification channel introduced at v11; coherent and recurrent, figural rather than verbal.

echoes.text: For then I will purify the lips of the peoples, that they may all call on Yahweh’s name, to serve him shoulder to shoulder.
echoes.note: Peoples serving the LORD 'with one accord' echoes the unity 'that the world may believe' (vv21-23). The purified-and-unified-nations motif coheres with the missional aim of the unity but the Volume is faint.

echoes.text: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him. When Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, behold, the skin of his face shone; and they were afraid to come near him. Moses called to them, and Aaron and all the rulers of the congregation returned to him; and Moses spoke to them. […]
echoes.note: 'The glory which you have given me, I have given to them' (v22) faintly mirrors Moses' face shining with reflected divine glory after Sinai. The motif of communicated/derivative glory is coherent, but John speaks of indwelling glory rather than facial radiance; low Volume.

echoes.text: For you have made him a little lower than God, and crowned him with glory and honor.
echoes.note: Glory bestowed on the disciples (v22) loosely recalls humanity 'crowned with glory and honor.' Generic glory-conferral idiom; supportive but faint and contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.
echoes.note: 'You... loved them, even as you loved me' (v23) echoes the LORD setting his love on Israel not for their greatness but because he loved them. The gratuitous divine love for the elect community coheres with the prayer, though John extends it to the disciples through the Son; low Volume.

pericopes.text: Father, I desire that they also whom you have given me be with me where I am, that they may see my glory, which you have given me, for you loved me before the foundation of the world. Righteous Father, the world hasn’t known you, but I knew you; and these knew that you sent me. I made known to them your name, and will make it known; that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.”

echoes.text: “Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed. When there were no depths, I was born, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains were settled in place, before the hills, I was born; while as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the beginning of the dust of the world. When he established the heavens, I was […]
echoes.note: 'You loved me before the foundation of the world' and 'see my glory' (v24) figure the Son after Wisdom delighted in by God before creation. The pre-cosmic love/glory shared between Father and agent is the same Wisdom channel that frames v5; coherent and recurrent within the prayer.

echoes.text: Before the mountains were born, before you had formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, you are God.
echoes.note: 'Before the foundation of the world' (v24) reuses the pre-creation eternity idiom of 'from everlasting... before... you had formed the earth.' Matches the temporal frame asserted of the Father-Son love and glory; moderate Volume via the recurring formula.

echoes.text: He said, “Please show me your glory.”
echoes.note: 'That they may see my glory' (v24) figures Moses' request 'Show me your glory' and the Sinai vision tradition. John transposes the longed-for sight of divine glory into the disciples' eschatological seeing of the Son's glory; coherent with the chapter's glory and Name theology.

echoes.text: but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Righteous Father, the world has not known you, but I knew you' (v25) recalls the LORD who 'practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness' and the boast of knowing him from 9:23-24. The righteousness-plus-knowledge cluster ties v25 back to v3's eternal-life-as-knowledge; coherent, moderate Volume.

echoes.text: Pour out your wrath on the nations that don’t know you; on the kingdoms that don’t call on your name;
echoes.note: 'The world has not known you' (v25) echoes 'the nations that do not know you,' the contrast between God's people and the ignorant nations. Coherent with John's world/disciples antithesis but the phrasing is generic; low Volume.

echoes.text: He said, “I will make all my goodness pass before you, and will proclaim Yahweh’s name before you. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy.”
echoes.note: 'I made known to them your name, and will make it known' (v26) reprises 'I will proclaim before you my name, the LORD,' closing the inclusio with v6. The ongoing proclamation of the Name as the vehicle of God's presence and love is coherent and recurrent across the prayer.

echoes.text: I will sanctify my great name, which has been profaned among the nations, which you have profaned in their midst; and the nations shall know that I am Yahweh, says the Lord Yahweh, when I shall be sanctified in you before their eyes.
echoes.note: 'I made known to them your name... that the love... may be in them' (v26) resonates with God's resolve to 'vindicate the holiness of my great name' so the nations know him, paired in Ezekiel with the indwelling Spirit (36:26-27). The hallowing-of-the-Name leading to interior transformation coheres with John's Name-and-indwelling climax; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: I will declare your name to my brothers. In the midst of the assembly, I will praise you.
echoes.note: 'I made known to them your name, and will make it known' (v26) restates the psalmist's vow 'I will tell of your name to my brothers,' bracketing the prayer with v6. The repeated declaration of the Name to the community gives strong Coherence and Recurrence within John.

echoes.text: My holy name will I make known in the midst of my people Israel; neither will I allow my holy name to be profaned any more: and the nations shall know that I am Yahweh, the Holy One in Israel.
echoes.note: 'I made known to them your name' (v26) echoes 'I will make my holy name known in the midst of my people Israel.' Reinforces the make-known-the-Name channel alongside Exod 33 and Isa 52:6; lower independent Volume, contested.

pericopes.text: When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples over the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, into which he and his disciples entered. Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples. Judas then, having taken a detachment of soldiers and officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, came there with lanterns, torches, and weapons. Jesus therefore, knowing all the things that were happening to him, went out, and said to them, “Who are you looking for?” They answered him, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus said to them, “I am he.” Judas also, who betrayed him, was standing with them. When therefore he said to them, “I am he,” they went backward, and fell to the ground. Again therefore he asked them, “Who are you looking for?” They said, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus answered, “I told you that I am he. If therefore you seek me, let these go their way,” that the word might be fulfilled which he spoke, “Of those whom you have given me, I have lost none.” Simon Peter therefore, having a sword, drew it, and struck the high priest’s servant, and cut off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus. Jesus therefore said to Peter, “Put the sword into its sheath. The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not surely drink it?”

echoes.text: All the country wept with a loud voice, and all the people passed over: the king also himself passed over the brook Kidron, and all the people passed over, toward the way of the wilderness.
echoes.note: Jesus crosses the brook Kidron with his disciples to a garden where he is betrayed, deliberately retracing David's flight across the Kidron under the betrayal of his counselor Ahithophel. The verbal anchor cheimarros tou Kedron (LXX) is exact and singular, and John alone of the evangelists names the wadi, signaling a typological David-suffers-betrayal pattern with high Volume and Coherence.

echoes.text: David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, and wept as he went up; and he had his head covered, and went barefoot: and all the people who were with him covered every man his head, and they went up, weeping as they went up.
echoes.note: David ascends the Mount of Olives weeping, head covered, abandoned by intimates, the very topography to which Jesus 'often met' (Gethsemane lies on Olivet's slope). The shared geography plus the betrayed-king-in-anguish motif coheres with the Kidron crossing of v.1, strengthening the Davidic typology though John omits the agony itself.

echoes.text: When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey, and arose, and went home, to his city, and set his house in order, and hanged himself; and he died, and was buried in the tomb of his father.
echoes.note: Ahithophel the betrayer hangs himself once his counsel fails, a fate the Synoptic Judas shares; the Kidron-crossing frame invites the reader to map Judas onto Ahithophel. Faint here because John does not narrate Judas's death, so the link rests on the larger Davidic matrix rather than this pericope's wording.

echoes.text: Yahweh God planted a garden eastward, in Eden, and there he put the man whom he had formed.
echoes.note: The arrest in a 'garden' (kepos), a setting unique to John among the passion accounts and reprised at the tomb (19:41; 20:15), evokes Eden as the place where humanity's fall began and where the new Adam now reverses it through obedience. The Coherence with John's new-creation theology (cf. 20:22) gives the figural reading weight despite no verbal quotation.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”
echoes.note: Jesus' absolute 'I am' (ego eimi) before the arresting party, at which they fall back, deploys the divine self-naming of the burning bush as rendered in the LXX (ego eimi ho on). The soldiers' collapse functions as a theophanic reaction, and John's repeated, climactic placement of ego eimi gives high Volume and Coherence with the Gospel's I-am Christology.

echoes.text: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me.
echoes.note: Deutero-Isaiah's 'that you may know and believe... that I am he' (ego eimi) supplies the monotheistic confessional sense John attaches to Jesus' self-declaration. The Isaianic ego eimi formula is the most plausible Second-Temple background for the absolute usage, reinforcing Exodus 3:14 and adding Recurrence across John's I-am sayings.

echoes.text: When evildoers came at me to eat up my flesh, even my adversaries and my foes, they stumbled and fell.
echoes.note: 'When evildoers came against me... they stumbled and fell' matches the soldiers going backward and falling to the ground at Jesus' word. The psalm of the righteous sufferer whose assailants collapse gives strong thematic Coherence; the falling-enemies motif is the verbal hinge linking the scene to the lament tradition.

echoes.text: Let those who seek after my soul be disappointed and brought to dishonor. Let those who plot my ruin be turned back and confounded.
echoes.note: 'Let them be turned back and brought to confusion who plot my hurt' supplies the enemies-driven-backward motif (apostrapheien eis ta opiso, LXX) that matches the arrest party's recoil (eis ta opiso). The shared lexeme eis ta opiso strengthens Volume above a merely thematic link in this cluster of persecution psalms.

echoes.text: Then my enemies shall turn back in the day that I call. I know this, that God is for me.
echoes.note: 'Then my enemies will turn back in the day when I call' offers another lament instance of foes turning back before the trusting sufferer, coherent with the soldiers' collapse. Low confidence as one of several overlapping psalm parallels rather than a distinct verbal source.

echoes.text: Let them be disappointed and confounded together who seek after my soul to destroy it. Let them be turned backward and brought to dishonor who delight in my hurt.
echoes.note: 'Let them be turned back and put to shame who seek my life' pairs the very verbs John uses (seek/zetein, turn back) as the soldiers 'seek' Jesus and go backward. Faint and contested, included for Recurrence within the righteous-sufferer psalm pattern behind the recoil.

echoes.text: For in the hand of Yahweh there is a cup, full of foaming wine mixed with spices. He pours it out. Indeed the wicked of the earth drink and drink it to its very dregs.
echoes.note: Jesus' 'the cup which the Father has given me, shall I not drink it?' draws on the prophetic cup of wrath, here the cup in the LORD's hand of foaming wine that the wicked must drain. The cup-of-judgment metaphor is the controlling image, and John's substitution of obedience-unto-death for the Synoptic prayer to remove the cup gives the figural reading high Volume and Coherence.

echoes.text: Awake, awake, stand up, Jerusalem, that have drunk at the hand of Yahweh the cup of his wrath; you have drunken the bowl of the cup of staggering, and drained it.
echoes.note: 'You have drunk... the cup of his wrath, the bowl of staggering' names the cup Jerusalem must drink, the background for the cup the Father gives Jesus to drink in the people's place. The Isaianic cup of staggering is a primary source of the metaphor, and Jesus' willing acceptance coheres with the Servant's vicarious suffering.

echoes.text: Thus says your Lord Yahweh, and your God who pleads the cause of his people, “Behold, I have taken out of your hand the cup of staggering, even the bowl of the cup of my wrath; you shall no more drink it again:
echoes.note: The LORD takes the cup of staggering from Jerusalem's hand and gives it to her tormentors; Jesus, drinking the cup, figurally takes it back so the people need not drink. The removal-and-transfer logic coheres with the substitution theme, supplementing 51:17 as the cup-of-wrath source.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, to me: take this cup of the wine of wrath at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send you, to drink it.
echoes.note: 'Take this cup of the wine of wrath from my hand, and make all the nations drink it' provides the most explicit OT 'cup the LORD gives to drink' formula, matching John's 'cup the Father has given.' The giving-of-the-cup wording strengthens the wrath-cup background behind Jesus' question.

echoes.text: Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Edom, that dwell in the land of Uz: The cup shall pass through to you also; you shall be drunken, and shall make yourself naked.
echoes.note: 'The cup shall pass to you also; you shall become drunk' continues the cup-of-judgment idiom, reinforcing the figural cup Jesus accepts. Low confidence as a secondary witness within the broader prophetic cup tradition rather than a direct source.

pericopes.text: So the detachment, the commanding officer, and the officers of the Jews, seized Jesus and bound him, and led him to Annas first, for he was father-in-law to Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. Now it was Caiaphas who advised the Jews that it was expedient that one man should perish for the people.

echoes.text: They came to the place which God had told him of. Abraham built the altar there, and laid the wood in order, bound Isaac his son, and laid him on the altar, on the wood.
echoes.note: Jesus is 'bound' (edesan) and led to the priests, faintly echoing the binding (aqedah) of Isaac, the beloved son bound for sacrifice. Low and contested: John supplies no verbal Isaac marker, so the link rests on the bound-sacrificial-son typology that informs Johannine atonement theology elsewhere.

echoes.text: The priest, who is anointed and who is consecrated to be priest in his father’s place, shall make the atonement, and shall put on the linen garments, even the holy garments. Then he shall make atonement for the Holy Sanctuary; and he shall make atonement for the Tent of Meeting and for the altar; and he shall make atonement for the priests and for all the people of the assembly.
echoes.note: Caiaphas the high priest 'that year' unwittingly presides over the death that atones for the people, mirroring the high priest's Day of Atonement role of securing the nation's expiation. The priestly-mediator framing coheres with John's irony that Caiaphas prophesies the saving death, though the connection is conceptual rather than verbal.

pericopes.text: Simon Peter followed Jesus, as did another disciple. Now that disciple was known to the high priest, and entered in with Jesus into the court of the high priest; but Peter was standing at the door outside. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to her who kept the door, and brought in Peter. Then the maid who kept the door said to Peter, “Are you also one of this man’s disciples?” He said, “I am not.” Now the servants and the officers were standing there, having made a fire of coals, for it was cold. They were warming themselves. Peter was with them, standing and warming himself.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;
echoes.note: Peter stands and warms himself among the servants and officers ranged against Jesus, faintly inverting the blessed man who does not 'stand in the way of sinners.' Faint and contested; the standing-among-the-wicked motif is suggestive of the first psalm's contrast but lacks verbal anchor.

echoes.text: Now the king was sitting in the winter house in the ninth month: and there was a fire in the brazier burning before him.
echoes.note: The charcoal fire (anthrakia) at which the company warms itself in the cold recalls the brazier before which the king burns Jeremiah's scroll, an image of hostility toward the prophetic word. Low confidence: a shared cold-weather brazier setting without further verbal contact, included for maximal coverage.

pericopes.text: The high priest therefore asked Jesus about his disciples, and about his teaching. Jesus answered him, “I spoke openly to the world. I always taught in synagogues, and in the temple, where the Jews always meet. I said nothing in secret. Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them. Behold, these know the things which I said.” When he had said this, one of the officers standing by slapped Jesus with his hand, saying, “Do you answer the high priest like that?” Jesus answered him, “If I have spoken evil, testify of the evil; but if well, why do you beat me?” Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas, the high priest.

echoes.text: I have not spoken in secret, in a place of the land of darkness. I didn’t say to the seed of Jacob, ‘Seek me in vain.’ I, Yahweh, speak righteousness. I declare things that are right.
echoes.note: Jesus' 'I spoke openly to the world... I said nothing in secret' closely matches the LORD's 'I have not spoken in secret, in a place of a land of darkness' (LXX ouk en kruphe... en topo skoteino). The shared 'not in secret' (en kruphe) idiom and the public-revelation claim give strong Volume, casting Jesus' testimony in the voice of the self-revealing God of Isaiah.

echoes.text: “Come near to me and hear this: “From the beginning I have not spoken in secret; from the time that it was, there am I.” Now the Lord Yahweh has sent me, with his Spirit.
echoes.note: 'From the beginning I have not spoken in secret' provides a second Isaianic 'not in secret' declaration reinforcing Jesus' open-teaching claim. The Recurrence of the formula across Isaiah 45 and 48 strengthens the allusion's plausibility as deliberate adoption of divine speech.

echoes.text: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting.
echoes.note: An officer strikes Jesus on the face for his answer, enacting the Servant's 'I gave my back to the smiters... I did not hide my face from shame and spitting.' The striking-of-the-cheek of the obedient Servant gives high Coherence with the Johannine passion's Servant Christology, and the blow on the innocent witness matches the Servant's non-resistance.

echoes.text: Now you shall gather yourself in troops, daughter of troops. He has laid siege against us. They will strike the judge of Israel with a rod on the cheek.
echoes.note: 'With a rod they strike the judge of Israel on the cheek' supplies a prophetic oracle of the ruler struck on the face, matching the officer's slap of Jesus. The cheek-striking of the messianic judge gives Coherence with John's royal-Christology trial scene, though the verbal contact is through the shared act rather than quotation.

echoes.text: Let him give his cheek to him who strikes him; let him be filled full with reproach.
echoes.note: 'Let him give his cheek to the one who strikes him; let him be filled with insults' commends the silent acceptance of the blow that Jesus models when struck and then reasons quietly rather than retaliating. The give-the-cheek motif coheres with the righteous-sufferer pattern shaping the interrogation scene.

echoes.text: Then Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near, and struck Micaiah on the cheek, and said, “Which way did the Spirit of Yahweh go from me to speak to you?”
echoes.note: Zedekiah strikes the true prophet Micaiah on the cheek for his testimony before the king, a striking-the-faithful-prophet parallel to the officer's blow on Jesus. Low confidence; one of several OT cheek-blow scenes, included for the prophet-struck-for-truth Recurrence.

echoes.text: “You shall not blaspheme God, nor curse a ruler of your people.
echoes.note: The officer's rebuke 'Do you answer the high priest like that?' invokes the Torah prohibition against reviling a ruler of the people, ironically applied to silence the true Lord. Faint and contested; the link is the legal premise behind the officer's charge rather than a quotation.

pericopes.text: Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. They said therefore to him, “You aren’t also one of his disciples, are you?” He denied it, and said, “I am not.” One of the servants of the high priest, being a relative of him whose ear Peter had cut off, said, “Didn’t I see you in the garden with him?” Peter therefore denied it again, and immediately the rooster crowed.

echoes.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
echoes.note: Peter's threefold denial by the charcoal fire belongs to the cluster of intimate-betrayal motifs John draws from Psalm 41:9 ('my close friend in whom I trusted... has lifted his heel against me'), already cited at 13:18. Low here because the psalm's primary referent is Judas; Peter's failure echoes the broader friend-failure pattern rather than the verse directly.

echoes.text: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is close to me,” says Yahweh of Armies. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; and I will turn my hand against the little ones.
echoes.note: 'Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered' undergirds the disciples' collapse, of which Peter's denial is the sharpest instance. Faint in John, which lacks the Synoptic citation, so the scattering-of-the-flock motif is conceptual support rather than a marked allusion.

pericopes.text: They led Jesus therefore from Caiaphas into the Praetorium. It was early, and they themselves didn’t enter into the Praetorium, that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover. Pilate therefore went out to them, and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?” They answered him, “If this man weren’t an evildoer, we wouldn’t have delivered him up to you.” Pilate therefore said to them, “Take him yourselves, and judge him according to your law.” Therefore the Jews said to him, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death,” that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spoke, signifying by what kind of death he should die.

echoes.text: They shall eat the flesh in that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread. They shall eat it with bitter herbs.
echoes.note: The accusers avoid defilement so they may 'eat the Passover,' even as they deliver the true Passover lamb to slaughter, a Johannine irony tied to the Exodus 12 paschal meal. The Coherence with John's paschal-lamb chronology (19:14, 19:36) gives the figural Passover framing real weight in this transitional pericope.

echoes.text: There were certain men, who were unclean because of the dead body of a man, so that they could not keep the Passover on that day, and they came before Moses and before Aaron on that day. Those men said to him, “We are unclean because of the dead body of a man. Why are we kept back, that we may not offer the offering of Yahweh in its appointed season among the children of Israel?” Moses answered them, “Wait, that I may hear what Yahweh will command […]
echoes.note: The concern over ritual defilement that would bar one from keeping the Passover reflects the purity legislation of Numbers 9, sharpening the irony of scrupulous purity beside judicial murder. Low confidence; the purity premise is conceptual background rather than an evoked text.

pericopes.text: Pilate therefore entered again into the Praetorium, called Jesus, and said to him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” Jesus answered him, “Do you say this by yourself, or did others tell you about me?” Pilate answered, “I’m not a Jew, am I? Your own nation and the chief priests delivered you to me. What have you done?” Jesus answered, “My Kingdom is not of this world. If my Kingdom were of this world, then my servants would fight, that I wouldn’t be delivered to the Jews. But now my Kingdom is not from here.” Pilate therefore said to him, “Are you a king then?” Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.” Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” When he had said this, he went out again to the Jews, and said to them, “I find no basis for a charge against him.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: Jesus' kingship 'not of this world,' a dominion not delivered by force, enacts the everlasting, non-earthly kingdom given to the one like a son of man. John's royal trial coheres with Daniel's vision of a heaven-bestowed, indestructible reign that 'shall not pass away,' giving the figural Son-of-Man kingship high Coherence with Johannine Christology.

echoes.text: The kingdom and the dominion, and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole sky, shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High: his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.
echoes.note: The kingdom given to the saints of the Most High, an everlasting dominion all peoples shall serve, supplies the otherworldly-sovereignty register behind Jesus' claim that his servants do not fight for an earthly realm. Recurrence within Daniel 7 reinforces the Son-of-Man kingdom background of the Pilate dialogue.

echoes.text: “Yet I have set my King on my holy hill of Zion.”
echoes.note: Pilate's interrogation of Jesus' kingship before the nations replays the royal psalm in which the LORD installs his anointed king on Zion while rulers conspire against him. The king-versus-the-rulers-of-the-earth frame gives Coherence with the Barabbas/Pilate scene, casting Jesus as the Messiah-king the nations reject.

echoes.text: The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,
echoes.note: 'The kings of the earth set themselves... against the LORD and his anointed' frames the rulers' collusion against the true king, matching Pilate and the chief priests arrayed against Jesus the King of the Jews. The conspiracy-of-rulers motif strengthens the messianic-king reading of the trial.

echoes.text: Behold, I have given him for a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander to the peoples.
echoes.note: 'I have given him as a witness (martys) to the peoples, a leader and commander' resonates with Jesus' 'I have come... that I should testify to the truth.' Low confidence; the witness-to-the-nations idea coheres with the kingship dialogue but lacks decisive verbal contact.

echoes.text: Micaiah said, “As Yahweh lives, what Yahweh says to me, that I will speak.”
echoes.note: Micaiah's resolve to speak only what is true before the king parallels Jesus' mission to 'testify to the truth' before Pilate, the true-witness-before-the-ruler motif. Faint and contested, included for the prophet-bears-truth Recurrence behind the trial.

echoes.text: All of your words are truth. Every one of your righteous ordinances endures forever.
echoes.note: 'The sum of your word is truth' stands behind Pilate's question 'What is truth?' and Jesus' truth-witness, since for John truth (aletheia) is the revelation of God enacted in Jesus. Faint; the link is thematic to John's truth motif rather than to a quoted verse.

pericopes.text: Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” When he had said this, he went out again to the Jews, and said to them, “I find no basis for a charge against him. But you have a custom, that I should release someone to you at the Passover. Therefore do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?” Then they all shouted again, saying, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a robber.

echoes.text: He shall take the two goats, and set them before Yahweh at the door of the Tent of Meeting. Aaron shall cast lots for the two goats; one lot for Yahweh, and the other lot for the scapegoat. Aaron shall present the goat on which the lot fell for Yahweh, and offer him for a sin offering. But the goat, on which the lot fell for the scapegoat, shall be presented alive before Yahweh, to make atonement for him, to send him away for the scapegoat into the […]
echoes.note: Pilate's Passover custom of releasing one prisoner while Jesus goes to death evokes the two-goats rite: one set free, the other slain to bear the people's sin. The released-Barabbas/condemned-Jesus pairing gives the scapegoat typology real Coherence with John's substitutionary 'one man for the people' (11:50; 18:14).

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all' frames the swap by which the guilty robber goes free and the innocent one is condemned in his place. The Servant who bears others' sin coheres tightly with the Barabbas substitution, strengthening John's vicarious-death reading.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: The Servant 'numbered with the transgressors' resonates with Jesus condemned in the place of Barabbas the robber/insurrectionist. Low confidence here since John does not crucify Jesus between criminals as the Synoptics do; the link rests on the with-the-transgressors theme.

echoes.text: Your lamb shall be without defect, a male a year old. You shall take it from the sheep, or from the goats: and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month; and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it at evening.
echoes.note: The Passover-release custom set against the choice of the lamb-king to die deepens John's paschal irony, in which the unblemished lamb is rejected while a 'robber' is freed. Faint; the paschal framing is structural to the pericope but the connection to the lamb selection is conceptual.

pericopes.text: So Pilate then took Jesus, and flogged him. The soldiers twisted thorns into a crown, and put it on his head, and dressed him in a purple garment. They kept saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and they kept slapping him.

echoes.text: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting.
echoes.note: The flogging and the slapping ('they kept slapping him') strongly recall the Servant who gives his back to those who strike and his cheeks to those who pluck the beard, not hiding his face from shame and spitting. High volume of shared imagery (back smitten, face struck) and coherence with John's Servant-passion frame.

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.
echoes.note: The Servant despised, wounded, and bruised stands behind the whole scourging scene; John reads the passion through the Suffering Servant. Coherence is strong across the chapter even where no formula is used.

echoes.text: But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people. All those who see me mock me. They insult me with their lips. They shake their heads, saying, “He trusts in Yahweh; let him deliver him. Let him rescue him, since he delights in him.”
echoes.note: The mockery of the crowned 'king' echoes the scorned righteous sufferer who is a reproach and despised, mocked by onlookers. Recurrence is high since John quotes Psalm 22:18 later in the chapter, raising the availability and coherence of the whole psalm.

echoes.text: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your King comes to you! He is righteous, and having salvation; lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
echoes.note: The ironic crowning and hailing of a humble king may faintly invoke Zechariah's king who comes lowly; John used Zech 9:9 explicitly at the entry (12:15), making it available. Faint and contested as background coloring only.

pericopes.text: Then Pilate went out again, and said to them, “Behold, I bring him out to you, that you may know that I find no basis for a charge against him.” Jesus therefore came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment. Pilate said to them, “Behold, the man!” When therefore the chief priests and the officers saw him, they shouted, saying, “Crucify! Crucify!” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves, and crucify him, for I find no basis for a charge against him.” The Jews answered him, “We have a law, and by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.”

echoes.text: and speak to him, saying, ‘Thus says Yahweh of Armies, “Behold, the man whose name is the Branch: and he shall grow up out of his place; and he shall build Yahweh’s temple;
echoes.note: Pilate's 'Behold, the man!' (idou ho anthropos) may echo 'Behold, the man whose name is the Branch' who shall build the temple, a messianic-royal-priestly figure. John has a temple-body theme (2:19-21); coherence is suggestive though contested, since the Greek wording differs.

echoes.text: When Samuel saw Saul, Yahweh said to him, “Behold, the man of whom I spoke to you! this same shall have authority over my people.”
echoes.note: The LORD's word to Samuel, 'Behold the man... he shall reign over my people,' offers an ironic royal echo to Pilate's presentation of the true (rejected) king. Faint; offered as alternative to the Zechariah Branch reading.

echoes.text: He who blasphemes Yahweh’s name, he shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall certainly stone him. The foreigner as well as the native-born, when he blasphemes the Name, shall be put to death.
echoes.note: 'We have a law, and by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God' invokes the Torah blasphemy statute commanding death for one who blasphemes the Name. The charge is legally grounded in this verse; high coherence with the trial logic.

echoes.text: But the prophet who speaks a word presumptuously in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or who speaks in the name of other gods, that same prophet shall die.”
echoes.note: The death sentence for a presumptuous prophet who speaks in God's name may secondarily inform 'by our law he ought to die.' Lower volume than Lev 24:16, offered as supplementary legal background.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: The title 'Son of God' adjacent to the heavenly 'one like a son of man' may stand faintly behind the Jewish leaders' accusation. Contested and faint; the divine-sonship charge is the chapter's pivot.

pericopes.text: When therefore Pilate heard this saying, he was more afraid. He entered into the Praetorium again, and said to Jesus, “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer. Pilate therefore said to him, “Aren’t you speaking to me? Don’t you know that I have power to release you, and have power to crucify you?” Jesus answered, “You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above. Therefore he who delivered me to you has greater sin.” At this, Pilate was seeking to release him, but the Jews cried out, saying, “If you release this man, you aren’t Caesar’s friend! Everyone who makes himself a king speaks against Caesar!”

echoes.text: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding;
echoes.note: Jesus' 'You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above' echoes Daniel's confession that God removes and sets up kings and gives authority. Coherent with John's theology of derived earthly power; medium volume.

echoes.text: The sentence is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones; to the intent that the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will, and sets up over it the lowest of men.
echoes.note: 'The Most High rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he will' directly grounds the claim that Pilate's authority is given 'from above.' Strong conceptual coherence; paired with Dan 2:21.

echoes.text: By me kings reign, and princes decree justice.
echoes.note: 'By me kings reign and rulers decree justice' (Wisdom speaking) faintly supports the notion that governing authority is divinely delegated. Lower volume than Daniel; offered as wisdom-tradition background.

echoes.text: Because your dominion was given you from the Lord, And your sovereignty from the Most High; Who will search out your works, And will make inquisition of your counsels:
echoes.note: Deuterocanonical: 'your dominion was given you from the Lord, and your sovereignty from the Most High,' addressed to rulers, closely matches 'given to you from above.' Available in the Second-Temple period; faint but apt.

pericopes.text: When Pilate therefore heard these words, he brought Jesus out, and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called “The Pavement”, but in Hebrew, “Gabbatha.” Now it was the Preparation Day of the Passover, at about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, “Behold, your King!” They cried out, “Away with him! Away with him! Crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your King?” The chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar!” So then he delivered him to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus and led him away.

echoes.text: and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month; and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it at evening.
echoes.note: The handing over at the Preparation of Passover, 'about the sixth hour,' coincides with the time the Passover lambs began to be slain; John times the sentence to the lamb-slaughter. High coherence with John's lamb Christology (1:29) and the unbroken-bones citation later.

echoes.text: Yahweh will be King over all the earth. In that day Yahweh will be one, and his name one.
echoes.note: 'The LORD shall be king over all the earth' may be ironically inverted by 'We have no king but Caesar.' Faint; the kingship motif is dense here but the verbal link is loose.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they tell you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not be king over them.
echoes.note: Israel's rejection of God as king ('they have rejected me from being king over them') resonates with the priests' 'We have no king but Caesar.' Coherent theological irony, but contested as a deliberate echo.

pericopes.text: He went out, bearing his cross, to the place called “The Place of a Skull”, which is called in Hebrew, “Golgotha”, where they crucified him, and with him two others, on either side one, and Jesus in the middle.

echoes.text: Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. He took in his hand the fire and the knife. They both went together.
echoes.note: Jesus 'bearing his cross' to the place of execution evokes Isaac carrying the wood of his own sacrifice up the mount. The Aqedah was a live Second-Temple typology; medium volume and good coherence with the lamb/son themes.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: Crucifixion 'with him two others, on either side one' enacts the Servant being 'numbered with the transgressors.' John shares the Servant frame though, unlike Luke 22:37, he does not cite it; coherence is strong.

pericopes.text: Pilate wrote a title also, and put it on the cross. There was written, “JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.” Therefore many of the Jews read this title, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city; and it was written in Hebrew, in Latin, and in Greek. The chief priests of the Jews therefore said to Pilate, “Don’t write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but, ‘he said, I am King of the Jews.’” Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.”

echoes.text: “Yet I have set my King on my holy hill of Zion.”
echoes.note: The inscription proclaiming Jesus 'King of the Jews,' published in three languages, ironically broadcasts the enthronement of God's king ('I have set my king on Zion'). Faint; the royal-psalm coloring is thematic rather than verbal.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day that the nations will seek the root of Jesse, who stands as a banner of the peoples; and his resting place will be glorious.
echoes.note: The trilingual title heralding the king to all peoples ('many of the Jews read it') faintly recalls the root of Jesse standing as a signal to the nations. Faint and contested; offered for the universal-proclamation motif.

pericopes.text: Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also the coat. Now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout. Then they said to one another, “Let’s not tear it, but cast lots for it to decide whose it will be,” that the Scripture might be fulfilled, which says, “They parted my garments among them. For my cloak they cast lots.” Therefore the soldiers did these things.

echoes.text: They divide my garments among them. They cast lots for my clothing.
echoes.note: Explicit fulfillment citation: 'They parted my garments among them, and for my cloak they cast lots,' verbatim from the LXX. John reads the two clauses as distinct acts (dividing the garments, casting lots for the tunic). Maximum volume and the chapter's anchor citation.

echoes.text: “You shall make the robe of the ephod all of blue. It shall have a hole for the head in its midst: it shall have a binding of woven work around its hole, as it were the hole of a coat of mail, that it not be torn.
echoes.note: The seamless tunic 'woven from the top throughout' recalls the high priest's robe of the ephod, woven in one piece with a reinforced opening so it would not tear. Suggests Jesus as priest-victim; medium volume, debated but coherent with John's temple-body theme.

echoes.text: He shall put on the holy linen coat. He shall have the linen breeches on his body, and shall put on the linen sash, and he shall be clothed with the linen turban. They are the holy garments. He shall bathe his body in water, and put them on.
echoes.note: The high priest's holy linen tunic worn on the Day of Atonement adds priestly resonance to the seamless coat. Faint; offered alongside the Exodus 28 robe reading.

pericopes.text: But there were standing by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. Therefore when Jesus saw his mother, and the disciple whom he loved standing there, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold your son!” Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home.

echoes.text: The man called his wife Eve because she would be the mother of all the living.
echoes.note: Jesus addressing his mother as 'Woman' and constituting a new family at the cross may echo Eve as 'the mother of all living,' with Mary as a new-Eve figure. Faint and contested; the 'Woman' address recurs in John (2:4).

echoes.text: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is close to me,” says Yahweh of Armies. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; and I will turn my hand against the little ones.
echoes.note: The scattering implied by the cross scene (shepherd struck, family reordered) faintly invokes 'strike the shepherd and the sheep will be scattered.' Very faint here; the verse is more at home in the arrest narratives.

pericopes.text: After this, Jesus, seeing that all things were now finished, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said, “I am thirsty.” Now a vessel full of vinegar was set there; so they put a sponge full of the vinegar on hyssop, and held it at his mouth. When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished.” He bowed his head, and gave up his spirit.

echoes.text: They also gave me gall for my food. In my thirst, they gave me vinegar to drink.
echoes.note: 'I am thirsty,' said 'that the Scripture might be fulfilled,' and the answering vinegar (oxos) draw directly on 'for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.' John signals fulfillment explicitly; high volume and the primary referent.

echoes.text: My strength is dried up like a potsherd. My tongue sticks to the roof of my mouth. You have brought me into the dust of death.
echoes.note: 'My tongue cleaves to my jaws' / 'my strength is dried up' supplies the thirst motif alongside Psalm 69. Recurrence is high (Ps 22:18 already quoted), so coherence is strong; medium volume secondary source.
