echoes.text: You shall take a bunch of hyssop, and dip it in the blood that is in the basin, and strike the lintel and the two door posts with the blood that is in the basin; and none of you shall go out of the door of his house until the morning.
echoes.note: The vinegar is raised on 'hyssop,' the very plant used to apply the Passover blood to the doorposts. John alone names hyssop, fusing the drink-offering with Passover typology; high coherence with the chapter's lamb framing.

echoes.text: The heavens, the earth, and all their vast array were finished. On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done.
echoes.note: 'It is finished' (tetelestai) echoes the completion of creation, 'the heavens and the earth were finished... God finished his work,' presenting the cross as the consummation of God's work. Coherent with John's new-creation framing (cf. 20:22); medium volume.

pericopes.text: Therefore the Jews, because it was the Preparation Day, so that the bodies wouldn’t remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a special one), asked of Pilate that their legs might be broken, and that they might be taken away. Therefore the soldiers came, and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who was crucified with him; but when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was already dead, they didn’t break his legs. However one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out. He who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true. He knows that he tells the truth, that you may believe. For these things happened, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, “A bone of him will not be broken.” Again another Scripture says, “They will look on him whom they pierced.”

echoes.text: In one house shall it be eaten; you shall not carry out anything of the flesh abroad out of the house; neither shall you break a bone of it.
echoes.note: 'A bone of him will not be broken' fulfills the Passover-lamb statute that no bone of it shall be broken. John's wording matches the LXX prohibition; this is the chapter's clearest Passover-typology citation, making Jesus the true paschal lamb.

echoes.text: They shall leave none of it until the morning, nor break a bone of it. According to all the statute of the Passover they shall keep it.
echoes.note: The second-Passover law repeats 'they shall not break a bone of it,' reinforcing the lamb identification behind John's unbroken-bones citation. Paired with Exodus 12:46 as the dual Torah source.

echoes.text: He protects all of his bones. Not one of them is broken.
echoes.note: 'He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken,' spoken of the righteous sufferer the LORD delivers, is the likeliest source if John intends the righteous-one rather than (or as well as) the lamb. Strong verbal match; many read this as the primary referent.

echoes.text: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn.
echoes.note: 'They will look on him whom they pierced,' the second explicit fulfillment formula, cites the mourning over the pierced one in Zechariah. John follows a textual tradition reading 'pierced' (cf. Rev 1:7); high volume and the climactic citation.
echoes.lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son.

echoes.text: “In that day there will be a spring opened to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for sin and for uncleanness.
echoes.note: Immediately after the piercing in Zechariah, 'a fountain shall be opened... for sin and uncleanness,' resonates with the blood and water flowing from the pierced side. Adjacent context to the quoted 12:10; medium volume and coherent.

echoes.text: He brought me back to the door of the house; and behold, waters issued out from under the threshold of the house eastward; (for the forefront of the house was toward the east;) and the waters came down from under, from the right side of the house, on the south of the altar. Then he brought me out by the way of the gate northward, and led me round by the way outside to the outer gate, by the way of the gate that looks toward the east; and behold, there ran […]
echoes.note: The water from the pierced side may evoke the temple stream flowing from the sanctuary to give life, supporting John's body-as-temple motif. Faint and contested; thematic rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock in Horeb. You shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it, that the people may drink.” Moses did so in the sight of the elders of Israel.
echoes.note: Water issuing from the struck rock at Horeb offers a faint typological background to the water from Jesus' side. Low volume; Paul (1 Cor 10:4) develops the rock typology more than John.

echoes.text: Moses lifted up his hand, and struck the rock with his rod twice, and water came out abundantly. The congregation and their livestock drank.
echoes.note: The water gushing when the rock is struck twice parallels the flow from the struck side; faint, offered alongside Exodus 17:6 as wilderness-water background.

pericopes.text: After these things, Joseph of Arimathaea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked of Pilate that he might take away Jesus’ body. Pilate gave him permission. He came therefore and took away his body. Nicodemus, who at first came to Jesus by night, also came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred Roman pounds. So they took Jesus’ body, and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as the custom of the Jews is to bury. Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden. In the garden was a new tomb in which no man had ever yet been laid. Then because of the Jews’ Preparation Day (for the tomb was near at hand) they laid Jesus there.

echoes.text: They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.
echoes.note: Burial by the wealthy Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, with a lavish hundred pounds of spices in a new tomb, fulfills 'they made his grave... with a rich man in his death.' Strong coherence with John's pervasive Servant typology; high volume.

echoes.text: They buried him in his own tombs, which he had dug out for himself in the city of David, and laid him in the bed which was filled with sweet odors and various kinds of spices prepared by the perfumers’ art: and they made a very great burning for him.
echoes.note: King Asa's burial laid on a bier filled with spices prepared by the perfumer's art parallels the royal, spice-laden entombment of Jesus, underscoring his kingship even in death. Medium volume; matches the regal scale of the myrrh and aloes.

echoes.text: spikenard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with every kind of incense tree; myrrh and aloes, with all the best spices,
echoes.note: The myrrh and aloes recall the garden spices ('myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices') of the beloved, and the burial 'in a garden' invites Song-of-Songs garden resonance. Faint; develops more fully in John 20's garden encounter.

echoes.text: Yahweh God planted a garden eastward, in Eden, and there he put the man whom he had formed.
echoes.note: Burial in a garden may echo Eden, supporting John's new-creation/new-Adam reading of the resurrection that follows. Faint and contested; thematic link to the garden setting.

echoes.text: All your garments smell like myrrh, aloes, and cassia. Out of ivory palaces stringed instruments have made you glad.
echoes.note: The royal wedding psalm's 'myrrh and aloes and cassia' on the king's garments offers a faint regal-spice background to the myrrh-and-aloes burial. Low volume; reinforces the king motif.

pericopes.text: Now on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene went early, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and saw the stone taken away from the tomb. Therefore she ran and came to Simon Peter, and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb, and we don’t know where they have laid him!”

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters. God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. God saw the light, and saw that it was good. God divided the light from the darkness. God called the light “day”, and the darkness he called “night”. There was evening and there was morning, the first day.
echoes.note: The resurrection occurs on 'the first day of the week' 'while it was still dark,' deliberately echoing the first day of creation when light dawns over darkness (Gen 1:3-5). John, who opened his Gospel 'In the beginning' (Jn 1:1 = Gen 1:1), frames the resurrection as inaugurated new creation; high Coherence with the Gospel's creation Christology and strong Volume in the temporal marker.

echoes.text: Yahweh God planted a garden eastward, in Eden, and there he put the man whom he had formed. Out of the ground Yahweh God made every tree to grow that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food, including the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. A river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from there it was parted, and became the source of four rivers. The name of the first is Pishon: it flows […]
echoes.note: The tomb is in a garden (Jn 19:41), and the empty-tomb scene is staged there, recalling Eden where God placed the man (Gen 2:8,15). The garden setting binds the whole pericope to a new-Adam/new-creation typology that surfaces explicitly when Mary mistakes Jesus for the gardener (20:15).

echoes.text: By night on my bed, I sought him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but I didn’t find him. I will get up now, and go about the city; in the streets and in the squares I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but I didn’t find him. The watchmen who go about the city found me; “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” I had scarcely passed from them, when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him […]
echoes.note: Mary comes seeking 'the Lord' in the dark and finds the place empty, mirroring the bride who 'on my bed by night sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but found him not.' The Song's seeking-not-finding-then-finding pattern unfolds across 20:1-16; medium Volume but strong Coherence given Jewish nuptial readings of the Song available in the Second-Temple period.

pericopes.text: Therefore Peter and the other disciple went out, and they went toward the tomb. They both ran together. The other disciple outran Peter, and came to the tomb first. Stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths lying, yet he didn’t enter in. Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying, and the cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but rolled up in a place by itself. So then the other disciple who came first to the tomb also entered in, and he saw and believed. For as yet they didn’t know the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. So the disciples went away again to their own homes.

echoes.text: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.
echoes.note: The narrator notes 'they didn't know the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead' (20:9); the OT warrant most plausibly in view is 'you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor allow your holy one to see corruption,' the standard apostolic resurrection proof-text. The reference is generic ('the Scripture') so the source is reconstructed from early Christian usage.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: The third-day raising ('after two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up') is a candidate background for the conviction that Jesus 'must rise.' Faint and contested: John never cites Hosea, and the day-count is implicit, lowering Volume.

pericopes.text: But Mary was standing outside at the tomb weeping. So, as she wept, she stooped and looked into the tomb, and she saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head, and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain. They told her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “Because they have taken away my Lord, and I don’t know where they have laid him.”

echoes.text: You shall make two cherubim of hammered gold. You shall make them at the two ends of the mercy seat. Make one cherub at the one end, and one cherub at the other end. You shall make the cherubim on its two ends of one piece with the mercy seat. The cherubim shall spread out their wings upward, covering the mercy seat with their wings, with their faces toward one another. The faces of the cherubim shall be toward the mercy seat. You shall put the mercy seat […]
echoes.note: Mary sees 'two angels in white sitting, one at the head, and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain' — a striking image of the two cherubim of beaten gold facing each other over the mercy seat of the ark, between whom God's presence dwelt. The empty slab framed by two angels figures the tomb as the new holy of holies; high Coherence with Johannine temple typology.

echoes.text: I lifted up my eyes, and looked, and behold, a man clothed in linen, whose thighs were adorned with pure gold of Uphaz: his body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as flaming torches, and his arms and his feet like burnished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude.
echoes.note: The dazzling angelic figures 'in white' draw on the Danielic vision of the man clothed in linen with a face like lightning. Volume is modest since John specifies only white garments, but the radiant-angel topos is widely available in apocalyptic.

echoes.text: I opened to my beloved; but my beloved left; and had gone away. My heart went out when he spoke. I looked for him, but I didn’t find him. I called him, but he didn’t answer. The watchmen who go about the city found me. They beat me. They bruised me. The keepers of the walls took my cloak away from me. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, If you find my beloved, that you tell him that I am faint with love. Friends
echoes.note: Mary's lament 'they have taken away my Lord, and I don't know where they have laid him' continues the bride-seeking-her-beloved pattern of the Song (5:6 'I sought him, but I could not find him'). Reinforces the 20:1 allusion through Recurrence within the same scene.

pericopes.text: When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, and didn’t know that it was Jesus. Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Who are you looking for?” She, supposing him to be the gardener, said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.” Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him, “Rabboni!” which is to say, “Teacher!” Jesus said to her, “Don’t hold me, for I haven’t yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brothers, and tell them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’” Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had said these things to her.

echoes.text: Yahweh God planted a garden eastward, in Eden, and there he put the man whom he had formed. Out of the ground Yahweh God made every tree to grow that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food, including the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. A river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from there it was parted, and became the source of four rivers. The name of the first is Pishon: it flows […]
echoes.note: Mary supposes the risen Jesus to be 'the gardener' in the garden of the tomb — John's deliberate irony casting Jesus as the new Adam who tends the garden (Gen 2:15), undoing Eden's loss. The garden + gardener convergence raises Volume and Coherence above the faint garden echo of 20:1.

echoes.text: I had scarcely passed from them, when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother’s house, into the room of her who conceived me.
echoes.note: 'Scarcely had I passed them when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go' lies behind Mary's recognition and Jesus' 'Don't hold me' (20:16-17). The seeking-then-clinging sequence completes the Canticle pattern begun at 20:1; medium confidence on the cumulative force of the recurrence.

echoes.text: Ruth said, “Don’t entreat me to leave you, and to return from following after you, for where you go, I will go; and where you lodge, I will lodge; your people shall be my people, and your God my God;
echoes.note: Jesus' covenant formula 'my Father and your Father, my God and your God' (20:17) echoes Ruth's pledge 'your people shall be my people, and your God my God,' a paradigmatic statement of incorporative belonging. Faint verbal contact ('your God / my God') with strong thematic Coherence to adoption.

echoes.text: I will declare your name to my brothers. In the midst of the assembly, I will praise you.
echoes.note: 'Go to my brothers' (20:17) recalls the vindicated sufferer's vow 'I will declare your name to my brothers,' the turn from passion to proclamation in the psalm John has quoted at the cross (19:24). The Psalm 22 frame gives 'my brothers' high Coherence and Recurrence within the Johannine passion.

echoes.text: He will call to me, ‘You are my Father, my God, and the rock of my salvation!’
echoes.note: The royal-messianic 'He will call to me, You are my Father, my God' supplies covenantal background for 'my Father... my God,' linking Jesus' filial claim to the Davidic adoption oracle. Low Volume; one of several candidate Father/God formulae.

pericopes.text: When therefore it was evening, on that day, the first day of the week, and when the doors were locked where the disciples were assembled, for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the midst, and said to them, “Peace be to you.” When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. The disciples therefore were glad when they saw the Lord. Jesus therefore said to them again, “Peace be to you. As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.” When he had said this, he breathed on them, and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit! If you forgive anyone’s sins, they have been forgiven them. If you retain anyone’s sins, they have been retained.”

echoes.text: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The risen Jesus' threefold greeting 'Peace be to you' (20:19,21,26) functions as the eschatological enactment of the Aaronic priestly blessing 'the LORD lift up his countenance on you and give you peace.' Medium Volume (shared 'peace') with strong Coherence as the resurrected high-priestly Lord blesses his gathered people.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: Jesus 'breathed on them' and said 'Receive the Holy Spirit' — the verb (enephysesen, LXX of Gen 2:7) directly evokes God breathing the breath of life into Adam's nostrils so he became a living being. John presents the Spirit-impartation as new creation/new Adam; very high Volume given the rare shared verb and high Coherence with the Gospel's creation theology.

echoes.text: Then he said to me, Prophesy to the wind, prophesy, son of man, and tell the wind, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Come from the four winds, breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live. So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army.
echoes.note: 'Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live' stands behind Jesus breathing Spirit into the disciples after the resurrection. Ezekiel's vivified corpses give the scene its resurrection-and-Spirit valence; high Coherence and shared breath/Spirit (ruach/pneuma) vocabulary reinforce the Genesis 2:7 figure.

echoes.text: Because he was ignorant of him that moulded him, And of him that inspired into him an active soul, And breathed into him a vital spirit.
echoes.note: 'He failed to know the one who formed him and inspired him with an active soul and breathed into him a living spirit' restates Gen 2:7 in Second-Temple idiom, evidencing the availability of the breath-of-life motif John reworks. Deuterocanonical witness rather than a direct source.

echoes.text: I will lay the key of the house of David on his shoulder. He will open, and no one will shut. He will shut, and no one will open.
echoes.note: The authority to forgive or retain sins ('he shall open, and no one shall shut; he shall shut, and no one shall open') parallels the key-of-the-house-of-David grant of binding/loosing power. The remit-or-retain antithesis matches the open/shut structure of the oracle; medium confidence on the structural rather than verbal link.

echoes.text: I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake; and I will not remember your sins.
echoes.note: 'I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake' grounds the forgiveness of sins as a divine prerogative now delegated to the disciples (20:23). Faint background highlighting that sin-forgiveness is God's act, sharpening the Christological claim.

pericopes.text: But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, wasn’t with them when Jesus came. The other disciples therefore said to him, “We have seen the Lord!” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.” After eight days again his disciples were inside, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, the doors being locked, and stood in the midst, and said, “Peace be to you.” Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.” Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen me,you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed.”

echoes.text: Wake up! Rise up to defend me, my God! My Lord, contend for me!
echoes.note: Thomas' confession 'My Lord and my God!' (20:28) reproduces the psalmist's vocative 'my God and my Lord' (LXX Ps 34:23: ho theos mou kai ho kyrios mou). The unusual paired address gives high Volume; John climaxes the Gospel by directing to Jesus the cry the psalmist directs to YHWH.

echoes.text: But you, Lord, are a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth.
echoes.note: Thomas addresses Jesus with the divine titles 'Lord... God' that the psalter repeatedly couples ('you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious'), reinforcing the deliberate transfer of YHWH-language to the risen Christ. Supporting Recurrence behind the primary Ps 35:23 allusion.

echoes.text: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.
echoes.note: 'Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed' (20:29) coheres with 'the righteous shall live by his faith,' the OT charter of faith-not-sight. Thematic rather than verbal; faint and one of several wisdom/faith backgrounds.

pericopes.text: Therefore Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book; but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.

echoes.text: Yahweh answered me, “Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it. For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hurries toward the end, and won’t prove false. Though it takes time, wait for it; because it will surely come. It won’t delay.
echoes.note: 'These are written, that you may believe' enacts the prophetic command 'Write the vision; make it plain... it awaits its appointed time,' grounding the inscribed witness-for-faith in the OT theology of the written vision that calls for belief. Medium Coherence with the Gospel's purpose statement; verbal contact is on the writing-for-faith motif.

echoes.text: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book. Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. Those who are wise shall […]
echoes.note: The notion of words 'written in this book' so that the faithful 'may have life' faintly recalls Daniel's sealed book and those 'found written in the book' who awake to everlasting life. Low Volume; offered as a faint life-through-the-book resonance.

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: The confessional goal 'that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God' draws on the royal-messianic decree 'You are my Son,' the OT title-cluster (Messiah / Son of God) John affirms. Background to the titulature rather than a quotation.

pericopes.text: After these things, Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples at the sea of Tiberias. He revealed himself this way. Simon Peter, Thomas called Didymus, Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together. Simon Peter said to them, “I’m going fishing.” They told him, “We are also coming with you.” They immediately went out, and entered into the boat. That night, they caught nothing. But when day had already come, Jesus stood on the beach, yet the disciples didn’t know that it was Jesus. Jesus therefore said to them, “Children, have you anything to eat?” They answered him, “No.” He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” They cast it therefore, and now they weren’t able to draw it in for the multitude of fish. That disciple therefore whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It’s the Lord!” So when Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he wrapped his coat around him (for he was naked), and threw himself into the sea. But the other disciples came in the little boat (for they were not far from the land, but about two hundred cubits away), dragging the net full of fish. So when they got out on the land, they saw a fire of coals there, and fish laid on it, and bread. Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish which you have just caught.” Simon Peter went up, and drew the net to land, full of great fish, one hundred fifty-three; and even though there were so many, the net wasn’t torn. Jesus said to them, “Come and eat breakfast.” None of the disciples dared inquire of him, “Who are you?” knowing that it was the Lord. Then Jesus came and took the bread, gave it to them, and the fish likewise. This is now the third time that Jesus was revealed to his disciples, after he had risen from the dead.

echoes.text: It shall happen, that every living creature which swarms, in every place where the rivers come, shall live; and there shall be a very great multitude of fish; for these waters have come there, and the waters of the sea shall be healed, and everything shall live wherever the river comes. It shall happen, that fishermen shall stand by it: from En Gedi even to En Eglaim shall be a place for the spreading of nets; their fish shall be after their kinds, as the […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel's temple river makes the sea teem with fish 'of every kind,' with fishermen spreading nets from Engedi to Eneglaim. John's miraculous catch of fish 'of every kind' (the 153 traditionally read as the count of fish species) and the unbroken net coheres with Ezekiel's eschatological ingathering. Volume is moderate but the thematic coherence (river/sea, abundance, fishing, no-loss) is strong; contested but widely proposed.

echoes.text: God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
echoes.note: The mandate to subdue and have dominion over 'the fish of the sea' lurks behind a restored humanity gathering the fish at the creative word of the risen Lord. Faint: shared lexeme 'fish of the sea' and a new-creation framing (resurrection 'after these things'), but no verbal citation and the link is thematic.

echoes.text: Shall flocks and herds be slaughtered for them, to be sufficient for them? Shall all the fish of the sea be gathered together for them, to be sufficient for them?”
echoes.note: Moses asks whether all the fish of the sea could be gathered to feed the people; John presents an answering abundance gathered by Jesus' word. Faint association on the motif of impossible provision of fish answered by divine sufficiency; offered only as a contested resonance.

echoes.text: Yahweh prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
echoes.note: Peter is addressed as 'Simon, son of Jonah' (vv.15-17) amid a sea/fish narrative; the Jonah-the-prophet sea imagery may color the scene of disciples on the deep at night. Faint and largely onomastic; included honestly as contested.

echoes.text: Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves. They heard the voice of Yahweh God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden. Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?” The man said, “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I […]
echoes.note: Peter, 'naked,' covers himself before encountering the Lord (v.7), recalling the shame/covering of Eden when the man hid from the LORD's presence. Faint verbal touch ('naked') with a coherent theme of standing exposed before the divine; contested.

pericopes.text: So when they got out on the land, they saw a fire of coals there, and fish laid on it, and bread. Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish which you have just caught.” Simon Peter went up, and drew the net to land, full of great fish, one hundred fifty-three; and even though there were so many, the net wasn’t torn. Jesus said to them, “Come and eat breakfast.” None of the disciples dared inquire of him, “Who are you?” knowing that it was the Lord. Then Jesus came and took the bread, gave it to them, and the fish likewise. This is now the third time that Jesus was revealed to his disciples, after he had risen from the dead.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]
echoes.note: The LORD appears and a meal is set before him/by him; here the risen Lord hosts a theophanic breakfast none dare question. Faint typological resonance of divine appearance plus prepared food; coherence with John's revelation motif ('revealed himself') but no verbal anchor.

echoes.text: He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, “Arise and eat!” He looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on the coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and lay down again. Yahweh’s angel came again the second time, and touched him, and said, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.” He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty […]
echoes.note: Elijah, exhausted, is given bread baked on coals by the LORD's messenger and strengthened for the journey; Jesus provides bread and fish from a charcoal fire to strengthen the disciples for mission. Faint but coherent provision-meal-after-failure motif; contested.

pericopes.text: So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.” He said to him again a second time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.” He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?” Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, “Do you have affection for me?” He said to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.

echoes.text: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd.
echoes.note: God promises to set up 'one shepherd' to feed and tend the flock. Jesus' triple charge to Peter—'feed my lambs / tend my sheep / feed my sheep'—delegates this messianic shepherd office. High volume of shepherd language, strong coherence with Johannine 'good shepherd' (ch.10), and clear availability in Ezekiel 34's feed/tend vocabulary.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.
echoes.note: The LORD as shepherd who feeds and leads the flock supplies the foundational pastoral imagery taken up in the commission to feed and tend sheep. Coherent and available, though general; the verbal link is thematic (shepherd/feed) rather than a citation.

echoes.text: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says Yahweh. Therefore thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, against the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them; behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings, says Yahweh. I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they […]
echoes.note: Against false shepherds who scatter, God will raise shepherds who 'feed' the flock so none is missing. Peter's reinstatement as a true shepherd who feeds coheres tightly with Jeremiah's contrast; moderate volume in shared feed/shepherd vocabulary.

echoes.text: He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.
echoes.note: The LORD 'will feed his flock like a shepherd' and gently carry the lambs—matching the specific pairing of lambs and sheep in Peter's threefold charge. Strong coherence and the distinctive lamb/sheep doublet raise volume above the generic shepherd topos.

echoes.text: “Let Yahweh, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation, who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: Moses asks God to appoint a successor so the congregation is not 'as sheep without a shepherd'; Joshua is commissioned over the flock. Jesus' commissioning of Peter to shepherd reprises this succession-of-shepherd pattern; coherent with the leadership-transfer theme of John 21.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh my God: “Feed the flock of slaughter. Their buyers slaughter them, and go unpunished. Those who sell them say, ‘Blessed be Yahweh, for I am rich;’ and their own shepherds don’t pity them. For I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land,” says Yahweh; “but, behold, I will deliver the men everyone into his neighbor’s hand, and into the hand of his king. They will strike the land, and out of their hand I will not deliver them.” So I fed […]
echoes.note: The prophet is told to 'feed the flock' destined for slaughter, foreshadowing a shepherd's costly office immediately before Peter's death-prophecy (vv.18-19). Faint but coherent given the adjoining martyrdom prediction; contested.

echoes.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
echoes.note: The thrice-repeated 'Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?' echoes the testing/love idiom of the Aqedah where God names the beloved son in a graduated demand. Faint structural resonance (threefold address, love, testing); offered as contested.

pericopes.text: Most certainly I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself, and walked where you wanted to. But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you, and carry you where you don’t want to go.” Now he said this, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God. When he had said this, he said to him, “Follow me.”

echoes.text: I have spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts;
echoes.note: 'I have stretched out my hands all day long' supplies a possible scriptural backdrop for 'you will stretch out your hands,' read by early Christians as crucifixion imagery. Faint verbal touch ('stretch out hands'); coherent with the death-prophecy but contested as the source.

echoes.text: My eyes are dim from grief. I have called on you daily, Yahweh. I have spread out my hands to you.
echoes.note: The afflicted 'spread out my hands' to God in a context of approaching death; resonates with Peter's foretold death by stretched-out hands and being led where he does not wish. Faint, generic gesture-language; contested.

echoes.text: Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come, and the years draw near, when you will say, “I have no pleasure in them”;
echoes.note: Qoheleth's contrast of youth and the days of trouble in old age frames the 'when you were young... when you are old' antithesis of Peter's prophecy. Faint thematic parallel of life-stage contrast; offered as contested.

pericopes.text: Then Peter, turning around, saw a disciple following. This was the disciple whom Jesus sincerely loved, the one who had also leaned on Jesus’ breast at the supper and asked, “Lord, who is going to betray You?” Peter seeing him, said to Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?” Jesus said to him, “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you? You follow me.” This saying therefore went out among the brothers, that this disciple wouldn’t die. Yet Jesus didn’t say to him that he wouldn’t die, but, “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you?” This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and wrote these things. We know that his witness is true.

echoes.text: Moses answered them, “Wait, that I may hear what Yahweh will command concerning you.”
echoes.note: Peter's 'Lord, what about this man?' and Jesus' deferral ('what is that to you? You follow me') faintly mirror the pattern of deferred answers awaiting the Lord's will. Very faint structural resonance; included only as low-confidence and contested.

pericopes.text: There are also many other things which Jesus did, which if they would all be written, I suppose that even the world itself wouldn’t have room for the books that would be written.

echoes.text: We may say many things, yet shall we not attain; And the sum of our words is, He is all. How shall we have strength to glorify him? For he is himself the great one above all his works.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's doxological hyperbole—'we could say more but could never say enough... he is greater than all his works'—matches John's closing topos that the world could not contain the books recording Jesus' deeds. Strong coherence in the inexhaustible-divine-works rhetoric; a recognized Second-Temple parallel to the hyperbole.

echoes.text: Furthermore, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
echoes.note: 'Of making many books there is no end' supplies the proverbial frame for John's hyperbole about innumerable books. Moderate volume via the shared 'books' motif and a fitting scribal-colophon function closing the work; coherent with an editorial epilogue.

echoes.text: To none has he given power to declare his works: And who will trace out his mighty deeds? Who shall number the strength of his majesty? And who shall also tell out his mercies? As for the wondrous works of the Lord, it is not possible to take from them nor add to them, Neither is it possible to track them out. When a man has finished, then he is but at the beginning; And when he ceaseth, then will he be in perplexity.
echoes.note: 'To whom has he given power to declare his works? Who can search out his mighty deeds?'—the immeasurability of God's works that no one can fully recount. Faint but coherent with John's claim that the world cannot hold the record of Jesus' deeds; contested.

echoes.text: Many, Yahweh, my God, are the wonderful works which you have done, and your thoughts which are toward us. They can’t be declared back to you. If I would declare and speak of them, they are more than can be numbered.
echoes.note: God's wondrous deeds 'are more than can be numbered'—the same hyperbole of innumerable divine works underlying John's uncontainable books. Faint and generic; offered as a contested resonance.
